If the seller is authorized to send the goods, it may ship them under reservation and may tender the documents of title, but the buyer may inspect the goods after their arrival before payment is due, unless inspection is inconsistent with the contract (§ 2-513).

If delivery is authorized and made by documents of title other than under (b), payment is due, regardless of where the goods are received, (i) at the time and place the buyer is to receive the tangible documents, or (ii) for electronic documents, at the time the buyer is to receive them and at the seller's place of business (or residence).

Where the seller is required or authorized to ship on credit, the credit period runs from the time of shipment, but post-dating the invoice or delaying its dispatch correspondingly delays the start of the credit period.
c: Payment is due where and when the buyer is to receive the goods, not at the point of delivery (except documentary sales). This preserves the buyer's right to inspect before paying even when risk of loss has already passed or credit has begun running under the delivery term.

The seller is protected too: absent credit, it need not give up possession before payment and may collect by a sight draft against an order bill of lading ("hold until arrival; inspection allowed"). If it ships under reservation, payment is due where and when the buyer is to receive the documents.
Unless otherwise agreed, documents are delivered and paid for in the buyer's city, but payment is due only after the goods arrive, because the buyer need not pay before inspection (§§ 2-512, 2-513).

If goods must be unloaded too fast for inspection on arrival, a seller wanting payment before inspection must put such a term in the contract. But under C.I.F., C.O.D., or cash-against-documents terms payment may be due before inspection.

An agreed credit period runs from shipment or from the invoice date commonly taken as the shipment date; delaying the invoice delays the credit period, since it deprives the buyer of notice of when to pay.

statutes.t: Options and Cooperation Respecting Performance
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: An agreement for sale that is otherwise sufficiently definite (§ 2-204(3)) is not invalid because it leaves particulars of performance to be specified by one of the parties. Any such specification must be made in good faith and within limits set by commercial reasonableness.

Unless otherwise agreed, specifications relating to assortment of the goods are at the buyer's option and, except as provided in § 2-319(1)(c) and (3), specifications or arrangements relating to shipment are at the seller's option.

Where a specification would materially affect the other party's performance but is not seasonably made, or where one party's cooperation is necessary to the other's agreed performance but is not seasonably forthcoming, the other party, in addition to all other remedies, (a) is excused for any resulting delay in its own performance; and (b) may either proceed to perform in any reasonable manner or, after the time for a material part of its own performance, treat the failure to specify or cooperate as a breach by failure to deliver or accept the goods.
c: Parties may leave details of performance for one of them to fill in without the contract failing for indefiniteness. The specifying party must act in good faith and by commercial standards, so there is no surprise and variation stays within commercial reasonableness. The power to specify may come from course of dealing, usage, or circumstances as well as express words.
Absent other arrangement, assortment is the buyer's option and shipping arrangements are the seller's. The old mechanical test giving the option to the party "first under a duty to move" is rejected.

When a needed option or cooperation is not seasonably forthcoming, the other party's delay is excused and it may proceed in any commercially reasonable manner rather than wait. All other remedies remain, especially the right to demand assurance for insecurity; good faith also allows a request for a reasonable indication of the time and manner of performance.

This remedy does not apply where § 2-614 (substituted performance) governs; there, the other party must offer or demand the substitute performance before claiming rights against the noncooperating party.

statutes.t: Warranty of Title and Against Infringement; Buyer's Obligation Against Infringement
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: Subject to (2), a contract for sale includes a warranty by the seller that (a) the title conveyed shall be good, and its transfer rightful; and (b) the goods shall be delivered free from any security interest or other lien or encumbrance of which the buyer at the time of contracting has no knowledge.

A warranty under (1) is excluded or modified only by specific language or by circumstances which give the buyer reason to know that the seller does not claim title in itself or that it is purporting to sell only such right or title as it or a third person may have.

Unless otherwise agreed, a seller that is a merchant regularly dealing in goods of the kind warrants that the goods shall be delivered free of the rightful claim of any third person by way of infringement or the like; but a buyer who furnishes specifications to the seller must hold the seller harmless against any such claim arising from compliance with the specifications.
c: The buyer is entitled to a good, clean title transferred in a rightful manner, so it will not be exposed to a lawsuit to protect it. The warranty applies whether or not the seller had possession when it sold. The separate warranty of quiet possession is abolished; disturbance of possession is just one way to prove breach of the title warranty. "Knowledge" in (1)(b) means actual knowledge, not notice.

The buyer must notify the seller of a title breach within a reasonable time after discovery if the seller's breach was innocent; if the seller acted in bad faith, it cannot claim prejudice from delay, and "reasonable time" is read very liberally. Either way, under § 2-725 the cause of action accrues at tender of delivery, since title is not a warranty of "future performance."

A dealer selling from normal stock must ensure no third-party patent or trademark claim mars the buyer's title. A non-dealer's sale carries no such warranty. When the buyer orders goods made to its own specifications, liability for infringement runs from buyer to seller: the buyer tacitly represents the seller will be safe following the specs and must indemnify in good faith.

"Eviction" is not required: the buyer's remedy arises when it receives notice of an infringement claim; cases denying a remedy unless the buyer was expressly prevented from using the goods are rejected.

Sales by sheriffs, executors, certain foreclosing lienors, and similar sellers are so out of the ordinary that the buyer knows only an unknown or limited right is being sold, so no personal title obligation arises (restitution questions are left open). Article 9 foreclosure sales are different: under § 9-610 a disposition of collateral carries the warranties of this section unless properly excluded under (2) or § 9-610's special rules.
The title warranty is not an "implied" warranty, so § 2-316(3) (as is, course of dealing, examination) does not disclaim it. Only specific language or the circumstances in (2) can.

statutes.t: Express Warranties by Affirmation, Promise, Description, Sample
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: Express warranties by the seller are created as follows: (a) any affirmation of fact or promise made by the seller to the buyer which relates to the goods and becomes part of the basis of the bargain creates an express warranty that the goods shall conform to the affirmation or promise; (b) any description of the goods which is made part of the basis of the bargain creates an express warranty that the goods shall conform to the description; (c) any sample or model which is made part of the basis of the bargain creates an express warranty that the whole of the goods shall conform to the sample or model.

It is not necessary that the seller use formal words such as "warrant" or "guarantee" or have a specific intention to make a warranty, but an affirmation merely of the value of the goods, or a statement purporting to be merely the seller's opinion or commendation of the goods, does not create a warranty.
c: Express warranties rest on the "dickered" aspects of the bargain and go so clearly to its essence that form disclaimers are repugnant to them. Implied warranties rest on a common factual situation and arise unless unmistakably negated. Warranties of description and sample are classed as express.

The section covers seller-to-buyer warranties in sales, but the warranty sections do not stop case law from extending warranties beyond sales contracts (for example, bailments for hire or containers) or beyond the direct parties; § 2-318 recognizes one such development, and the rest is left to the courts.

No specific intention to warrant is needed if the affirmation, description, or sample is part of the basis of the bargain. Affirmations made during the bargain are treated as part of the description of the goods, so no particular reliance need be shown to weave them into the agreement; rather, any fact that is to take such an affirmation out of the agreement requires clear affirmative proof. The issue is normally one of fact.

Warranty law decides what the seller has in essence agreed to sell, so courts refuse, except in unusual circumstances, to recognize a material deletion of the seller's obligation. A contract is normally for something described; a clause disclaiming "all warranties, express or implied" cannot reduce the seller's obligation as to that description and so cannot be given literal effect under § 2-316. Parties can consciously make a different bargain, but good faith counts and it is unlikely a real price was meant to buy a pseudo-obligation.

A description need not be in words: technical specifications and blueprints can be more exact than language. Past deliveries may set the quality described, expressly or by course of dealing. Merchants' descriptions are read against trade usage, with the merchantability rules resolving doubts.

Both a "sample" (drawn from the bulk being sold) and a "model" (offered when the goods are not at hand) can warrant. Any sample or model is presumed to be part of the basis of the bargain, but it is a fact question whether it was meant to "suggest" or to "be" the goods. A sample drawn from an existing bulk must be fairly drawn and describes the goods unless accompanied by an unmistakable denial of responsibility; the presumption is weaker for a model of goods not on hand, especially if the buyer's requested modifications affect it.

The timing of the words or samples does not matter; the question is whether they are fairly part of the contract. Language used after the deal closes (an assurance given at delivery) operates as a modification, which needs no consideration if otherwise reasonable (§ 2-209).

For value statements, opinion, or commendation (puffing), the question is still which statements, objectively, became part of the basis of the bargain - all of the seller's statements do unless good reason is shown. Some statements or predictions cannot fairly be viewed as part of the bargain, but even false statements of value may still support a fraud or misrepresentation claim.

statutes.t: Implied Warranty: Merchantability; Usage of Trade
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: Unless excluded or modified (§ 2-316), a warranty that the goods shall be merchantable is implied in a contract for their sale if the seller is a merchant with respect to goods of that kind. Serving food or drink for value, to be consumed on the premises or elsewhere, is a sale.

Goods to be merchantable must be at least such as (a) pass without objection in the trade under the contract description; (b) in the case of fungible goods, are of fair average quality within the description; (c) are fit for the ordinary purposes for which such goods are used; (d) run, within the variations permitted by the agreement, of even kind, quality, and quantity within each unit and among all units involved; (e) are adequately contained, packaged, and labeled as the agreement may require; and (f) conform to the promises or affirmations of fact made on the container or label, if any.
Unless excluded or modified (§ 2-316), other implied warranties may arise from course of dealing or usage of trade.
c: The warranty applies to present sales and contracts to sell, subject to the effect of examining specific goods (§ 2-316(2)); it applies to sales for use and for resale.

Whether the warranty is met turns on the agreement's terms as understood in the trade: goods must be of a quality comparable to what is generally acceptable in that line of trade under the contract description. It binds any merchant-seller, grower or manufacturer or not.

A buyer's specific designation of goods does not exclude the seller's obligation that they be fit for their general purposes. A sale of second-hand goods carries only the obligation appropriate to such goods, since that is their description. A person making an isolated sale is not a merchant for this section, so no merchantability warranty arises - but good faith still requires that person to disclose known material hidden defects.

Even a non-merchant who says goods are "guaranteed" makes an express warranty whose content this section may help define - important in second-hand sales and in limiting fine-print disclaimers that conflict with a large-print "guarantee."
Serving food or drink for value is a sale; contrary cases are rejected. The main warranty is fitness for ordinary purposes under (2)(c).
Subsection (2) is not exhaustive ("at least such as"); other attributes may come from usage of trade or case law.

(a) and (b) are read together, measured by the standards of the trade line that fits the deal. "Fair average" (for agricultural bulk products) means the middle belt of quality, not the worst passable; some low-end goods are fine, but not all. The contract price is an excellent index of the quality obligation.
Fitness for ordinary purposes is the core concept. A buyer for resale is equally protected: goods must be honestly resalable in the normal course because they are what they purport to be.
Evenness of kind, quality, and quantity follows case law, subject to trade usages that permit substantial variation.

(e) applies only where the goods or transaction require a certain container or label; (f) applies whenever a label or container makes representations, even if not required, because good faith forbids delivering goods under false labels. No extra consideration is needed.

Exclusion or modification is governed by § 2-316 (read with its remedy-limitation subsection). Merchantability is so commonly assumed that excluding it threatens surprise and needs special precaution.
Usage of trade and course of dealing can create implied (not express) warranties, so § 2-316 can exclude them - for example, a duty to supply pedigree papers with a pedigreed dog.

The buyer must prove the warranty, its breach, and that the breach proximately caused the loss. The seller can defend by showing the loss came from something after delivery. Evidence of the seller's care in making or selecting the goods is relevant to whether the warranty was broken, and a buyer's use after an examination that should have revealed the defect bears on causation.
k: merchant with respect to goods of that kind

statutes.t: Implied Warranty: Fitness for Particular Purpose
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: Where the seller at the time of contracting has reason to know any particular purpose for which the goods are required and that the buyer is relying on the seller's skill or judgment to select or furnish suitable goods, there is, unless excluded or modified under § 2-316, an implied warranty that the goods shall be fit for such purpose.
c: Whether the warranty arises is basically a question of fact. The buyer need not prove the seller actually knew the purpose or the reliance if the seller had reason to realize them - but the buyer must actually rely on the seller.

A "particular purpose" is a specific use peculiar to the buyer's business, unlike the ordinary purposes covered by merchantability. Shoes are generally for walking on ordinary ground, but a seller may know a particular pair was chosen for mountain climbing. A contract can carry both warranties. If warranties conflict, fact questions about which was intended are resolved in favor of fitness for a particular purpose, except where the buyer furnished the technical specifications.

Where the purpose combines quality requirements with compliance with laws or regulations, how the parties divided that risk is a fact question decided from the agreement, circumstances, usage of trade, and course of performance.

The seller need not be a grower or manufacturer. The warranty normally arises only when the seller is a merchant with the relevant skill or judgment, but it can arise for a non-merchant when the circumstances justify it.

The old "patent or trade name" exception is gone. Buying by brand name is only one fact bearing on reliance. A buyer who insists on a particular brand is not relying on the seller, so no warranty arises; but if the seller recommended the branded item as adequate for the buyer's purpose, the brand name alone does not show nonreliance.
The warranty can be excluded under § 2-316, but only by a conspicuous writing.

statutes.t: Exclusion or Modification of Warranties
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: Words or conduct relevant to the creation of an express warranty, and words or conduct tending to negate or limit warranty, shall be construed wherever reasonable as consistent with each other; but, subject to the parol evidence rule (§ 2-202), negation or limitation is inoperative to the extent that such construction is unreasonable.

Subject to (3), to exclude or modify the implied warranty of merchantability or any part of it, the language must mention merchantability and, in case of a writing, must be conspicuous; and to exclude or modify any implied warranty of fitness, the exclusion must be by a writing and conspicuous. Language to exclude all implied warranties of fitness is sufficient if it states, for example, "There are no warranties which extend beyond the description on the face hereof."

Notwithstanding (2): (a) unless the circumstances indicate otherwise, all implied warranties are excluded by expressions like "as is," "with all faults," or other language which in common understanding calls the buyer's attention to the exclusion of warranties and makes plain that there is no implied warranty; (b) when the buyer before contracting has examined the goods or the sample or model as fully as it desired, or has refused to examine the goods, there is no implied warranty as to defects which an examination ought in the circumstances to have revealed; and (c) an implied warranty can also be excluded or modified by course of dealing, course of performance, or usage of trade.
Remedies for breach of warranty can be limited under §§ 2-718 and 2-719 (liquidation or limitation of damages and contractual modification of remedy).
c: The section targets clauses excluding "all warranties, express or implied." It protects the buyer from unexpected, unbargained disclaimer language by denying it effect when inconsistent with an express warranty, and by allowing implied warranties to be excluded only by conspicuous language or other circumstances that protect against surprise.

The seller is protected from false claims of oral warranties by the parol evidence rule, and from unauthorized representations by customary "lack of authority" clauses. Limiting consequential damages is treated as limiting remedies (§§ 2-718, 2-719), separate from whether a warranty exists.
Merchantability may be disclaimed, but the disclaimer must mention merchantability and, if written, be conspicuous.
Unlike merchantability, fitness for a particular purpose may be excluded by general language, but only in a conspicuous writing.

Disclaimer language that fails this section may still matter elsewhere - for example, an oral disclaimer (if not barred by § 2-202) may show the buyer did not rely or the seller lacked reason to know under § 2-315.
The exceptions in (3)(a)-(c) are common situations where the circumstances themselves alert the buyer that no implied warranty is made.

"As is," "as they stand," "with all faults" and the like are commonly understood to mean the buyer takes the entire risk as to quality. Paragraph (a) is really a particular instance of exclusion by usage of trade under (c).

"Examination" in (b) means examination before contracting, not inspection after the contract. A buyer who finds a defect and uses the goods anyway, or unreasonably fails to examine before use, may be the cause of its own injury (§§ 2-314, 2-715). "Refused to examine" requires more than the goods being available: the seller must demand that the buyer examine them fully, putting the buyer on notice that it assumes the risk. Caveat emptor is rejected: if the seller offers examination while making statements about merchantability or specific attributes, and the buyer clearly relies on those statements, an express warranty arises. What examination excludes depends on the buyer's skill and the normal method of examination: obvious defects are excluded; defects detectable only by chemical or other testing, or latent defects, are not. A professional buyer assumes the risk of defects a professional ought to notice; a layperson only those a layperson would.

When the buyer gives precise and complete specifications, fitness for a particular purpose usually does not arise (no reliance), and under § 2-317(c) the express warranty of conformity to specifications displaces an inconsistent merchantability warranty - so neither implied quality warranty normally applies unless consistent with the specs.
On records other than writings, see § 2-207, Comment 8; on conspicuousness (including electronic records), see § 1-201, Comment 10.

statutes.t: Cumulation and Conflict of Warranties Express or Implied
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: Warranties, express or implied, shall be construed as consistent with each other and as cumulative, but if such construction is unreasonable the intention of the parties determines which warranty is dominant. In ascertaining that intention: (a) exact or technical specifications displace an inconsistent sample or model or general language of description; (b) a sample from an existing bulk displaces inconsistent general language of description; (c) express warranties displace inconsistent implied warranties other than an implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose.
c: No warranty arises except from some conduct of the seller (affirmative action or failure to disclose), so all warranties are cumulative unless that construction is impossible or unreasonable. For brand-name sales, whether fitness is excluded depends only on whether the buyer relied on the seller; the brand name is just one factor.

These rules apply only where the seller in perfect good faith made warranties that later prove inconsistent and no equitable estoppel applies. A seller who led the buyer to believe all warranties could be performed is estopped from pleading their inconsistency.

The rules look to the factor that probably first claimed the parties' attention. They are not absolute and can be overcome by evidence that conditions at contracting make them inconsistent or unreasonable.

statutes.t: Third Party Beneficiaries of Warranties Express or Implied
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: Alternative A

A seller's warranty, express or implied, extends to any natural person who is in the family or household of the buyer or who is a guest in the buyer's home, if it is reasonable to expect that person may use, consume, or be affected by the goods and the person is injured in person by breach of the warranty. A seller may not exclude or limit the operation of this section.
Alternative B

A seller's warranty, express or implied, extends to any natural person who may reasonably be expected to use, consume, or be affected by the goods and who is injured in person by breach of the warranty. A seller may not exclude or limit the operation of this section.
Alternative C

A seller's warranty, express or implied, extends to any person who may reasonably be expected to use, consume, or be affected by the goods and who is injured by breach of the warranty. A seller may not exclude or limit the operation of this section with respect to injury to the person of an individual to whom the warranty extends.
Note
Each state selects one alternative.
c: The last sentence does not stop the seller from disclaiming warranties under § 2-316 or limiting remedies under §§ 2-718 and 2-719; those provisions bind the beneficiaries just as they bind the buyer. What it forbids is excluding liability to the persons to whom the buyer's warranties extend under this section.

The section gives certain beneficiaries the same warranty the buyer received, freeing them from technical privity rules, without affecting negligence rights. It rests mainly on the merchant-seller's warranty of merchantability (fitness for ordinary purposes), not fitness for a particular purpose. A beneficiary may sue the seller directly.

Alternative A covers family, household, and guests (horizontal privity) and is neutral on whether warranties run up the distributive chain (vertical privity), leaving that to case law. Alternative B is for states wanting a wider class. Alternative C goes further, following the trend of Restatement (Second) of Torts § 402A, by extending beyond personal injury.

statutes.t: F.O.B. and F.A.S. Terms
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: Unless otherwise agreed, the term F.O.B. ("free on board") at a named place, even though used only with the stated price, is a delivery term under which: (a) when the term is F.O.B. the place of shipment, the seller must at that place ship the goods as provided in § 2-504 and bear the expense and risk of putting them into the possession of the carrier; (b) when the term is F.O.B. the place of destination, the seller must at its own expense and risk transport the goods to that place and there tender delivery as provided in § 2-503; (c) when under (a) or (b) the term is also F.O.B. vessel, car, or other vehicle, the seller must in addition at its own expense and risk load the goods on board. If the term is F.O.B. vessel, the buyer must name the vessel, and in an appropriate case the seller must comply with § 2-323 on the form of bill of lading.

Unless otherwise agreed, the term F.A.S. vessel ("free alongside") at a named port, even though used only with the stated price, is a delivery term under which the seller must (a) at its own expense and risk deliver the goods alongside the vessel in the manner usual in that port or on a dock designated and provided by the buyer; and (b) obtain and tender a receipt for the goods in exchange for which the carrier must issue a bill of lading.

Unless otherwise agreed, in cases under (1)(a) or (c) or (2), the buyer must seasonably give any needed instructions for delivery, including, for F.A.S. or F.O.B., the loading berth of the vessel and in an appropriate case its name and sailing date. The seller may treat the failure of needed instructions as a failure of cooperation under § 2-311, and may at its option move the goods in any reasonable manner preparatory to delivery or shipment.

Under F.O.B. vessel or F.A.S., unless otherwise agreed, the buyer must pay against tender of the required documents, and the seller may not tender nor the buyer demand delivery of the goods in substitution for the documents.
c: The section rejects the line of cases treating "F.O.B." as "merely a price term": F.O.B. is a delivery term even if it appears only next to the price, and it fixes where the seller's delivery obligation (and, with § 2-509, the risk) ends. Related issues are handled by § 2-311(2) (seller's option on shipping arrangements) and §§ 2-614, 2-615.
Subsection (1)(c) spells out the extra loading duty of F.O.B. vessel and the like; a contract contemplating reshipment from a port that just says "F.O.B." that place is poorly drawn.

The buyer's duties to name the vessel and give instructions are duties of cooperation. Pending instructions, the seller may make preparatory moves such as shipping from the interior to the named point. If the buyer has repudiated, § 2-704 (mitigation) applies instead.

Requiring payment against documents for F.O.B. vessel and F.A.S. matches standard practice; F.O.B. vessel by its terms calls for an "on board" document, so it is stricter than an ordinary overseas shipment contract (C.I.F., § 2-320).

statutes.t: C.I.F. and C. & F. Terms
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: C.I.F. means the price includes in a lump sum the cost of the goods and the insurance and freight to the named destination. C. & F. (or C.F.) means the price includes cost and freight to the named destination.

Unless otherwise agreed, and even though used only with the stated price and destination, C.I.F. destination requires the seller at its own expense and risk to: (a) put the goods into the possession of a carrier at the port for shipment and obtain a negotiable bill or bills of lading covering the entire transportation to the named destination; (b) load the goods and obtain a receipt from the carrier showing that the freight has been paid or provided for; (c) obtain a policy or certificate of insurance, including any war risk insurance, of a kind and on terms then current at the port of shipment, in the usual amount and the currency of the contract, covering the same goods as the bill of lading and payable to the buyer's order or for the account of whom it may concern (the seller may add war-risk premiums to the price); (d) prepare an invoice and procure any other documents required to effect shipment or comply with the contract; and (e) forward and tender with commercial promptness all the documents in due form with any indorsement necessary to perfect the buyer's rights.
Unless otherwise agreed, C. & F. has the same effect and imposes the same obligations and risks as C.I.F., except the obligation as to insurance.

Under C.I.F. or C. & F., unless otherwise agreed, the buyer must pay against tender of the required documents, and the seller may not tender nor the buyer demand delivery of the goods in substitution for the documents.
c: A C.I.F. contract is a shipment contract, not a destination contract: risk passes to the buyer on shipment if the seller properly performed. Delivery to the carrier is delivery to the buyer for risk and title. On tender of documents the buyer must pay without waiting for the goods; if they were lost after proper shipment, the buyer looks to the carrier or insurer. The buyer has no right to inspect before paying for or accepting the documents.
The seller's duties are the same even if C.I.F. appears only with the price and destination.
The insurance is for the buyer's benefit; "insurance for the account of sellers" means the seller pays for it.
The bill of lading must cover the whole transport and only the contract quantity, so the buyer can deal with the goods afloat.
The seller may pay or "provide for" freight but may not ship freight collect unless agreed; the buyer gets documentary proof it need not pay freight.
Insurance must be the kind usual at the port of shipment for the goods, vessel, and route - not coverage of every risk; uncovered risks fall on the buyer. It must cover the whole voyage.
The seller must procure customary war-risk insurance at the buyer's expense, changing the common law.

Insurance covers value at the time and place of shipment, not increases in market value or the buyer's resale profit; sub-buyers on C.I.F. resales take the original policy and must buy extra coverage themselves.

Insurance "for the account of whom it may concern" is fine, and negotiable certificates of insurance are good tender, but broker's cover notes need usage or course of dealing. Defective insurance tender may be waived or cured, but safe arrival alone does not cure failure to insure.
The invoice is a usual and necessary document.
Documents must be forwarded with "commercial promptness," which is more urgent than "reasonable time."

The buyer pays on documents before inspecting, but payment is not acceptance and does not impair later inspection or remedies; the point of the term is to protect the seller from unjustified rejection at a distant port.
A C.I.F. contract may combine rail to a port and sea carriage under a through bill of lading.

Express terms are usually a fuller statement of normal C.I.F. terms, not a departure, and variations should be read within C.I.F.'s dominant outlines (a contract for proper shipment, not delivery at destination); C.I.F. terms prevail over repugnant printed clauses on a form made for another kind of contract.
A seller that performed may tender documents even knowing the goods were lost; it cannot perform by tendering landed goods.
Under C. & F., title and risk also pass on shipment; insurance may be arranged by either side.
The French "C.A.F." means C.I.F. ("A" is assurance - insurance).
statutes.note: A Week 5 slide cites "§ 2-329" for C.I.F. and C. & F.; there is no § 2-329 - this is the correct section.

statutes.t: C.I.F. or C. & F.: "Net Landed Weights"; "Payment on Arrival"; Warranty of Condition on Arrival
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: Under a C.I.F. or C. & F. contract, where the price is based on or adjusted by "net landed weights," "delivered weights," "out turn" quantity or quality, or the like, unless otherwise agreed the seller must reasonably estimate the price. The estimate is payable on tender of the documents, and after final adjustment a settlement must be made with commercial promptness.

Such an agreement, or any warranty of quality or condition of the goods on arrival, puts on the seller the risk of ordinary deterioration, shrinkage, and the like in transportation, but does not change the place or time of identification or delivery or the passing of the risk of loss.

Unless otherwise agreed, where the contract provides for payment on or after arrival of the goods, the seller must before payment allow such preliminary inspection as is feasible; but if the goods are lost, delivery of the documents and payment are due when the goods should have arrived.
c: Two common C.I.F. variations. Subsections (1) and (2) shift to the seller the risk of quality and weight deterioration during shipment, without changing the rule that marine risks pass to the buyer at shipment. Subsection (3) treats "payment on arrival" as merely postponing payment - not a "no arrival, no sale" term (§ 2-324). If the goods are lost, the buyer still pays when they should have arrived; the clause is not a condition that excuses payment and leaves the loss on the seller.

statutes.t: Delivery "Ex-Ship"
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: Unless otherwise agreed, a term for delivery "ex-ship" (from the carrying vessel) is not restricted to a particular ship and requires delivery from a ship that has reached a place at the named port of destination where goods of the kind are usually discharged.

Unless otherwise agreed, (a) the seller must discharge all liens arising out of the carriage and furnish the buyer a direction that puts the carrier under a duty to deliver the goods; and (b) the risk of loss does not pass to the buyer until the goods leave the ship's tackle or are otherwise properly unloaded.
c: "Ex-ship" is the reverse of F.A.S.: the seller bears the voyage.
Delivery need not come from any particular vessel unless the agreement restricts it to a named vessel.
The place and manner of unloading depend on the goods and the port's facilities and usages.

With "cash against documents," only documents appropriate to an ex-ship contract are needed (a delivery order and freight receipt). The seller need not tender a bill of lading or insure for the buyer, because the goods are not at the buyer's risk during the voyage.

statutes.t: "No Arrival, No Sale" Term
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: Under a term "no arrival, no sale" or like terms, unless otherwise agreed, the seller must properly ship conforming goods and, if they arrive by any means, must tender them on arrival, but it assumes no obligation that the goods will arrive unless it caused the non-arrival.

Where without fault of the seller the goods are in part lost, or have so deteriorated as no longer to conform, or arrive after the contract time, the buyer may proceed as if there had been casualty to identified goods (§ 2-613).
c: In a destination contract, the term leaves risk of loss on the seller but exempts it from liability for non-delivery. Good faith requires the seller not to interfere with arrival; if it is responsible for shipping, it must ship, and the shipment must conform - the exemption covers only transportation hazards. A seller reselling goods shipped by others, with the buyer's knowledge, gets the full exemption.
The exemption applies only after the goods are identified to a particular shipment or ship.
Delay or transshipment does not relieve the seller of the duty to tender goods that do arrive.
"To arrive" often means the same thing, but added to a C.I.F. or C. & F. contract it usually covers only risks not covered by insurance; intent is a fact question.
Paragraph (b) applies the casualty rules of § 2-613 to partial loss or damage in transit; the term protects the seller from loss beyond its control, not to give it a windfall.

statutes.t: Sale on Approval and Sale or Return; Rights of Creditors
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: Unless otherwise agreed, if delivered goods may be returned by the buyer even though they conform to the contract, the transaction is (a) a "sale on approval" if the goods are delivered primarily for use, and (b) a "sale or return" if the goods are delivered primarily for resale.
Goods held on approval are not subject to the claims of the buyer's creditors until acceptance; goods held on sale or return are subject to such claims while in the buyer's possession.

Any "or return" term of a contract for sale is treated as a separate contract for sale under the statute of frauds (§ 2-201) and as contradicting the sale aspect of the contract under the parol evidence rule (§ 2-202).
c: A sale on approval ("on trial," "on satisfaction"): the seller takes a risk to satisfy a prospective buyer; the goods stay the seller's property until the buyer accepts; the buyer's willingness to receive and test them is consideration. A sale or return is typically to a merchant who is induced to buy by the seller's promise to take back unsold goods instead of payment - a present sale the buyer can undo. Every presumption runs against a delivery to a consumer being a sale or return and against a delivery to a merchant for resale being a sale on approval.

A right to return nonconforming goods is not a sale on approval or sale or return; this section concerns a contractual power to return goods that are wholly as warranted. If the buyer's obligation depends on the goods passing an objective test, risk of casualty pending the test is on the seller.
An "or return" term is so at odds with an ordinary sale that, under (3), it must satisfy the statute of frauds on its own and counts as contradicting a written sale for parol evidence purposes.
The section covers only sales to buyers. Delivery to a non-buyer for the purpose of selling is a consignment (a bailment), now governed in part by Article 9 (§§ 9-109(a)(4), 9-103(d), 9-319).

statutes.t: Special Incidents of Sale on Approval and Sale or Return
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: Under a sale on approval, unless otherwise agreed: (a) although the goods are identified to the contract, the risk of loss and the title do not pass to the buyer until acceptance; (b) use of the goods consistent with the purpose of trial is not acceptance, but failure seasonably to notify the seller of election to return the goods is acceptance, and if the goods conform, acceptance of any part is acceptance of the whole; and (c) after due notification of election to return, the return is at the seller's risk and expense, but a merchant buyer must follow any reasonable instructions.

Under a sale or return, unless otherwise agreed: (a) the option to return extends to the whole or any commercial unit of the goods while in substantially their original condition, but must be exercised seasonably; and (b) the return is at the buyer's risk and expense.
c: In a sale on approval, if all goods conform, accepting part accepts the whole; the partial-acceptance policy for defective deliveries does not apply. Taking home two dresses to choose one is usually two contracts, or covered by "unless otherwise agreed."

In a sale or return, returning an unsold unit just because it did not sell is the normal intent. Returns for breach (including goods returned by the buyer's customers for defects) are governed instead by the rules on acceptance and revocation.
Risk: on approval, the risk stays on the seller until acceptance; in a sale or return, the risk is on the buyer throughout.
On approval, notice of election to return ends the buyer's liability; in a sale or return, actual return is required. "Seasonable" has its § 1-205 meaning, read with commercial reason and good faith.

statutes.t: Passing of Title; Reservation for Security; Limited Application of This Section
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 4 - Title, Creditors and Good Faith Purchasers
x: Preamble

Each Article 2 provision on the rights, obligations, and remedies of seller, buyer, purchasers, or third parties applies irrespective of title, except where the provision refers to title. Where title becomes material in a situation not otherwise covered, these rules apply:

Title cannot pass before the goods are identified to the contract (§ 2-501), and unless otherwise explicitly agreed the buyer acquires by identification a special property. Any retention or reservation by the seller of title in goods shipped or delivered to the buyer is limited in effect to a reservation of a security interest. Subject to these rules and Article 9, title passes in any manner and on any conditions explicitly agreed.

Unless otherwise explicitly agreed, title passes to the buyer at the time and place at which the seller completes its performance with reference to the physical delivery of the goods, despite any reservation of a security interest and even though a document of title is to be delivered at a different time or place. In particular: (a) if the contract requires or authorizes the seller to send the goods but does not require delivery at destination, title passes at the time and place of shipment; (b) if the contract requires delivery at destination, title passes on tender there.

Unless otherwise explicitly agreed, where delivery is to be made without moving the goods: (a) if the seller is to deliver a tangible document of title, title passes when and where it delivers the document (for an electronic document, when it delivers it); or (b) if the goods are already identified at contracting and no documents are to be delivered, title passes at the time and place of contracting.

A rejection or other refusal by the buyer to receive or retain the goods, justified or not, or a justified revocation of acceptance, revests title in the seller. Revesting occurs by operation of law and is not a "sale."
c: Article 2 resolves buyer-seller issues step by step through performance, not by asking whether "title" passed. The section says where title is only for cases (such as public regulation or tax laws) that turn on title or a "sale."
Future goods cannot be presently sold; goods must be identified under § 2-501 before title passes. Parties may agree on when title to existing goods passes.

The buyer's "special property" in identified goods is not a security interest; its incidents appear in provisions on seller's creditors, good faith purchase, the buyer's rights on seller insolvency, and specific performance or replevin.
The test is when the seller finally commits itself to specific goods: in a shipment contract, by shipping; if no shipment is contemplated, by delivering documents or making the contract.

statutes.t: Rights of Seller's Creditors Against Sold Goods
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 4 - Title, Creditors and Good Faith Purchasers
x: Except as provided in (2) and (3), the rights of the seller's unsecured creditors in goods identified to a contract for sale are subject to the buyer's rights to recover the goods under §§ 2-502 and 2-716.

A creditor of the seller may treat a sale or identification as void if, as against it, the seller's retention of possession is fraudulent under the law of the state where the goods are located - except that retention of possession in good faith and current course of trade by a merchant-seller for a commercially reasonable time after a sale or identification is not fraudulent.

Article 2 does not impair the rights of the seller's creditors (a) under Article 9; or (b) where identification or delivery is made not in current course of trade but in satisfaction of or as security for a pre-existing claim, under circumstances that would make it a fraudulent transfer or voidable preference under local law.
c: Local law on hindering creditors by a seller's retained possession is outside Article 2, but retention in the current course of trade is legitimate; improper preferences are not protected.

A merchant seller's retention of possession for a commercially reasonable time after a sale or identification in current course cannot be attacked as fraudulent, and (3) does not reach identification or delivery in the current course of trade.

statutes.t: Power to Transfer; Good Faith Purchase of Goods; "Entrusting"
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 4 - Title, Creditors and Good Faith Purchasers
x: A purchaser of goods acquires all title which its transferor had or had power to transfer, except that a purchaser of a limited interest acquires rights only to the extent of the interest purchased. A person with voidable title has power to transfer a good title to a good faith purchaser for value. When goods have been delivered under a transaction of purchase, the purchaser has that power even though (a) the transferor was deceived as to the identity of the purchaser; (b) the delivery was in exchange for a check which is later dishonored; (c) it was agreed that the transaction was to be a "cash sale"; or (d) the delivery was procured through fraud punishable as larcenous under the criminal law.
Any entrusting of possession of goods to a merchant who deals in goods of that kind gives it power to transfer all rights of the entruster to a buyer in ordinary course of business.

"Entrusting" includes any delivery and any acquiescence in retention of possession, regardless of any condition expressed between the parties and regardless of whether the procurement of the entrusting or the possessor's disposition of the goods was larcenous under the criminal law.
The rights of other purchasers of goods and of lien creditors are governed by Article 9 and Article 7 (and Article 6, Bulk Sales, where still in force).
c: The basic rule that a transferor passes the title it has is continued and expanded, for any form of "purchase." Rights under agency, apparent agency or ownership, and estoppel remain, as do the powers of factors. Subsection (1) protects good faith purchasers for value in several troublesome situations (impostor, bad check, cash sale, larcenous fraud). A limited purchase (a pledge, a fractional interest) passes only that interest.

Subsections (2)-(4) protect a person buying in ordinary course out of a merchant's inventory against hidden interests; consignors and inventory lenders cannot complain, since inventory exists to be sold. Entrusting is freed from technicalities of larceny law and extends to any bailor's entrusting. For secured parties, § 9-320 controls (no protection for buyers of farm products from a farmer).

The definition of "buyer in ordinary course of business" (§ 1-201(b)(9)) keeps the sensible case-law limits, so the protection does not extend to results that outrage common sense, without hurting normal market dealings.
Except under (1), rights of purchasers other than buyers in ordinary course are left to Articles 9, 7, and (if not repealed) 6.
k: merchant who deals in goods of that kind

statutes.t: Insurable Interest in Goods; Manner of Identification of Goods
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 5 - Performance
x: The buyer obtains a special property and an insurable interest in goods by identification of existing goods as goods to which the contract refers, even though the goods are nonconforming and the buyer has an option to return or reject them. Identification can be made at any time and in any manner explicitly agreed. Absent explicit agreement, identification occurs: (a) when the contract is made, if it is for the sale of goods already existing and identified; (b) for future goods other than those in (c), when goods are shipped, marked, or otherwise designated by the seller as goods to which the contract refers; (c) when the crops are planted or otherwise become growing crops, or the young are conceived, if the contract is for unborn young to be born within twelve months after contracting or for crops to be harvested within twelve months or the next normal harvest season after contracting, whichever is longer.

The seller retains an insurable interest so long as title to or any security interest in the goods remains in it, and where the identification is by the seller alone, it may substitute other goods until default, insolvency, or notification to the buyer that the identification is final.
This section does not impair any insurable interest recognized under other law.
c: The section says how goods become identified so the buyer gets an insurable interest and the rights in § 2-502. Explicit agreement controls; (a)-(c) apply only without it.
Identification is usually unambiguous, but it may be tentative or contingent. Because identification has limited effect, doubts are resolved in favor of identification.
"Explicit agreement" is required to displace (a)-(c) - for example, a term letting the buyer select the goods. Trade rules incorporated by reference count as explicit.
Goods need not be in deliverable state for identification. Despite identification, risk of loss stays with the seller until it completes its duties under the risk-of-loss rules.

Undivided shares in an identified fungible bulk (grain in an elevator, oil in a tank) can be sold; making the contract identifies the share, though the seller's duty to segregate and deliver is unaffected.

Crops are identified on planting only if to be harvested within the year or next normal harvest season (including quick-harvest nursery stock, but not timber). Wool and young born within twelve months are covered. Lumbering, mining, and fishing output is not "growing," but identification under an output contract can happen early in the operation.

statutes.t: Buyer's Right to Goods on Seller's Repudiation, Failure to Deliver, or Insolvency
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 5 - Performance
x: Subject to (2) and (3), and even though the goods have not been shipped, a buyer who has paid part or all of the price of goods in which it has a special property under § 2-501 may, on making and keeping good a tender of any unpaid portion of the price, recover them from the seller if: (a) for goods bought for personal, family, or household purposes, the seller repudiates or fails to deliver as required by the contract; or (b) in all cases, the seller becomes insolvent within ten days after receipt of the first installment on their price.
The buyer's right under (1)(a) vests upon acquisition of a special property, even if the seller had not then repudiated or failed to deliver.
If the identification creating the special property was made by the buyer, it may recover the goods only if they conform to the contract.
c: The buyer gets a right to recover identified goods (on tendering the unpaid price) in two limited cases: consumer goods when the seller repudiates or fails to deliver, and any goods when the seller becomes insolvent within 10 days after receiving the first installment. This is an exception to the usual rule that a disappointed buyer sues for damages.
Whether the buyer also has a security interest, and rights on insolvency after the ten days, depends on Article 9.

Because the consumer buyer's right vests on identification, the buyer takes free of a security interest created by the seller that attaches after identification, even if the buyer is not in ordinary course and the security interest is perfected; payments made after attachment are the secured party's proceeds.
Subsection (3) prevents unjust enrichment from recovering goods far better or more plentiful than the contract called for.

statutes.t: Manner of Seller's Tender of Delivery
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 5 - Performance
x: Tender of delivery requires that the seller put and hold conforming goods at the buyer's disposition and give the buyer any notification reasonably necessary to enable it to take delivery. The manner, time, and place for tender are determined by the agreement and Article 2, and in particular (a) tender must be at a reasonable hour, and goods must be kept available for the period reasonably necessary to enable the buyer to take possession; but (b) unless otherwise agreed the buyer must furnish facilities reasonably suited to the receipt of the goods.
Where the case is within § 2-504 (shipment), tender requires that the seller comply with that section.
Where the seller is required to deliver at a particular destination, tender requires that it comply with (1) and, in an appropriate case, tender documents as described in (4) and (5).

Where goods are in the possession of a bailee and are to be delivered without being moved: (a) tender requires that the seller either tender a negotiable document of title covering the goods or procure acknowledgment by the bailee of the buyer's right to possession; but (b) tender of a non-negotiable document of title or a record directing the bailee to deliver is sufficient unless the buyer seasonably objects, and (except under Article 9) the bailee's receipt of notice of the buyer's rights fixes those rights against the bailee and all third persons; but the risk of loss and of the bailee's failure to honor the document or obey the direction stays on the seller until the buyer has had a reasonable time to present it, and a bailee's refusal to honor defeats the tender.

Where the contract requires the seller to deliver documents, (a) it must tender all such documents in correct form (except as § 2-323(2) provides for bills of lading in a set); and (b) tender through customary banking channels is sufficient, and dishonor of a draft accompanying or associated with the documents is non-acceptance or rejection.
c: "Tender" has two senses. "Due tender" is an offer coupled with a present ability to fulfill all conditions, followed by actual performance if the other side is ready; this is the usual meaning. Elsewhere it means an offer of goods or documents as if in fulfillment, even if defective. Either way, tender puts the other party in default if it fails to proceed.

Tender has two primary requirements: (1) put and hold conforming goods at the buyer's disposition, and (2) give any notice reasonably necessary for the buyer to take delivery. If payment is due on delivery, the seller may keep control until payment, but must first allow inspection unless the terms (C.I.F., C.O.D., cash against documents) negate inspection before payment. With documents, tendering documents that give complete control of the goods satisfies (1).
Trade usage and the circumstances decide what is a reasonable hour and a reasonable holding period.
The buyer must furnish reasonable receiving facilities; that duty is not part of the seller's tender.

The old rule that a seller's promise to pay freight makes the contract a destination contract is rejected. The shipment contract is the normal one and the destination contract the variant: the seller is not bound to deliver at a destination and bear risk until arrival unless it specifically agreed so or the commercial understanding of the terms contemplates it.

Under (4)(b), as between the parties risk stays on the seller for a reasonable time to obtain the bailee's acknowledgment, while against everyone else the buyer's rights are fixed when the bailee gets notice.

Documents are "required" only by express term, plain implication, or usage. When required: "all" documents, "such" documents as the contract calls for, in "correct form." If a document cannot be had, § 2-614 (substituted performance) may apply.

statutes.t: Shipment by Seller
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 5 - Performance
x: Where the seller is required or authorized to send the goods to the buyer and the contract does not require it to deliver them at a particular destination, then unless otherwise agreed it must: (a) put the goods in the possession of such a carrier and make such a contract for their transportation as may be reasonable having regard to the nature of the goods and other circumstances; (b) obtain and promptly deliver or tender in due form any document necessary to enable the buyer to obtain possession of the goods or otherwise required by the agreement or usage of trade; and (c) promptly notify the buyer of the shipment. Failure to notify the buyer under (c) or to make a proper contract under (a) is a ground for rejection only if material delay or loss ensues.
c: The section covers only shipment contracts (not destination contracts or delivery where the goods are), including F.O.B. point of shipment, C.I.F., and C. & F. Due tender under § 2-503 requires compliance with it.
The carrier contract must follow the agreement's express terms (subject to substituted performance), read in their commercial rather than literal sense.

Absent agreement, the seller chooses any reasonable carrier and routing (§ 2-311), and must make reasonable arrangements such as refrigeration, watering livestock, protection from cold, or specialized cars - relaxed if the buyer can make them and gets reasonable notice. Agreeing with the carrier to a limited valuation below true value, cutting off the buyer's recovery when the buyer bears the risk, is an improper contract.
The duty to deliver necessary documents is in addition to (a). For pool car shipments, a delivery order usually suffices.

The seller must always notify the buyer of shipment, but failure justifies rejection only if material delay or loss follows. Sending an invoice (open credit) or forwarding documents (documentary sales) is standard notice. Parties may make prompt notice a term of the essence, but it should be a dickered term or called sharply to the seller's attention.

Rejection is justified only when the seller's lapse actually leads to material delay or damage. The seller bears the burden, on matters outside the buyer's special knowledge, of showing its error was not followed by events justifying rejection.

statutes.t: Seller's Shipment Under Reservation
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 5 - Performance
x: Where the seller has identified goods to the contract by or before shipment: (a) its procurement of a negotiable bill of lading to its own order or otherwise reserves in it a security interest in the goods; procuring the bill to the order of a financing agency or of the buyer indicates in addition only the seller's expectation of transferring that interest to the person named; (b) a non-negotiable bill of lading to itself or its nominee reserves possession of the goods as security, but (except for conditional delivery under § 2-507(2)) a non-negotiable bill naming the buyer as consignee reserves no security interest even if the seller keeps the bill.

When shipment with reservation of a security interest violates the contract, it is an improper contract for transportation under § 2-504, but it impairs neither the buyer's rights from shipment and identification nor the seller's powers as holder of a negotiable document of title.
c: The reserved security interest only secures the buyer's payment or performance; it does not affect where title is, and the parties' rights rest on the contract, not presumptions about title.
Every shipment of identified goods under a negotiable bill reserves a security interest in the seller; making the bill to a nominee (agent, bank, buyer) is common.
A non-negotiable bill to someone other than the buyer reserves possession as security, but the buyer can tender payment and recover the goods if the seller wrongly withholds them.

A non-negotiable bill to the buyer leaves the seller no security interest or control (except stoppage in transit); demanding immediate payment can make delivery conditional, but the buyer can still pass title to a good faith purchaser under § 2-403.
An improper reservation does not impair the buyer's rights from identification, and the reservation does not let the seller hold the goods to extract more than it is owed.

statutes.t: Effect of Seller's Tender; Delivery on Condition
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 5 - Performance
x: Tender of delivery is a condition to the buyer's duty to accept the goods and, unless otherwise agreed, to its duty to pay for them. Tender entitles the seller to acceptance of the goods and to payment according to the contract.

Where payment is due and demanded on the delivery to the buyer of goods or documents of title, the buyer's right as against the seller to retain or dispose of them is conditional upon making the payment due.
c: Subsection (1) continues prior law on tender and delivery and applies equally to present sales and contracts to sell, read together with the other sections on delivery and payment.
"Unless otherwise agreed" mainly covers advance payment or letter-of-credit terms. Payment "according to the contract" may be immediate, at the end of a credit term, by time acceptance, and so on.

Subsection (2) makes the buyer's rights against the seller conditional on payment in a cash sale, codifying the cash seller's right of reclamation (in the nature of a lien). There is no fixed time limit, but delay that prejudices the buyer, waiver, estoppel, or ratification defeats it; good faith purchasers are protected by § 2-403(1).

statutes.t: Cure by Seller of Improper Tender or Delivery; Replacement
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 5 - Performance
x: Where any tender or delivery by the seller is rejected because nonconforming and the time for performance has not yet expired, the seller may seasonably notify the buyer of its intention to cure and may then within the contract time make a conforming delivery.

Where the buyer rejects a nonconforming tender which the seller had reasonable grounds to believe would be acceptable with or without money allowance, the seller may, if it seasonably notifies the buyer, have a further reasonable time to substitute a conforming tender.
c: Under (1), a seller may cure within the contract time after seasonable notice, even if it took back the goods and refunded the price. The closer to the deadline, the more prompt the notice must be. If a later modification shortened the delivery period (the buyer asked for early-month shipment under a June contract), cure must fit the modified time.

Subsection (2) protects the seller from a surprise rejection, but only if it had reasonable grounds to believe the tender would be acceptable - grounds that may come from course of dealing, course of performance, usage of trade, or the circumstances of contracting. A seller is charged with knowing when strict compliance is needed (documents in overseas shipments, precision parts, manufacturing chemicals). If the buyer signals strictness (rigorous past inspections, a deliberate "no replacement" clause), the seller must comply rigidly - though a form clause out of line with usage and not called to the seller's attention may still leave reasonable grounds.
"A further reasonable time" limits the seller to protect the buyer; what is reasonable depends on the circumstances (compare § 2-511).
Trade usages allowing variations with a price allowance are part of the agreement as contractual limits on remedy, not cure under this section.

statutes.t: Risk of Loss in the Absence of Breach
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 5 - Performance
x: Where the contract requires or authorizes the seller to ship the goods by carrier: (a) if it does not require delivery at a particular destination, the risk of loss passes to the buyer when the goods are duly delivered to the carrier, even though the shipment is under reservation (§ 2-505); but (b) if it does require delivery at a particular destination and the goods are there duly tendered while in the carrier's possession, the risk passes to the buyer when the goods are there duly so tendered as to enable the buyer to take delivery.

Where the goods are held by a bailee to be delivered without being moved, the risk of loss passes to the buyer (a) on its receipt of possession or control of a negotiable document of title covering the goods; or (b) on acknowledgment by the bailee of the buyer's right to possession; or (c) after its receipt of possession or control of a non-negotiable document of title or other direction to deliver in a record, as provided in § 2-503(4)(b).
In any case not within (1) or (2), the risk of loss passes to the buyer on its receipt of the goods if the seller is a merchant; otherwise the risk passes to the buyer on tender of delivery.
This section is subject to contrary agreement of the parties and to §§ 2-327 (sale on approval) and 2-510 (effect of breach on risk of loss).
c: Risk of loss follows a contractual approach, not the location of "property" or title. This section applies only where the seller has not breached; if the tender or delivery fails to conform, § 2-510 governs.

"Requires or authorizes" shipment is read like § 2-504. "Duly delivered to the carrier" requires a proper carrier contract under § 2-504 and delivery that lets the seller complete a due tender. Shipment need not follow contracting, but if the seller buys goods afloat and diverts them to the buyer, the goods must be identified before risk passes, and risk does not pass retroactively to shipment.

Whether delivery is at the seller's place or where the goods are, a merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer actually receives the goods - even if the buyer paid in full and was told the goods were at its disposal. The merchant still controls the goods and can be expected to insure them; the buyer has no control and is unlikely to insure goods it does not possess. The seller is protected against a buyer's breach by § 2-510.
For goods held by a bailee, delivery of a negotiable document or the bailee's acknowledgment completes delivery and passes the risk.

"Contrary agreement" means "unless otherwise agreed"; parties may reallocate risk any way they like, and agreement may be found in the circumstances, trade usage, course of dealing, or course of performance.

statutes.t: Effect of Breach on Risk of Loss
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 5 - Performance
x: Where a tender or delivery of goods so fails to conform to the contract as to give a right of rejection, the risk of their loss remains on the seller until cure or acceptance.
Where the buyer rightfully revokes acceptance, it may, to the extent of any deficiency in its effective insurance coverage, treat the risk of loss as having rested on the seller from the beginning.

Where the buyer, as to conforming goods already identified to the contract, repudiates or is otherwise in breach before risk of their loss has passed to it, the seller may, to the extent of any deficiency in its effective insurance coverage, treat the risk of loss as resting on the buyer for a commercially reasonable time.
c: A seller cannot shift the risk of loss by its own action unless that action meets all the conditions resting on it under the contract.

"Cure" in (1) means changes to goods already tendered (repair, partial substitution, sorting); repossession and new tender does not affect risk on the original goods, and risk does not shift until cure is complete. For defective documents, cure or the buyer's waiver shifts the risk - but not if the goods were destroyed before cure or the buyer waived without knowing of the destruction.

After a breach, any loss not covered by the aggrieved party's insurance falls on the breaching party. "Effective" insurance addresses an insolvent insurer, and "deficiency" means the shortfall without subrogation; insurers' subrogation does not disturb this allocation.

statutes.t: Tender of Payment by Buyer; Payment by Check
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 5 - Performance
x: Unless otherwise agreed, tender of payment is a condition to the seller's duty to tender and complete any delivery.

Tender of payment is sufficient when made by any means or in any manner current in the ordinary course of business, unless the seller demands payment in legal tender and gives any extension of time reasonably necessary to procure it.
Subject to § 3-310, payment by check is conditional and is defeated as between the parties by dishonor of the check on due presentment.
c: Payment against delivery applies to noncommercial and ordinary retail sales and to documentary contracts and shipment contracts with no payment term; it does not apply to the many commercial contracts with credit terms. "Any delivery" ties in with delivery in lots (§ 2-307). Even before tender, § 2-609 protects the seller's expectation of payment.
Absent agreement, payment and delivery are concurrent conditions performed at one place and time, set by the delivery sections and the inspection section.
Subsection (2) avoids commercial surprise at performance; a seller demanding cash must allow time to get it.
Taking a seemingly solvent party's check is normal and is not penalized if collected diligently. The conditional character applies only between the parties.
Payment by check fails if the check is dishonored on due presentment, but if the seller has the check certified instead of cashing it, the buyer is discharged.
A credit instrument (a note or a post-dated check) is a delivery on credit as to third parties; between the parties, dishonor gives the seller rights on the instrument and for breach.

statutes.t: Payment by Buyer Before Inspection
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 5 - Performance
x: Where the contract requires payment before inspection, nonconformity of the goods does not excuse the buyer from making payment unless (a) the nonconformity appears without inspection; or (b) despite tender of the required documents, the circumstances would justify an injunction against honor under § 5-109(b).
Payment under (1) does not constitute an acceptance of the goods or impair the buyer's right to inspect or any of its remedies.
c: A pay-before-inspection term shifts to the buyer risks that usually rest on the seller; in most cases the buyer must pay first and litigate defects later.
"Inspection" means inspection reasonable for detecting defects in goods whose surface appearance is satisfactory.
Clause (a) is a common-sense exception for nonconformity evident in the mere process of taking delivery.
Clause (b) covers payment against documents where fraud would justify enjoining honor (§ 5-109).
Paying first does not impair any of the buyer's rights or remedies, including for total non-delivery after advance payment, and the buyer need not pay "under protest."
The section applies whether the pay-first requirement is express or results by law from the terms (see § 2-513(3)).

statutes.t: Buyer's Right to Inspection of Goods
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 5 - Performance
x: Unless otherwise agreed and subject to (3), where goods are tendered, delivered, or identified to the contract, the buyer has a right before payment or acceptance to inspect them at any reasonable place and time and in any reasonable manner. When the seller is required or authorized to send the goods, the inspection may be after their arrival.
Expenses of inspection must be borne by the buyer but may be recovered from the seller if the goods do not conform and are rejected.

Unless otherwise agreed and subject to § 2-321(3), the buyer is not entitled to inspect before paying the price when the contract provides (a) for delivery "C.O.D." or on like terms; or (b) for payment against documents of title, except where payment is due only after the goods are to become available for inspection.

A place or method of inspection fixed by the parties is presumed to be exclusive, but unless otherwise expressly agreed it does not postpone identification or shift the place for delivery or for passing the risk of loss. If compliance becomes impossible, inspection follows this section unless the agreed place or method was clearly an indispensable condition whose failure avoids the contract.
c: Agreement can limit inspection, but cannot displace the entire right except in a sale of "this thing." Even in an "as is" sale of boxed goods, if the boxes hold different merchandise the price can be recovered.

The right arises on tender, delivery, or identification with notice; it can come before payment (where payment is due on delivery) or be postponed for a reasonable time after receipt. Not inspecting before paying does not waive inspection after receipt.

Any reasonable time, place, and manner will do - not necessarily the best or the customary one; reasonableness depends on usage, past practice, and circumstances. The place of arrival is a reasonable place to inspect shipped goods.
The buyer pays for inspection at first, but if the goods are rightly rejected because of what inspection shows, reasonable inspection costs are incidental damages.

Payment against documents usually comes before inspection because documents arrive while goods are in transit; but if payment awaits arrival, or documents are tendered after arrival, the buyer may inspect first. Payment against storage documents or a delivery order normally does not bar inspection before payment.

An agreed place or method is presumed exclusive. If it becomes impossible, the question is intent: an indispensable condition ends the deal; a mere convenient method can be replaced by any reasonable one. Failing to inspect at the agreed place may be acceptance with knowledge of defects inspection would have revealed.
Clauses on time of inspection usually limit the time to inspect and give notice of defects, so they must be reasonable.
Inspection is not a "condition precedent to passing of title" that keeps risk on the seller; Article 2 settles such issues by specific provisions, not by locating title.
"Inspection" here (checking the seller's performance) is different from pre-contract "examination" that affects warranties under § 2-316(3)(b).

statutes.t: Buyer's Rights on Improper Delivery
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 6 - Breach, Repudiation and Excuse
x: Subject to § 2-612 (installment contracts) and unless otherwise agreed under §§ 2-718 and 2-719 (contractual limits on remedy), if the goods or the tender of delivery fail in any respect to conform to the contract, the buyer may (a) reject the whole; or (b) accept the whole; or (c) accept any commercial unit or units and reject the rest.
c: This is the perfect tender rule: any nonconformity lets the buyer reject. A buyer who accepts a nonconforming tender keeps its other remedies. Partial acceptance is allowed (whether or not the accepted part conforms) where the price can reasonably be apportioned, limited only by good faith and commercial reasonableness so the remainder is not unduly impaired - hence the "commercial unit" requirement. The test is not only what unit the contract used but whether the partial acceptance so harms the rest as to be bad faith.

An acceptance made with the seller's knowledge is final. A rejection can be withdrawn by later acceptance if the seller is holding the tender open; but a buyer who tries to accept after its rejection led the seller to arrange other disposition is liable for the resulting damage, since exercising ownership after rejection is wrongful (§ 2-602). Good faith efforts to dispose of defective goods when the seller gives no instructions are not acceptance.

statutes.t: Manner and Effect of Rightful Rejection
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 6 - Breach, Repudiation and Excuse
x: Rejection of goods must be within a reasonable time after their delivery or tender. It is ineffective unless the buyer seasonably notifies the seller.

Subject to §§ 2-603 and 2-604: (a) after rejection, any exercise of ownership by the buyer as to any commercial unit is wrongful as against the seller; (b) if the buyer has taken physical possession of goods in which it has no security interest under § 2-711(3), it must after rejection hold them with reasonable care at the seller's disposition for a time sufficient to permit the seller to remove them; but (c) the buyer has no further obligations as to goods rightfully rejected.
The seller's rights as to goods wrongfully rejected are governed by § 2-703.
c: Even a wholly nonconforming delivery requires affirmative action by the buyer to avoid acceptance. The buyer has a reasonable time (read with the inspection sections) to notify the seller, and without seasonable notice the rejection is ineffective. Contract limits on the time to reject are effective if they give a reasonable time to discover defects. "Notifies" is defined in § 1-202.
Beyond holding the goods with reasonable care for the seller, the rejecting buyer generally has no duties, except the limited salvage duty of § 2-603.
The section covers only rightful rejection. If the tender conforms in all respects, the buyer must accept, and refusing is a wrongful rejection giving the seller immediate remedies.
These rules are modified appropriately while negotiation is in progress.

statutes.t: Merchant Buyer's Duties as to Rightfully Rejected Goods
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 6 - Breach, Repudiation and Excuse
