Purposes: the merchant-confirmation rule of § 2-201(2) was left out because such lease transactions were thought to be few. There is no exception for payment made and accepted: a lessee pays only some rent, not the full price, and that is not a sufficient substitute for a memorandum. (5) supplies the term when the lease is enforceable under (4).

statutes.t: Final Written Expression: Parol or Extrinsic Evidence
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 2 - Formation and Construction of Lease Contract
x: Terms on which confirmatory memoranda agree, or that are set out in a record intended as a final expression of those terms, may not be contradicted by evidence of a prior agreement or a contemporaneous oral agreement. They may be explained or supplemented (a) by course of dealing, usage of trade, or course of performance; and (b) by consistent additional terms, unless the court finds the record was also intended as a complete and exclusive statement.
c: Taken from § 2-202, with "record" replacing "writing."

statutes.t: Formation in General
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 2 - Formation and Construction of Lease Contract
x: A lease contract may be made in any manner sufficient to show agreement, including conduct by both parties recognizing that a lease contract exists.
An agreement may be found although the moment of its making is undetermined.
With terms left open, a lease contract does not fail for indefiniteness if the parties intended a lease contract and there is a reasonably certain basis for an appropriate remedy.
c: Modeled on § 2-204, revised for leasing practice and terminology.

statutes.t: Firm Offers
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 2 - Formation and Construction of Lease Contract
x: A merchant's offer to lease goods to or from another in a signed record that by its terms gives assurance it will be held open is not revocable for lack of consideration, for the stated time or, if none, a reasonable time, but not more than 3 months. Such a term on a form supplied by the offeree must be separately signed by the offeror.
c: Modeled on § 2-205, with "record" replacing "writing."

statutes.t: Offer and Acceptance in Formation of Lease Contract
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 2 - Formation and Construction of Lease Contract
x: Unless otherwise unambiguously indicated, an offer to make a lease contract invites acceptance in any manner and by any medium reasonable in the circumstances.
If beginning a requested performance is a reasonable mode of acceptance, an offeror not notified of acceptance within a reasonable time may treat the offer as lapsed.
c: Modeled on § 2-206(1)(a) and (2). No analog to § 2-206(1)(b) on prompt-shipment orders, and Article 2A has no analog to § 2-207.
statutes.note: § 2A-207, once the course-of-performance section, has been deleted. See § 1-303, which now covers it.

statutes.t: Modification, Rescission and Waiver
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 2 - Formation and Construction of Lease Contract
x: An agreement modifying a lease contract needs no consideration to be binding.

A signed lease agreement excluding modification or rescission except by signed record can't otherwise be modified or rescinded, but, except between merchants, such a term on a merchant's form must be separately signed by the other party.
An attempt at modification or rescission that fails (2) may operate as a waiver.

A party who waived as to an executory portion may retract by reasonable notification that strict performance is required, unless retraction would be unjust given a material change of position in reliance.
c: Taken from § 2-209, except that § 2-209(3) was left out.

Purposes: § 2-209(3) was omitted because it would be unfair for an oral modification to make the whole lease unenforceable, e.g., by taking it a few dollars over the limit, while enforcing the pre-modification lease might sometimes be worse. Courts decide on the facts of each case.

statutes.t: Lessee Under Finance Lease as Beneficiary of Supply Contract
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 2 - Formation and Construction of Lease Contract
x: The benefit of a supplier's promises to the lessor under the supply contract, and of all warranties (express or implied, including a third party's given in connection with it), extends to the lessee to the extent of its leasehold interest under a related finance lease, subject to the terms of the warranty and supply contract and all related defenses and claims.
This extension doesn't change the rights and obligations of the parties to the supply contract or impose any duty under it on the lessee.

A modification or rescission of the supply contract by supplier and lessor is effective against the lessee unless, beforehand, the supplier received notice that the lessee entered into the finance lease. If it is effective, the lessor is deemed to assume the supplier's promises and warranties as they stood.
The lessee also keeps any rights it has against the supplier from an agreement with the supplier or under other law.
c: The finance lessor's role is extremely limited, and the lessee looks to the supplier. (1) is self-executing and its operation can't be excluded, but any exclusion, limitation, or defense effective against the lessor under the supply contract is also effective against the lessee. Only selective discrimination against the lessee is barred.
The benefit is enforced by action.
The benefit has a price: in a non-consumer finance lease, the lessee's promises become irrevocable and independent on acceptance (§ 2A-407).
(2) preserves the supplier's and lessor's rights against each other and frees the lessee of duties under the supply contract.
If a modification is effective, the lessor picks up what the lessee would lose. Example: an express warranty cut from four years to one; a breach in the later years is the lessor's liability.
(4) confirms that the section doesn't displace the lessee's other rights against the supplier.

statutes.t: Express Warranties
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 2 - Formation and Construction of Lease Contract
x: Express warranties by the lessor arise from (a) an affirmation of fact or promise to the lessee that relates to the goods and becomes part of the basis of the bargain; (b) a description of the goods made part of the basis of the bargain; (c) a sample or model made part of the basis of the bargain.
No formal words or specific intent are needed, but an affirmation merely of value, or a statement of the lessor's opinion or commendation, creates no warranty.
c: All of Article 2's express and implied warranties are carried over, revised for leases. "Value" in (2) includes rental value.

statutes.t: Warranties Against Interference and Against Infringement; Lessee's Obligation Against Infringement
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 2 - Formation and Construction of Lease Contract
x: A lease contract carries a warranty that for the lease term no person holds a claim or interest arising from an act or omission of the lessor, other than infringement or the like, that will interfere with the lessee's enjoyment of its leasehold interest.
Except in a finance lease, a merchant lessor regularly dealing in goods of the kind warrants the goods are delivered free of the rightful claim of any person by way of infringement or the like.
A lessee who furnishes specifications must hold the lessor and supplier harmless against infringement claims arising from compliance with them.
c: Modeled on § 2-312, with changes for the limited interest a lease transfers. (1) restores the warranty of quiet possession that was abolished for sales: a lessee needs more protection than a buyer, and the warranty is limited to claims arising from the lessor's own acts or omissions, which the lessor can evaluate and price. In a finance lease, apart from §§ 2A-210 and 2A-211(1), the lessee looks to the supplier or manufacturer.

statutes.t: Implied Warranty of Merchantability
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 2 - Formation and Construction of Lease Contract
x: Except in a finance lease, a warranty that the goods will be merchantable is implied if the lessor is a merchant with respect to goods of that kind.

Merchantable goods must at least (a) pass without objection in the trade under the description in the lease agreement; (b) for fungible goods, be of fair average quality; (c) be fit for ordinary purposes; (d) run of even kind, quality, and quantity within the agreement's variations; (e) be adequately contained, packaged, and labeled as required; (f) conform to promises or affirmations on the container or label.
Other implied warranties may arise from course of dealing or usage of trade.
c: Modeled on § 2-314.

statutes.t: Implied Warranty of Fitness for Particular Purpose
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 2 - Formation and Construction of Lease Contract
x: Except in a finance lease, if the lessor at the time of contracting has reason to know of a particular purpose for which the goods are required and that the lessee is relying on the lessor's skill or judgment to select or furnish suitable goods, there is an implied warranty that the goods will be fit for that purpose.
c: Modeled on § 2-315.

statutes.t: Exclusion or Modification of Warranties
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 2 - Formation and Construction of Lease Contract
x: Words creating an express warranty and words negating it are construed as consistent where reasonable; otherwise, subject to § 2A-202, the negation is inoperative.

To exclude or modify merchantability, the language must mention "merchantability," be by a writing, and be conspicuous. To exclude fitness, the exclusion must be by a writing and conspicuous; language such as "There is no warranty that the goods will be fit for a particular purpose" is sufficient.

Notwithstanding (2): (a) "as is," "with all faults," or similar language calling attention to the exclusion excludes implied warranties, if in writing and conspicuous, unless circumstances indicate otherwise; (b) if the lessee examined the goods or sample as fully as desired, or refused to, there is no implied warranty for defects an examination ought to have revealed; (c) course of dealing, course of performance, or usage of trade may exclude or modify an implied warranty.

To exclude or modify a warranty against interference or infringement, the language must be specific, by a writing, and conspicuous, unless the circumstances give the lessee reason to know the goods are leased subject to a claim or interest.
c: Unlike § 2-316(2), a merchantability disclaimer must be in writing and conspicuous, the same as for fitness. § 2-312(2)'s analog moved to (4) to treat disclaimers together. The sample fitness language differs from § 2-316(2) to promote understanding of its effect.

statutes.t: Third-Party Beneficiaries of Express and Implied Warranties
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 2 - Formation and Construction of Lease Contract
x: Alt. A

A warranty for a lessee extends to a natural person in the lessee's family or household, or a guest in the lessee's home, if it is reasonable to expect that person may use, consume, or be affected by the goods, and who is injured in person by breach.
Alt. B
Extends to any natural person who may reasonably be expected to use, consume, or be affected by the goods and who is injured in person.
Alt. C
Extends to any person who may reasonably be expected to use, consume, or be affected by the goods and who is injured by breach.
All

The section's operation can't be excluded, modified, or limited (Alt. C: as to injury to the person of an individual), but an exclusion or limitation of the warranty effective against the lessee is also effective against the beneficiary. Alts. A and B don't displace principles of law and equity extending warranties to others.
c: Taken from § 2-318, modified for leasing and to codify the comment on disclaimers. A state should consider matching its choice under § 2-318. Selective discrimination against beneficiaries is barred. Other law, including Article 2, may determine how a warranty to the lessor reaches the lessee.

statutes.t: Identification
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 2 - Formation and Construction of Lease Contract
x: Identification may be made at any time and manner the parties explicitly agree. Otherwise it occurs (a) when the lease contract is made, for goods existing and identified; (b) when goods are shipped, marked, or otherwise designated by the lessor, for goods not existing and identified; or (c) when the young are conceived.
c: Derived from § 2-501, leaving out special property. Ambiguity under (b), e.g., goods marked for delivery when the lessor is both selling and leasing to the same party, is left to the courts.

statutes.t: Insurance and Proceeds
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 2 - Formation and Construction of Lease Contract
x: A lessee obtains an insurable interest when existing goods are identified, even if nonconforming and the lessee may reject.
If the lessee's interest rests only on the lessor's identification, the lessor may substitute other goods until default, insolvency, or notice that identification is final.
The lessor keeps an insurable interest until an option to buy has been exercised and risk of loss has passed to the lessee.
Other insurable interests are not impaired.
The parties may agree who must obtain and pay for insurance and who takes the proceeds.
c: Derived from § 2-501. An option to buy counts as exercised when the sale closes, not when notice is given. (5) reflects the common shifting of insurance responsibility and cost.

statutes.t: Risk of Loss
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 2 - Formation and Construction of Lease Contract
x: Except in a finance lease, risk of loss is retained by the lessor and doesn't pass to the lessee. In a finance lease, risk of loss passes to the lessee.

Subject to § 2A-220, if risk is to pass and the time isn't stated: (a) if shipment by carrier is required or authorized, then (i) with no particular destination, on due delivery to the carrier; (ii) with a destination, when duly tendered there so the lessee can take delivery. (b) If held by a bailee to be delivered without being moved, on the bailee's acknowledgment of the lessee's right to possession. (c) Otherwise, on the lessee's receipt if the lessor or, in a finance lease, the supplier is a merchant; if not, on tender.
c: (1) reflects current lease practice, and (2) draws on § 2-509(1)-(3). The section doesn't address loss caused by either party's wrongful act.

statutes.t: Effect of Default on Risk of Loss
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 2 - Formation and Construction of Lease Contract
x: Where risk is to pass and the time isn't stated: (a) if tender or delivery fails to conform so as to give a right of rejection, risk stays with the lessor or, in a finance lease, the supplier, until cure or acceptance. (b) A lessee who rightfully revokes may, to the extent of any deficiency in its insurance, treat the risk as having stayed with the lessor from the beginning.

Whether or not risk is to pass, if the lessee repudiates or defaults as to conforming identified goods, the lessor or, in a finance lease, the supplier may, to the extent of any deficiency in its insurance, treat risk as resting on the lessee for a commercially reasonable time.
c: Modeled on § 2-510. Under (1)(b), a finance lessee can't treat the risk as having stayed with the supplier, which fits the limited revocation right in finance leases.

statutes.t: Casualty to Identified Goods
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 2 - Formation and Construction of Lease Contract
x: If a lease contract requires goods identified at contracting, and the goods suffer casualty without fault of the lessee, lessor, or supplier before delivery, or before risk passes to the lessee: (a) if the loss is total, the lease contract is avoided; (b) if partial, or the goods no longer conform, the lessee may demand inspection and either treat the contract as avoided or, except in a non-consumer finance lease, accept the goods with due allowance from the rent for the balance of the term, with no further right against the lessor.
c: Modeled on § 2-613. Because the allowance is hard to measure, the section doesn't say how to recapture it across rent payments.

statutes.t: Alienability of Party's Interest Under Lease Contract or of Lessor's Residual Interest in Goods; Delegation of Performance; Transfer of Rights
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 3 - Effect of Lease Contract
x: Except as in (3) and § 9-407, a provision prohibiting a voluntary or involuntary transfer of a party's interest or the lessor's residual, or making it a default, gives rise to the (4) remedies, but the transfer is otherwise effective.

A provision prohibiting a transfer of a right to damages for default on the whole lease, or of a right to payment from the transferor's due performance of its entire obligation, or making that a default, is not enforceable. Such a transfer doesn't materially impair return performance or materially change the other party's duty, burden, or risk.

Subject to (3) and § 9-407: (a) if the transfer is made an event of default, the other party has § 2A-501(2) rights and remedies unless it waives or agrees otherwise. (b) If (a) doesn't apply, and the transfer is prohibited, or materially impairs return performance or materially changes duties, burdens, or risks, then, unless the other party agrees, the transferor is liable for damages the other party couldn't reasonably prevent, and a court may grant other relief, including cancellation or an injunction.

A transfer of "the lease" or "all my rights under the lease" is a transfer of rights and, unless the language or circumstances show otherwise, as in a transfer for security, a delegation of duties. Acceptance is a promise to perform, enforceable by the transferor or the other party.
Unless the lessor and lessee agree otherwise, delegation doesn't relieve the transferor of any duty or liability.
In a consumer lease, language prohibiting a transfer or making it a default must be specific, written, and conspicuous.
c: Transfers are effective despite a prohibition, but the provision is still enforceable through (4). If the transfer is an event of default, default remedies apply. If merely prohibited, damages apply, or cancellation or an injunction if damages would be ineffective.
Under § 9-407, a provision barring a security interest or making it a default is generally not enforceable.

A right to payment that is due or will come due with no further performance can't be restricted. A duty to let the lessee remain in possession, or potential warranty liability, is not remaining performance; a duty to maintain or upgrade is. Think operating vs. non-operating leases.
Relief for material prejudice where the lease doesn't prohibit the transfer is only for extreme circumstances.
Example of (4)(b): a sublease or assignment to a party using the goods improperly.
(7) protects a consumer lessee from surprise defaults.
(5) separates a commercial assignment, which moves rights and duties, from an assignment for security or financing, which moves only rights.

statutes.t: Subsequent Lease of Goods by Lessor
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 3 - Effect of Lease Contract
x: Subject to § 2A-303, a subsequent lessee from a lessor gets, to the extent of the interest transferred, the leasehold interest the lessor had or had power to transfer, and, except under (2) and § 2A-527(4), takes subject to the existing lease. A lessor with voidable title can transfer a good leasehold to a good-faith subsequent lessee for value. With goods delivered under a transaction of purchase, the lessor has that power even if its transferor was deceived about its identity, the delivery was for a check later dishonored, it was agreed to be a "cash sale," or the delivery was procured by larcenous fraud.

A subsequent lessee in ordinary course from a merchant lessor dealing in goods of that kind, to whom the existing lessee entrusted the goods before the subsequent lessee's interest became enforceable, gets, to the extent transferred, all the lessor's and existing lessee's rights, and takes free of the existing lease.
For goods covered by a certificate of title, the subsequent lessee takes no greater rights than this section and the title statute provide.
c: Read with § 2-403. A person who buys goods to lease, or a lessee from that buyer, is protected under § 2-403.

An entrustment outside these sections: M sells to B, who leaves the goods with M, and M leases them to L. L isn't a buyer in ordinary course, and B isn't an existing lessee or M's lessor. § 2A-307(2) resolves it: B, a creditor of M through its common-law claim, takes subject to the lease to L. B's recourse is against M for proceeds and M's interest as lessor, including the residual.
A subsequent lessee keeps rights under agency, apparent agency, or estoppel, but generally takes subject to the existing lease.
(1) protects a good-faith subsequent lessee for value in specific situations that troubled prior law.
An existing lessee who entrusts goods to its lessor is like any other entruster. The lessor keeps the residual, and entrustment must come before the subsequent lessee's interest is enforceable.
If a title statute is silent on the transfer, this section controls.

statutes.t: Sale or Sublease of Goods by Lessee
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 3 - Effect of Lease Contract
x: Subject to § 2A-303, a buyer or sublessee from a lessee gets, to the extent transferred, the leasehold interest the lessee had or had power to transfer, and, except under (2) and § 2A-511(4), takes subject to the existing lease. A lessee with a voidable leasehold can transfer a good leasehold to a good-faith buyer or sublessee for value, even if the lessor was deceived about the lessee's identity, delivery was for a check later dishonored, or delivery was procured by larcenous fraud.

A buyer or sublessee in ordinary course from a lessee who is a merchant dealing in goods of that kind, to whom the lessor entrusted the goods, gets all the lessor's and lessee's rights, and takes free of the existing lease.
For titled goods, the transferee takes no greater rights than this section and the title statute provide.
c: Companion to § 2A-304, and consistent with cases refusing to let a bailee pass title under § 2-403(1). Unlike § 2A-304(2), (2) has no timing requirement for entrustment, because the equities between competing interests were seen as balanced.

statutes.t: Priority of Certain Liens Arising by Operation of Law
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 3 - Effect of Lease Contract
x: If a person in the ordinary course of business furnishes services or materials for goods under a lease, a lien on those goods in that person's possession, given by statute or rule of law, takes priority over any interest of the lessor or lessee, unless the statute or rule provides otherwise.
c: The reference to statute includes applicable regulations and cases, which must be reviewed in a priority dispute.

statutes.t: Priority of Liens Arising by Attachment or Levy on, Security Interests in, and Other Claims to Goods
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 3 - Effect of Lease Contract
x: Except under § 2A-306, a creditor of a lessee takes subject to the lease contract.
Except under (3) and §§ 2A-306 and 2A-308, a creditor of a lessor takes subject to the lease contract unless it holds a lien that attached before the lease contract became enforceable.
Except under §§ 9-317, 9-321, and 9-323, a lessee takes its leasehold subject to a security interest held by a creditor of the lessor.
c: "Lessee" includes a sublessee, and "creditor" includes general, secured, and lien creditors and their representatives.
The same scope applies for a lessor's creditors under (2).
To beat the lease, a creditor must fit (2), an earlier-attached lien, or an Article 9 provision named in (3).
The rules protect whichever party may enforce the lease, even if the other may not.

statutes.t: Special Rights of Creditors
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 3 - Effect of Lease Contract
x: A creditor of a lessor in possession may treat the lease as void if retention of possession is fraudulent under other law, but retention in good faith and current course of trade for a commercially reasonable time after the lease becomes enforceable is not fraudulent.

Article 2A doesn't impair a lessor's creditors' rights if the lease is made, not in current course of trade, but for a pre-existing claim, under circumstances that make it a fraudulent transfer or voidable preference under other law.

A creditor of a seller may treat a sale as void if the seller's retention of possession is fraudulent under other law, but retention under a lease from buyer as lessor to seller as lessee is not fraudulent if the buyer bought for value and in good faith.
c: (3) is a new rule protecting sale-leasebacks and overrides § 2-402(2) to that extent.

statutes.t: Insecurity: Adequate Assurance of Performance
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 4 - Performance of Lease Contract: Repudiated, Substituted and Excused
x: A lease contract obliges each party not to impair the other's expectation of due performance.

If reasonable grounds for insecurity arise, the insecure party may demand adequate assurance in writing and, if commercially reasonable, suspend any performance for which it hasn't received the agreed return.
Repudiation occurs if adequate assurance isn't provided within a reasonable time, not exceeding 30 days after receipt of a demand.
Between merchants, grounds and adequacy are judged by commercial standards.
Accepting a nonconforming delivery or payment doesn't prejudice the right to demand assurance.
c: Modeled on § 2-609. The word "justified" before "demand" was dropped as unnecessary, with no change in substance.

statutes.t: Anticipatory Repudiation
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 4 - Performance of Lease Contract: Repudiated, Substituted and Excused
x: If either party repudiates as to a performance not yet due, the loss of which will substantially impair the lease contract's value to the other, the aggrieved party may (a) await retraction and performance for a commercially reasonable time; (b) demand assurance under § 2A-401 and await it; or (c) resort to any remedy, even after urging retraction. It may also suspend performance or, if the lessor, proceed under § 2A-524.
c: Modeled on § 2-610.

statutes.t: Retraction of Anticipatory Repudiation
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 4 - Performance of Lease Contract: Repudiated, Substituted and Excused
x: Until its next performance is due, the repudiating party may retract unless the aggrieved party has since cancelled, materially changed position, or otherwise indicated it considers the repudiation final.
Retraction may be by any method clearly showing the party will perform, and must include any assurance demanded under § 2A-401.
Retraction reinstates the repudiating party's rights, with due excuse and allowance for delay.
c: Modeled on § 2-611.

statutes.t: Substituted Performance
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 4 - Performance of Lease Contract: Repudiated, Substituted and Excused
x: If, without fault of the lessee, lessor, or supplier, the agreed facilities fail, the agreed carrier becomes unavailable, or the agreed manner of delivery becomes commercially impracticable, and a commercially reasonable substitute is available, it must be tendered and accepted.

If the agreed means of payment fails because of governmental regulation: (a) the lessor may withhold or stop delivery, or cause the supplier to, unless the lessee provides a commercially substantial equivalent; (b) if delivery has been taken, payment as the regulation provides discharges the lessee, unless the regulation is discriminatory, oppressive, or predatory.
c: Modeled on § 2-614.

statutes.t: Excused Performance
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 4 - Performance of Lease Contract: Repudiated, Substituted and Excused
x: Delay or nondelivery by a lessor or supplier who complies with (b) and (c) is not a default if performance was made impracticable by a contingency whose nonoccurrence was a basic assumption of the lease contract, or by good-faith compliance with a governmental regulation or order.
If only part of capacity is affected, it must allocate fairly and reasonably among customers, and may include regular customers and its own needs.
The lessor, and in a finance lease the supplier, must seasonably notify of the delay or nondelivery and any quota.
c: Modeled on § 2-615.

statutes.t: Procedure on Excused Performance
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 4 - Performance of Lease Contract: Repudiated, Substituted and Excused
x: On notice of a material or indefinite delay or an allocation under § 2A-405, the lessee may by written notification, for the goods involved (or all goods if the whole installment lease is substantially impaired), (a) terminate; or (b) except in a non-consumer finance lease, accept the available quota with due allowance from the rent, with no further right against the lessor.
If the lessee doesn't modify within a reasonable time not exceeding 30 days, the lease contract lapses as to the affected deliveries.
c: A finance lessee may terminate, but a non-consumer finance lessee may not modify, for the same policy as § 2A-407.

statutes.t: Irrevocable Promises: Finance Leases
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 4 - Performance of Lease Contract: Repudiated, Substituted and Excused
x: In a finance lease that is not a consumer lease, the lessee's promises become irrevocable and independent on acceptance of the goods.

Such a promise (a) is enforceable between the parties and by or against third parties, including assignees; and (b) isn't subject to cancellation, termination, modification, repudiation, excuse, or substitution without the consent of the party to whom it runs.
The validity under other law of a covenant making a lessee's promises irrevocable and independent on acceptance isn't affected.
c: This extends the classic "hell or high water" clause to non-consumer finance leases and is self-executing. It remains subject to good faith and to revocation of acceptance under § 2A-517.

The lessee must perform even if the lessor's performance after acceptance falls short, but it may have a claim against the lessor, e.g., under §§ 2A-210 and 2A-211(1). Consumer leases are excluded because obliging a consumer to pay despite defective goods isn't tenable.
Hypothetical: A (lessor) and B (lessee) sign a 60-month lease of equipment B ordered from C, and B assigns the purchase order to A. This should be a finance lease.
C installs, B tests and signs an acceptance certificate, and a year later the line malfunctions.

A gave no implied warranty. Absent an express term, §§ 2A-210 or 2A-211(1), or fraud or duress, B has no claim against A, keeps paying, and has no setoff. B may have a claim against C under § 2A-209(1), despite no privity.

The section doesn't say whether a hell-or-high-water clause is enforceable in a consumer lease or a non-finance lease; other law decides. Courts have enforced such clauses in non-consumer finance leases.
The promise is enforceable against third parties, so the lease can be assigned without disturbing it.

statutes.t: Default: Procedure
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: Whether a lessor or lessee is in default is determined by the lease agreement and this Article.
The party seeking enforcement has the rights and remedies in this Article and, except as limited, in the lease agreement.
It may reduce its claim to judgment or otherwise enforce the lease by self-help or any available judicial or nonjudicial procedure, including arbitration.
Except as § 1-305(a), this Article, or the lease provides, the rights and remedies are cumulative.
If the lease covers real property and goods, the party may proceed under this Part as to the goods, or under other law as to both.
c: Unlike Article 9, default depends on this Article as well as the agreement, and either party can default.
Remedies are cumulative to the extent needed to put the aggrieved party where full performance would have, but not in a better position.
Unlike Article 9's limits on waiver, there is no restraint on varying remedies, given freedom of contract in bailments for hire and the lessee's lack of an equity of redemption.

statutes.t: Notice After Default
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: Except as this Article or the lease provides, a party in default isn't entitled to notice of default or notice of enforcement from the other party.
c: Absent agreement or a contrary provision, such as § 2A-516(3)(a), no notice is due. Unlike Article 9's disposition notices, the common-law scheme for lessors and lessees generally needs no notice of enforcement, and due process doesn't require it.

statutes.t: Modification or Impairment of Rights and Remedies
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: Except as this Article provides, the lease may add remedies or substitute for those provided, and limit or alter the measure of damages.
A remedy is optional unless expressly exclusive. If an exclusive or limited remedy fails of its essential purpose, or an exclusive remedy is unconscionable, Article 2A remedies apply.

Consequential damages may be liquidated under § 2A-504, or otherwise limited, altered, or excluded unless unconscionable. For injury to the person with consumer goods, a limit is prima facie unconscionable; where the loss is commercial it is not.
Remedies for default on obligations collateral or ancillary to the lease contract aren't impaired.
c: Part 5 fills in for parties who don't provide remedies, or whose remedies fail. It doesn't restrict freedom of contract.
(2) makes explicit what is implicit in § 2-719: an unconscionable exclusive remedy falls away.
(3) makes clear that consequential damages may also be liquidated.
Example of an ancillary promise: the lessee as seller to the lessor as buyer in a sale-leaseback.

statutes.t: Liquidation of Damages
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: Damages for default or any other act or omission, including indemnity for lost tax benefits or harm to the residual, may be liquidated, but only at an amount or by a formula reasonable in light of the then anticipated harm.
If the provision fails (1), or an exclusive or limited remedy fails of its essential purpose, Article 2A remedies apply.

If the lessor justifiably withholds or stops delivery because of the lessee's default or insolvency, the lessee gets restitution of payments above (a) valid liquidated damages; or (b) without them, 20 percent of the then present value of total rent for the balance of the term or, in a consumer lease, the lesser of that or $500.
The right is offset to the extent the lessor establishes (a) a right to damages under other Article 2A provisions and (b) benefits the lessee received.
c: Lessors rely on agreed damages, so this rule is more flexible than § 2-718. Unlike § 2-718(1): an amount or a formula is allowed; it covers any act or omission, not only default; the tests of difficulty of proof and inconvenience of other remedy are dropped; and the sentence voiding unreasonably large damages as a penalty is dropped, because tax indemnities can dwarf the goods' price. Reasonableness still restrains the clause. Common formula: past-due payments + accelerated future payments + estimated residual, less net proceeds of disposition. Enforceability is judged by the harm anticipated when agreed. The $500 alternative in (3)(b) is kept only for consumer leases, as too low for others.

statutes.t: Cancellation and Termination and Effect of Cancellation, Termination, Rescission, or Fraud on Rights and Remedies
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: On cancellation, executory obligations on both sides are discharged, but rights based on prior default or performance survive, and the cancelling party keeps any remedy for default of the whole or any unperformed balance.
On termination, executory obligations are discharged, but rights based on prior default or performance survive.
Unless a contrary intention clearly appears, words of "cancellation" or "rescission" don't renounce a claim for antecedent default.
Remedies for material misrepresentation or fraud include all rights and remedies for default.
Rescission, a claim for rescission, or rejection or return of the goods doesn't bar a claim for damages or another remedy.

statutes.t: Statute of Limitations
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: An action for default, including breach of warranty or indemnity, must be brought within 4 years after the cause of action accrued. The original lease may reduce the period to not less than one year.

A default claim accrues when the act or omission is or should have been discovered, or when the default occurs, whichever is later. An indemnity claim accrues when the act or omission is or should have been discovered.
If a timely action ends leaving a remedy by another action, the new action may be brought within 6 months after, unless the end was voluntary or for failure to prosecute.
Tolling law isn't altered.
c: Unlike § 2-725(1), the parties aren't barred from extending the period. Accrual is more liberal than § 2-725(2): the later of default or when it was or should have been discovered.

statutes.t: Proof of Market Rent: Time and Place
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: Market-rent damages use the rent for a term identical to the remaining term of the original lease, at the times in §§ 2A-519 and 2A-528.
If that isn't readily available, a rent within a reasonable time before or after, at another place, or for a different term may be used if commercially a reasonable substitute, with proper allowance.
Evidence of such a rent isn't admissible without notice sufficient to prevent unfair surprise.
Published market reports of rents or values are admissible, and circumstances of preparation go to weight.
c: Combines §§ 2-723 and 2-724.

statutes.t: Lessee's Remedies
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: If the lessor fails to deliver conforming goods or repudiates, or the lessee rightfully rejects or justifiably revokes, then for the goods involved (all goods if an installment lease's value is substantially impaired) the lessee may (a) cancel; (b) recover so much of the rent and security paid as is just under the circumstances; (c) cover and recover damages (§§ 2A-518, 2A-520), or recover nondelivery damages (§§ 2A-519, 2A-520); (d) use any other right in the lease contract.
If the lessor fails to deliver or repudiates, the lessee may also (a) recover identified goods (§ 2A-522); or (b) in a proper case obtain specific performance or replevin (§ 2A-521).
If the lessor is otherwise in default, the lessee has the lease's remedies, which may include cancellation, and § 2A-519(3).
For breach of warranty, the lessee may recover damages (§ 2A-519(4)).

On rightful rejection or justifiable revocation, the lessee has a security interest in goods in its possession or control for rent and security paid and reasonable expenses, and may hold and dispose of them in good faith and in a commercially reasonable manner, subject to § 2A-527(5).
Subject to § 2A-407, a lessee on notifying the lessor may deduct damages from rent still due under the same lease contract.
c: An index to the lessee's remedies, which the parties may vary.

There's no general election of remedies; a remedy is barred only if it would put the lessee in a better position than performance. Unlike a sale, not all rent paid need come back: if a 36-month lease ends in month 12 for failure to maintain, it may be just to return little or none.
(3) covers defaults that don't deprive the lessee of the goods, and defaults where the lessee keeps the goods.
The lease may give cancellation for lesser defaults, and a right to cancel carries a right to reject or revoke.
(4) is for warranty breaches short of what justifies revocation.
The lien parallels § 2-711(3), and a good-faith purchaser takes free under § 2A-511(4).
The lessee must account for excess proceeds under § 2A-527(5).
Setoff is subject to § 2A-407 and to any enforceable hell-or-high-water clause.
No special finance-lease treatment here, but after acceptance a finance lessee will usually have no rights against the lessor and will look to the supplier.

statutes.t: Lessee's Rights on Improper Delivery; Rightful Rejection
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: Subject to § 2A-510, if the goods or tender or delivery fail in any respect to conform, the lessee may reject or accept, or accept any commercial units and reject the rest.
Rejection is ineffective unless within a reasonable time after tender or delivery and the lessee seasonably notifies the lessor.
c: Modeled on §§ 2-601 and 2-602(1).

statutes.t: Installment Lease Contracts: Rejection and Default
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: Under an installment lease, a lessee may reject a nonconforming delivery if the nonconformity substantially impairs that delivery's value and can't be cured, or is a defect in required documents. If it doesn't fall under (2) and the lessor or supplier gives adequate assurance of cure, the lessee must accept.

If nonconformity or default as to one or more deliveries substantially impairs the value of the whole, there is a default as to the whole. The aggrieved party reinstates the contract by accepting a nonconforming delivery without seasonably notifying of cancellation, or by suing only on past deliveries, or by demanding future performance.
c: Modeled on § 2-612.

statutes.t: Merchant Lessee's Duties as to Rightfully Rejected Goods
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: Subject to the lessee's security interest, if the lessor or supplier has no agent or place of business at the market of rejection, a merchant lessee must follow reasonable instructions and, without them, make reasonable efforts to sell, lease, or dispose of goods that threaten to decline in value speedily. Instructions aren't reasonable if indemnity for expenses isn't forthcoming on demand.
A lessee who disposes of goods gets reimbursement for reasonable expenses of care and disposition, and a usual commission or a reasonable sum up to 10 percent of gross proceeds.
The lessee is held only to good faith, and good-faith conduct is neither acceptance nor conversion nor a basis for damages.
A good-faith purchaser from a lessee under this section or § 2A-512 takes free of the lessor's and supplier's rights, even if the lessee failed a requirement.
c: Modeled on §§ 2-603 and 2-706(5).

statutes.t: Lessee's Duties as to Rightfully Rejected Goods
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: Except for goods that decline speedily, and subject to the lessee's security interest: (a) the lessee must hold rejected goods with reasonable care at the lessor's or supplier's disposition for a reasonable time after notice; (b) without instructions in a reasonable time, it may store, ship back, or dispose of them for the lessor's or supplier's account, with § 2A-511 reimbursement; (c) it has no further obligations for rightfully rejected goods.
Action under (1) is not acceptance or conversion.
c: Modeled on §§ 2-602(2)(b)-(c) and 2-604.

statutes.t: Cure by Lessor of Improper Tender or Delivery; Replacement
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: If a nonconforming tender is rejected and the time for performance hasn't expired, the lessor or supplier may seasonably notify of its intent to cure and make conforming delivery within the time provided.
If it had reasonable grounds to believe the tender would be acceptable, with or without money allowance, it may have a further reasonable time to substitute a conforming tender, on seasonable notice.
c: Modeled on § 2-508.

statutes.t: Waiver of Lessee's Objections
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: A lessee's failure to state a defect ascertainable by reasonable inspection bars relying on it to justify rejection or establish default (a) if, stated seasonably, it could have been cured; or (b) between merchants, if after rejection the lessor or supplier made a written request for a full and final statement of defects.
Failure to reserve rights when paying against documents bars recovery for defects apparent in the documents.
c: Modeled on § 2-605.

statutes.t: Acceptance of Goods
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: Acceptance occurs after a reasonable opportunity to inspect when the lessee (a) signifies, or acts in a way that signifies, that the goods conform or that it will keep them despite nonconformity; or (b) fails to make an effective rejection.
Accepting part of a commercial unit accepts the whole unit.
c: Based on § 2-606, but the lessee's conduct may signify acceptance, and § 2-606(1)(c), an act inconsistent with the seller's ownership, was dropped as irrelevant given the lessee's possession and use.

statutes.t: Effect of Acceptance of Goods; Notice of Default; Burden of Establishing Default After Acceptance; Notice of Claim or Litigation to Person Answerable Over
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: A lessee must pay rent for goods accepted, with allowance for goods rightfully rejected or not delivered.

Acceptance precludes rejection. In a finance lease, acceptance with knowledge of a nonconformity can't be revoked because of it. Otherwise it can't be unless made on the reasonable assumption of seasonable cure. Acceptance doesn't itself impair other remedies.

After acceptance: (a) within a reasonable time after it discovered or should have discovered any default, the lessee must notify the lessor and the supplier, if any, or be barred from any remedy against the party not notified; (b) except in a consumer lease, it must notify the lessor of infringement litigation or lose its remedy over; (c) the lessee bears the burden of establishing any default.

If sued for an obligation for which a lessor or supplier is answerable over, the lessee may give written notice to come in and defend, or be bound by common findings of fact; for infringement, the lessor or supplier may demand control of the litigation on agreeing to bear expense and any judgment.
(3) and (4) apply to a lessee's duty to hold harmless against infringement.
c: A special finance-lease rule bars revocation for known nonconformity with the lease agreement; the lessee still has a direct claim against the supplier. Revocation remains available if acceptance was without discovery and induced by the lessor's assurances, even after the promise is irrevocable.
In a finance lease, the essential notice is to the supplier, but remedy is barred against whichever party isn't notified, and notifying the lessor is good practice.
A finance lessee should consider notifying the supplier of infringement litigation, too.

statutes.t: Revocation of Acceptance of Goods
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: A lessee may revoke acceptance of a lot or commercial unit whose nonconformity substantially impairs its value to the lessee if accepted (a) except in a finance lease, on the reasonable assumption of cure, not seasonably made; or (b) without discovery, where acceptance was reasonably induced by the lessor's assurances or, except in a finance lease, by difficulty of discovery.
Except in a non-consumer finance lease, a lessee may revoke if the lessor defaults and the default substantially impairs the value of the lot or unit to the lessee.
If the lease so provides, the lessee may revoke because of other defaults.

Revocation must occur within a reasonable time after the lessee discovers or should have discovered the ground, and before any substantial change in condition not caused by the nonconformity. It isn't effective until the lessee notifies the lessor.
A revoking lessee has the same rights and duties as if it had rejected.
c: (2) recognizes continuing lessor duties, e.g., failing to maintain equipment or supply what it needs to run may justify revocation and cancellation.
The parties may agree on what defaults are serious enough to allow cancellation.
A finance lessee keeps only the limited (1)(b) right. See § 2A-516 comment.

statutes.t: Cover; Substitute Goods
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: After a § 2A-508(1) default, or other default if agreed, the lessee may cover by purchasing or leasing substitute goods.

Unless liquidated or otherwise agreed, if cover is by a lease substantially similar to the original, made in good faith and in a commercially reasonable manner, the lessee recovers (i) the present value, at the start of the new term, of new rent for the period comparable to the remaining original term, minus the present value of the rent for that remaining term; and (ii) incidental or consequential damages, less expenses saved.
If cover doesn't qualify under (2), or is by purchase or otherwise, § 2A-519 governs as if the lessee hadn't covered.
c: Whether to cover is a commercial judgment, with no sanction for failing to.
Three criteria: cover by lease, substantially similar, in good faith and commercially reasonable. Consequential damages may include loss of use between default and new lease.
"Substantially similar" was left undefined on purpose, and is decided case by case.
Look at the goods. If identical goods aren't available, more modern equipment may qualify as a reasonable substitute.
Look at the lease terms: options, warranties, covenants, services. If differences are easily valued, a court may adjust the rent and still find similarity, e.g., for who insures.
Take the factors as a whole, with commercial judgment and no scientific precision.

A new lease may run past the old term if the terms are commercially comparable and rent can be fairly apportioned. Dates needn't match. A one-month rental and a five-year lease are unlikely to be similar.

statutes.t: Lessee's Damages for Non-delivery, Repudiation, Default, and Breach of Warranty in Regard to Accepted Goods
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: Unless liquidated or otherwise agreed, if the lessee doesn't cover or cover doesn't qualify under § 2A-518(2), damages for non-delivery, repudiation, rejection, or revocation are the present value, at default, of market rent minus the present value of original rent, for the remaining term, plus incidental and consequential damages, less expenses saved.
Market rent is determined at the place for tender or, after rejection on arrival or revocation, the place of arrival.

Unless otherwise agreed, if the lessee accepted and gave notice, damages for nonconforming tender or other default are the loss in the ordinary course, determined in any reasonable manner, plus incidental and consequential damages, less expenses saved.

Unless otherwise agreed, damages for breach of warranty are the present value, at the time and place of acceptance, of the difference in the value of the use of the goods accepted and as warranted for the term, unless special circumstances show otherwise, plus incidental and consequential damages, less expenses saved.
c: Applies if there's no cover or cover doesn't qualify. There's no sanction for cover that doesn't qualify.
The reference is to the date of default, not an event of default, which becomes default only after grace and notice periods.
(3) applies to defaults at inception and later ones, such as failure to maintain.
(4) is a present-value version of § 2-714(2).
The parties may vary (1), (3), and (4).

statutes.t: Lessee's Incidental and Consequential Damages
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: Incidental damages include expenses reasonably incurred in inspection, receipt, transportation, and care of goods rightfully rejected or as to which acceptance was justifiably revoked; commercially reasonable charges of effecting cover; and other reasonable expense incident to the default.

Consequential damages include (a) loss from general or particular requirements the lessor had reason to know of at contracting and that couldn't reasonably be prevented by cover or otherwise; and (b) injury to person or property proximately resulting from breach of warranty.
c: Modeled on § 2-715. Neither list is exhaustive, and (1) covers revocation as well as rejection.

statutes.t: Lessee's Right to Specific Performance or Replevin
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: Specific performance may be decreed if the goods are unique or in other proper circumstances.
The decree may include terms on rent, damages, or other relief.
A lessee has a right of replevin or the like for goods identified to the lease contract if, after reasonable effort, it can't cover or the circumstances indicate the effort will be unavailing.
c: Modeled on § 2-716, with similar rights added to replevin.

statutes.t: Lessee's Right to Goods on Lessor's Insolvency
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: Subject to (2), a lessee who has paid part or all of the rent and security for identified goods, on tendering any unpaid portion due, may recover them if the lessor becomes insolvent within 10 days after receipt of the first installment.
The right exists only if the goods conform.
c: Modeled on § 2-502, without the consumer-goods rule in § 2-502(1)(a).

statutes.t: Lessor's Remedies
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: If the lessee wrongfully rejects or revokes, fails to make a payment when due, or repudiates, then for the goods involved (all goods if an installment lease's value is substantially impaired) the lessor may (a) cancel; (b) proceed as to unidentified goods (§ 2A-524); (c) withhold delivery and take possession of delivered goods (§ 2A-525); (d) stop delivery (§ 2A-526); (e) dispose of the goods and recover damages (§ 2A-527), retain them and recover damages (§ 2A-528), or in a proper case recover rent (§ 2A-529); (f) use other rights in the lease contract.

A lessor that doesn't fully exercise a right or obtain a remedy under (1) may recover the loss in the ordinary course from the default, determined in any reasonable manner, plus incidental damages, less expenses saved.

If the lessee is otherwise in default, the lessor has the lease's remedies, and unless the lease says otherwise: (a) if the default substantially impairs the lease's value, (1) or (2) remedies; (b) if not, recovery under (2).
c: An index to §§ 2A-524 to 2A-531. The doctrine of election of remedies is rejected: a lessor may change course unless that would actually be unreasonable to the lessee, and may use (1) and (2) together unless it ends up better off than performance.
The parties may agree on different remedies.
A remedy is barred only if it puts the lessor in a better position than performance.

A long bicycle-rental hypothetical runs through comments 5-18: a staged lease, default on rent after the first delivery, repossession, stopping and finishing later deliveries, then choosing among the damages measures.
The lessor may, but need not, dispose of the goods. It can't recover damages that put it ahead of performance or losses it could reasonably have avoided.
Retail leases are unlikely to be substantially similar to a wholesale lease.
Recovery of the rent isn't available if goods are repossessed or tendered back, unless they can't be disposed of.
Repossession doesn't bar a damages measure, since a lessor would have got the goods back anyway.
A lessor may choose (2) instead, e.g., not repossess, and sue for rent as it comes due plus lost interest.
No special finance-lease treatment. The supplier usually has no rights against a defaulting lessee.

statutes.t: Lessor's Right to Identify Goods to Lease Contract
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: After default, the lessor may (a) identify conforming goods in its or the supplier's possession or control when it learned of the default; and (b) dispose of goods demonstrably intended for the lease, even if unfinished.

If unfinished, the lessor or supplier may, in reasonable commercial judgment to avoid loss and for effective realization, complete and identify them, cease and dispose for scrap or salvage, or proceed in any other reasonable manner.
c: Modeled on § 2-704. The remedies apply on a § 2A-523(1) or (3)(a) default, or another default if the lease so provides, which it can do in general terms.

statutes.t: Lessor's Right to Possession of Goods
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: If the lessor discovers the lessee to be insolvent, it may refuse to deliver.

After a § 2A-523(1) or (3)(a) default, or other default if agreed, the lessor may take possession. If the lease so provides, it may require the lessee to assemble the goods at a reasonably convenient place. Without removal, it may render business goods unusable and dispose of goods on the lessee's premises.
The lessor may proceed without judicial process if that can be done without breach of the peace, or by action.
c: § 2-702(2) reclamation wasn't carried over, since (2) makes it unnecessary.
Because insolvency is a default in a standard lease, (2) works like reclamation. It also sanctions the crate-and-delivery clause.
Modeled on § 9-609. Action includes injunctive relief. These sections codify the lessor's common-law right to protect its reversion and supplement other law on the subject.

statutes.t: Lessor's Stoppage of Delivery in Transit or Otherwise
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: A lessor may stop delivery in a carrier's or bailee's possession if it discovers the lessee is insolvent, and may stop carload, truckload, planeload, or larger shipments if the lessee repudiates or fails to make a payment due before delivery, or for any other reason it may withhold or take possession.
It may stop until (a) the lessee's receipt; (b) a non-carrier bailee's acknowledgment that it holds for the lessee; or (c) a carrier's such acknowledgment by reshipment or as a warehouse.

The lessor must give notice enabling the bailee, by reasonable diligence, to prevent delivery. The bailee then follows the lessor's directions, and the lessor is liable for ensuing charges or damages. A carrier with a nonnegotiable bill needn't obey anyone but the consignor.
c: Modeled on § 2-705.

statutes.t: Lessor's Rights to Dispose of Goods
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: After a default, or after refusing delivery or taking possession, the lessor may dispose of the goods by lease, sale, or otherwise.

Unless liquidated or otherwise agreed, if disposition is by a lease substantially similar to the original, in good faith and in a commercially reasonable manner, the lessor recovers (i) accrued unpaid rent at the start of the new term; (ii) the present value of total rent for the remaining original term minus the present value of comparable new rent; and (iii) incidental damages, less expenses saved.
If the disposition doesn't qualify, or is by sale or otherwise, § 2A-528 governs.
A good-faith buyer or lessee for value takes free of the original lease and lessee, even if the lessor failed a requirement.
The lessor isn't accountable for any profit. A lessee who rightfully rejected or revoked must account for any excess over its security interest.
c: Disposition is a commercial judgment, not a duty; the lessee has no right of redemption.
The measure depends on how the lessor disposed of the goods.
Three criteria: disposition by lease, substantially similar, in good faith and commercially reasonable.
"Substantially similar" is decided case by case.
Weigh options, warranties, covenants, services. Easily valued differences can be adjusted.
Tractor hypothetical: a re-lease on identical terms except who insures; whether it is similar is a question of fact.
The new term may run longer if commercially comparable and apportionable. Dates needn't match.
(4) overrides the first-in-time rule of § 2A-304(1).
No accounting for profit, since a lessee has no equity of redemption.

statutes.t: Lessor's Damages for Non-acceptance, Failure to Pay, Repudiation, or Other Default
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: Unless liquidated or otherwise agreed, if the lessor keeps the goods, or disposes of them other than under § 2A-527(2), it recovers (i) accrued unpaid rent as of default if the lessee never took possession, or else as of repossession or an earlier tender of the goods; (ii) the present value at that date of total rent for the remaining term minus the present value of market rent at the place where the goods are located for the same term; and (iii) incidental damages, less expenses saved.

If (1) is inadequate to put the lessor in as good a position as performance, the measure is the present value of the profit, including reasonable overhead, from full performance, plus incidental damages, due allowance for costs reasonably incurred, and due credit for payments or proceeds of disposition.
c: Applies when the lessor keeps the goods or the disposition doesn't qualify. There's no sanction for a disposition that doesn't qualify.
The date is the date of default or, with possession, the earlier of repossession or tender, not an event of default.
Market rent is computed under § 2A-507.
The credit for proceeds must value the lessor's residual interest properly.
Lost profit includes expected appreciation of the goods, e.g., the foal of a leased mare, and present value must be applied.

statutes.t: Lessor's Action for the Rent
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: After default, a lessor complying with (2) may recover (a) for goods accepted and not repossessed by or tendered to it, and for conforming goods lost or damaged within a commercially reasonable time after risk passed, accrued unpaid rent at judgment, plus the present value of remaining rent, plus incidental damages, less expenses saved; and (b) the same for identified goods if, after reasonable effort, it can't dispose of them at a reasonable price or the effort would be unavailing.
Except as in (3), the lessor must hold for the lessee for the remaining term any identified goods in its control.
It may dispose of the goods any time before collecting the judgment. If that is before the term ends, recovery is governed by § 2A-527 or § 2A-528, and it must credit any excess against the judgment.
Payment of the judgment entitles the lessee to use and possession of goods not disposed of for the rest of the term.
A lessor held not entitled to rent must still be awarded § 2A-527 or § 2A-528 damages.
c: The full rent is available for goods not lost only if the lessee keeps them or the lessor can't dispose of them. Article 2's rule that the seller can recover the price of accepted goods is rejected. If the lessee tenders the goods back and the lessor refuses, the lessor is limited to the damages it would have had: it holds a residual and will re-let or sell anyway.

Lost profit under § 2A-528(2) can still reach full rent even with the goods back. Five backhoes, never all rented: an early return costs the lessor the two-week rental and gives it nothing it wouldn't have had.
If the lessor disposes before collecting, the measures in §§ 2A-527 and 2A-528 take over.
Only full satisfaction of the judgment restores use and possession.
Holding the goods usually means the lessor can't use them. Using them may count as a disposition.
(5) means suing for rent isn't an election of remedies.

statutes.t: Lessor's Incidental Damages
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: Incidental damages to an aggrieved lessor include commercially reasonable charges, expenses, or commissions in stopping delivery, in transportation, care, and custody of goods after default, in connection with return or disposition, or otherwise resulting from the default.
c: Modeled on § 2-710.

statutes.t: Lessor's Rights to Residual Interest
statutes.part: Article 2A, Part 5 - Default
x: In addition to other recovery, the lessor may recover an amount fully compensating it for loss of or damage to its residual interest caused by the lessee's default.
c: Covers failure to return the goods in the required condition, failure to return them at all, and any other default harming the residual.

statutes.t: Scope (excerpt)
statutes.part: Article 9 - Secured Transactions (excerpts)
x: Except as provided in (c) and (d), Article 9 applies to a transaction, regardless of its form, that creates a security interest in personal property or fixtures by contract.
It also applies to a sale of accounts, chattel paper, payment intangibles, or promissory notes; to a consignment; and to security interests arising under §§ 2-401, 2-505, 2-711(3), or 2A-508(5).

Article 9 does not apply to, among other things: (4) a sale of accounts or similar rights as part of a sale of the business out of which they arose; (5) an assignment for collection only; (6) an assignment of a right to payment under a contract to an assignee that is also obligated to perform under the contract; (7) an assignment of a single account or similar right in full or partial satisfaction of a preexisting debt.
statutes.note: Only the subsections cited in the outline are summarized. In this course: a sale that is really a secured loan is governed by Article 9, not Article 2 (§ 2-102(3)), and Article 9's anti-assignment override does not reach an assignment of a right to payment to an assignee that must also perform the contract (§ 9-109(d)(6)), so ordinary assignment law and § 2-210 govern there.

statutes.t: Interests That Take Priority Over or Take Free of Security Interest (excerpt)
statutes.part: Article 9 - Secured Transactions (excerpts)
x: A lessee of goods takes free of a security interest if it gives value and receives delivery without knowledge of the security interest and before it is perfected.
c: Certain purchasers beat an unperfected security interest. They must give value and take delivery without knowledge and before perfection; if perfection comes before delivery, they lose. A lessee in ordinary course takes free even of a perfected interest under § 9-321.
statutes.note: Subsection (c) is summarized from the casebook (p. 502) and comment 6. The statutes book's excerpt of § 9-317 omits its text.

statutes.t: Licensee of General Intangible and Lessee of Goods in Ordinary Course of Business (excerpt)
statutes.part: Article 9 - Secured Transactions (excerpts)
x: A lessee in ordinary course of business takes its leasehold free of a security interest in the goods created by the lessor, even if it is perfected and the lessee knows of it.
c: Contains the rule once found in § 2A-307(3) and works like § 9-320(a) for buyers.

statutes.t: Discharge of Account Debtor; Terms Restricting Assignment (excerpt)
statutes.part: Article 9 - Secured Transactions (excerpts)
x: Subject to (b)-(i), an account debtor (for example, a buyer that owes for goods) may discharge its obligation by paying the assignor until, but not after, it receives a notification, authenticated by the assignor or the assignee, that the amount due has been assigned and that payment is to be made to the assignee. After receiving the notification, the account debtor may discharge its obligation only by paying the assignee; paying the assignor no longer discharges it.

Except as provided in (e) and (k) and §§ 2A-303 and 9-407, and subject to (h), a term in an agreement between an account debtor and an assignor is ineffective to the extent that it (1) prohibits, restricts, or requires the account debtor's consent to the assignment or transfer of, or the creation, attachment, perfection, or enforcement of a security interest in, the account; or (2) provides that such an assignment or security interest may give rise to a default, breach, right of recoupment, claim, defense, termination, or remedy.
statutes.note: Cited with § 2-210(2): a seller's right to be paid for goods (an "account") stays assignable even if the sales contract forbids assignment.

statutes.t: Restrictions on Creation or Enforcement of Security Interest in Leasehold Interest or in Lessor's Residual Interest
statutes.part: Article 9 - Secured Transactions (excerpts)
x: A lease term is ineffective to the extent it prohibits, restricts, or requires consent to an assignment or transfer of, or a security interest in, a party's interest under the lease or the lessor's residual, or makes that a default or ground for a remedy.

A term making such a thing a default is effective to the extent there is a transfer by the lessee of its right of possession or use, or a delegation of a material performance of either party, in violation of the term.
A security interest in the lessor's interest or residual isn't a material impairment under § 2A-303(4), unless and to the extent enforcement actually delegates the lessor's material performance.
c: Reflects the policy of § 9-406(d).
Whether the lessor has remaining duties depends on the lease. If it does, ask whether a material performance was actually delegated.

statutes.t: Filing and Compliance With Other Statutes and Treaties for Consignments, Leases, Other Bailments, and Other Transactions
statutes.part: Article 9 - Secured Transactions (excerpts)
x: A lessor, consignor, or similar party may file a financing statement using terms such as "lessor" and "lessee" rather than "secured party" and "debtor."
The filing isn't itself a factor in deciding whether the collateral secures an obligation. If it does for another reason, the security interest is perfected by the filing.
c: A precautionary filing protects a party when it's unclear whether a "lease" creates a security interest, without affecting how the deal is classified.
Certificate-of-title law may affect this result.

statutes.t: Secured Party's Right to Take Possession After Default
statutes.part: Article 9 - Secured Transactions (excerpts)
x: After default a secured party may take possession of collateral and, without removal, may render equipment unusable and dispose of collateral on the debtor's premises.
It may proceed by judicial process, or without it if there is no breach of the peace.
If agreed, and in any event after default, it may require the debtor to assemble the collateral at a place reasonably convenient to both.
c: Breach of the peace is left to the courts. A secured party answers for those acting for it, including independent contractors. A law officer may not be used without judicial process.
Disabling equipment suits collateral that is impractical to remove, and any disposition must be commercially reasonable.
An agreement to assemble collateral is valid.

statutes.t: Disposition of Collateral After Default (excerpt)
statutes.part: Article 9 - Secured Transactions (excerpts)
x: A contract for sale, lease, license, or other disposition of collateral includes the warranties relating to title, possession, quiet enjoyment, and the like which by operation of law accompany a voluntary disposition of property of that kind.

A secured party may disclaim or modify those warranties (1) in a manner that would be effective in a voluntary disposition of that kind of property; or (2) by communicating to the purchaser a record evidencing the contract for disposition and including an express disclaimer or modification.

A record is sufficient to disclaim warranties under (e) if it says "There is no warranty relating to title, possession, quiet enjoyment, or the like in this disposition" or uses words of similar import.
statutes.note: Cited with § 2-312, Comment 5: unlike a sheriff's sale, a secured party's foreclosure sale of goods carries title warranties unless properly disclaimed.

statutes.t: Notification Before Disposition of Collateral (excerpt)
statutes.part: Article 9 - Secured Transactions (excerpts)
x: Except as otherwise provided, a secured party disposing of collateral must send a reasonable signed notification of disposition to those named in (c).
These include the debtor, any secondary obligor, and, for non-consumer goods, others who gave notice of a claim and certain perfected secured parties and lienholders.
c: The notice must be reasonable in manner, timing, and content.
Notice can be waived only by a signed post-default agreement.
statutes.note: Relevant to Article 2A only if a "lease" turns out to be a disguised sale. See casebook p. 493 n.16.

sections.title: I. The UCC & Which Law Governs
The UCC and the common law
sections.html:
• What it is: a model code (Uniform Law Commission (ULC) + American Law Institute (ALI)) adopted by the states to standardize commerce and protect those in business transactions. Not law until enacted; check each state's version. Louisiana never enacted Art. 2/2A.
  • § 1-103(a) purposes (construe liberally to promote):
    (1) simplify, clarify, modernize     commercial law;
    (2) permit continued expansion of commercial practices     through custom, usage, and agreement;
    (3) make the law uniform     among jurisdictions.
  • § 1-103(b): unless displaced by a particular UCC provision, common law and equity (capacity, agency, estoppel, fraud, misrepresentation, duress, coercion, mistake, bankruptcy, other validating/invalidating causes) supplement the Code.
  • Sales law is broader than commercial law — buying and selling goods by individuals, businesses, and others; a cumulative subject, not one law.
  • Role of sales systems: bring buyers and sellers together; supply standard terms; supply mechanisms for performing; supply mechanisms for resolving disputes.
  • Recurring themes: certainty · responsiveness · laissez-faire · simplicity · efficiency · international.

sections.title: Statutory interpretation (slides + text)
sections.html:
• Three rules:
    (1) read it all, then read it again — parse grammar, find the pauses, test hypotheticals;
    (2) find the definitions (§ 1-201 for all Articles; §§ 2-103 to 2-106; "purchase" includes a gift; "goods" includes unborn animals);
    (3) read in context of the provision's and the Code's purposes.
  • Then consult: Official Comments (most important aid, but not law — the text controls if they conflict), case law (other states are persuasive), treatises, state legislative history, earlier drafts; last resort, a tie-breaker policy.
  • Keep the client's goals in view. Good drafting: understand the deal; know the rules and risk-allocation options; attention to detail; concise, clear, simple language — goal: an enforceable agreement that clearly reflects the deal.

sections.title: Which law governs — four factors (in this order)
sections.html:
1. Type of property (goods, real estate, services, intellectual property (IP)…);

2. Nature of the rights transferred (sale, lease, license, lien, gift);

3. Location of the parties (domestic vs. international / United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods (CISG));

4. The parties' agreement on governing law.

Transaction in goods

Governing law

Sale

UCC Article 2 (or CISG if international)

Lease

UCC Article 2A

Security interest

UCC Article 9

Gift

Common law

Bequest/devise

Law of wills

Other columns of the slide chart: real property → real-property law; securities → Art. 8 (+ securities law; Art. 9 for security interests); negotiable instruments → Arts. 3 & 4; IP → common law & federal law; controllable electronic records → Art. 12.

sections.title: Is it a "good"? — § 2-105(1), § 2-107
sections.html:
rule

Goods = all things (including specially manufactured goods) movable at the time of identification to the contract, except
(1) the money in which the price is to be paid,
(2) investment securities (Art. 8), and
(3) things in action. Also includes unborn young of animals, growing crops, and things attached to realty under § 2-107.

  • § 2-107(1): minerals (oil, gas) or a structure to be removed from realty → goods only if severed by the SELLER.
  • § 2-107(2): growing crops, timber to be cut, other things severable without material harm → goods whether buyer or seller severs.

Problem 1-1 item

Goods?

Why

Isotopes in solution · oxygen

✓

Liquids and gases are movable things

Excess solar electricity

✓ (maybe)

Courts split — good once metered vs. a service

Gold coin from a coin dealer

✓

It's the subject of the sale, not the money paying the price

500 euro notes for a trip

Depends

Currency bought as a commodity vs. as money

Yen credited to a brokerage account

Unlikely

Not a movable thing — a financial asset/thing in action

Lottery ticket

✗

Thing in action

Microsoft stock (certificated)

✗

Investment security

Building — seller removes it

✓

Structure severed by seller (§ 2-107(1))

Timber — buyer cuts

✓

Timber is goods regardless (§ 2-107(2))

Oil & gas — buyer extracts

✗

Minerals are goods only if seller severs

sections.title: Hybrid transactions (goods + services/other property)
sections.html:
Test

Question

Notes

Predominant purpose (majority, pre-2022)

Is the predominant purpose goods or services? All-or-nothing.

Factors: contract language · nature of supplier's business · relative value of goods vs. services · whether applying Art. 2 makes sense. Hard to apply; why should services insulate goods from warranties?

Gravamen of the claim (Anthony Pools, Md.)

Does the claim relate to the goods or the services?

Anthony Pools (note case, casebook p. 24): an unmerchantable diving board, supplied under a pool-construction contract in which services predominated, caused personal injuries → Art. 2 applied to impose the merchantability warranty and to test the disclaimer. Outside class materials: the homeowner slipped off the board. Hard to apply (contact lenses — bad lens or bad exam?); multiple statutes of limitations may apply to one deal. Little traction.

2022 Amendments — § 2-102(2)

Two tiers

Goods predominate → Art. 2 applies. Goods don't predominate → only provisions relating primarily to the goods apply.

  • § 2-106(5) "hybrid transaction": a sale of goods plus services, a lease of other goods, or a sale/lease/license of non-goods property (provided by the seller).
  • Still apply when goods don't predominate (cmt. 5): warranties (§§ 2-312–2-318), tender & risk of loss, acceptance/rejection/cure, buyer's remedies for nondelivery/nonconforming goods. Don't apply: § 2-201, §§ 2-204–2-207, § 2-209.
  • Predominance factors (cmt. 3) weighed together:
    (1) agreement's language;
    (2) share of price     for the goods (an agreed allocation usually binds);
    (3) parties' purposes;
    (4) nature of businesses. Manufacturing services count toward goods;
    (5) design     services don't.
  • Problem 1-2 (Speedy Offset prints & binds 500 art books): printing/binding = services in manufacturing goods → goods predominate → Art. 2 applies; claims concern conformity of the books, so warranty rules apply either way.
  • Problem 1-4: Art. 2 governs merchant→merchant, merchant→consumer, consumer→merchant, and consumer→consumer (garage sale) — scope never depends on merchant status.
  • Disguised security interest: a "sale" with a mandatory repurchase at a higher price is really a secured loan → Art. 9, not Art. 2 (§ 2-102(3)(a)).

sections.title: Common law vs. UCC; agreement vs. contract
sections.html:
Common law

UCC Article 2

Mutual assent; based on promise

Based on bargain, as to goods

Mirror-image rule — acceptance must match the offer

Contract formed "in any manner sufficient to show agreement"; acceptance need not mirror

All material terms needed

Open terms OK; fewer formalities; many ways to form

  • "Agreement" (§ 1-201(b)(3)) = the parties' bargain in fact, from language and course of performance (CoP) / course of dealing (CoD) / usage of trade (UoT). "Contract" (§ 1-201(b)(12)) = the total legal obligation that results, as determined by the UCC and other law. The contract can be more (gap fillers, implied warranties) or less (statute of frauds (SOF), unconscionable term) than the agreement.
  • Questions to ask:
