  • Contracts allocate risk; excuse is applied sparingly. Foreseeability matters most but isn't decisive. All of these yield to contrary agreement (e.g., force majeure clauses). Excuse decides who pays damages; risk of loss decides who absorbs the goods' value.
rule

§ 2-613 — casualty to identified goods all required:
(1) goods identified when the contract was made,
(2) destroyed without fault of either party (negligence counts as fault)
(3) before risk passes → total loss: contract avoided; partial loss/deterioration: buyer may inspect and either avoid or accept with a price allowance (no further claim). Fungible goods → no excuse.

rule

§ 2-614 — substituted performance: if agreed loading/berthing facilities, carrier type, or manner of delivery becomes commercially impracticable without fault, a commercially reasonable substitute must be tendered and accepted. If the agreed payment method fails due to governmental regulation, seller may withhold delivery unless buyer offers a substantially equivalent payment method.

rule

§ 2-615 — impracticability (seller): delay or non-delivery isn't a breach if (1) performance became impracticable due to (2) a contingency whose non-occurrence was a basic assumption (or good-faith compliance with government regulation) — but seller must allocate fairly among customers if capacity is partly affected and seasonably notify buyers. Increased cost or market swings alone don't excuse (cmt. 4); war, embargo, crop failure, shutdown of major supply sources can. § 2-616: buyer may terminate or take its quota; silence for 30 days = contract lapses as to affected deliveries.

  • Buyer's excuse: common-law frustration of purpose (§ 1-103(b); R2d § 265); § 2-615 cmt. 9 — a supply contract tied to a specific construction venture may excuse the buyer. NIPSCO v. Carbon County Coal (7th Cir. 1986, Posner) (note case; the casebook quotes it, p. 256): a fixed-price contract (there, with a price floor and escalation) assigns the risk of market increases to the seller and decreases to the buyer; a buyer that misforecasts the market "has only himself to blame" and can't walk away when costs drop steeply. Outside class materials: NIPSCO was an Indiana electric utility locked into a 20-year coal contract; regulators wouldn't let it pass fuel costs through when cheaper power was available.

Problem

Answer

6-6(a) Art dealer's Picasso etching burns overnight before buyer's pickup

Merchant seller → risk not passed (no receipt) → identified goods, total loss → avoided — if no fault: a neglected coffee pot (negligence) = seller breaches; lightning = excused

6-6(b) Etching was stolen; true owner reclaims it

Not a casualty — a title failure → seller breaches (no § 2-613 excuse)

6-6(c) Print #10 water-damaged; seller has #12

If #10 specifically → § 2-613(b): buyer avoids or accepts with allowance; if prints are interchangeable → must deliver #12

6-6(d) Buyer's options under § 2-613

Total loss → avoided (refund); partial → inspect, then avoid or accept with allowance

6-8(a) Town cancels the sewer project; fittings have no other use

Frustration of purpose likely (shared basic assumption; § 2-615 cmt. 9)

6-8(b) Buyer's bank seized, account frozen

Not excused — § 2-614(2): buyer must provide a substantially equivalent payment method

note

Syllabus Weeks 8–14 start here. Sections XVII to XXXV follow the syllabus reading for Weeks 8–13 (Sepinuck pp. 261–312, 326–344, 397–430, 465–505) and the Week 14 review. The class slides on file end at Week 8, which finished Chapter 6 (a week later than the syllabus planned), so no slides support these sections, and the week labels below are syllabus weeks. Everything here comes from the casebook and the 2026 statutory supplement. Answers to the problems are worked from the casebook text and the statutes. The casebook prints no answers, so they are not the professor's answers; where the law is unsettled the outline says so. The syllabus says to skip the CISG and UNIDROIT materials, so they are left out. Pages 313–325 (risk of loss after a seller's breach, the statute of limitations, Mydlach, Problems 7-29 and 7-30) are not assigned; Section XXVII gives the short limitations rule from p. 430.

sections.title: XVII. Buyer's Remedies: Roadmap & Getting the Goods — §§ 2-711, 2-716, 2-502
Before you reach remedies
sections.html:
• Run the threshold questions first.
    (1) What are the contract's terms (agreement + course of performance, course of dealing, usage of trade + gap fillers)?
    (2) Who breached? Disputes often slide into breach, e.g., a buyer demands assurance, the seller is silent, the buyer cancels: if the buyer had no reasonable grounds for insecurity, the seller's silence is no repudiation and the buyer's cancellation is the breach.
    (3) Is the failure excused (Section XVI)?
    (4) Are remedies limited (Section XI)?
  • Seller's basic duty: deliver goods that conform to the contract (§ 2-301).
  • Goal of every remedy: the expectation interest, putting the aggrieved party in as good a position as full performance (§ 1-305(a)). Punitive damages are generally unavailable (§ 1-305). A breach is not a moral wrong, and the good-faith duty in § 1-304 is not an independent obligation.
  • Remedies turn on two things: what the breach was, and who has the goods.

How the seller breached

Buyer's basic options

Where

Repudiates or never tenders

(i) Get the goods by court order and pay the price, plus delay damages; or (ii) cancel, recover any price paid, and take cover or market damages

§§ 2-711, 2-502, 2-716, 2-712, 2-713, 2-715

Nonconforming tender or goods

(i) Reject, cancel, recover the price, take cover or market damages; or (ii) accept and take value-difference damages

§§ 2-601, 2-711, 2-714, 2-715

Hidden defect after acceptance

Revoke acceptance if the limits are met, then proceed as if rejected

§§ 2-608, 2-711

Conforming goods, but ancillary services (installation, repair) missing or poor

Damages for that harm. Article 2 has no specific rule, but it does not preclude common-law remedies

§ 1-103

rule

§ 2-711 is the roadmap for a seller's repudiation, failure to deliver, a rightful rejection, or a justified revocation. It is an incomplete list. Buyer may cancel, recover price paid, and then cover (§ 2-712) or take market damages (§ 2-713); or, where allowed, obtain the goods (§ 2-502, § 2-716). All damages carry § 2-715 incidental and consequential damages, less expenses saved.

sections.title: Three ways to force the goods out of the seller
sections.html:
• All three need a court order. None allows self-help. Contrast a secured party's repossession without breach of the peace under § 9-609 (p. 265 n.3).
rule

Specific performance, § 2-716(1)–(2): may be decreed where the goods are unique or in other proper circumstances. "May" keeps the remedy discretionary, so the common-law limits presumably remain: (i) damages inadequate, (ii) order not unduly hard to enforce, (iii) no undue hardship, unfairness, or harm to the public interest. Goods need not be identified. The decree may include terms on price, damages, or other relief.

rule

Replevin, § 2-716(3): a legal right, not equitable, so there is no judicial discretion. Requires goods identified to the contract and either (i) after reasonable effort buyer cannot cover, or circumstances reasonably indicate the effort would be unavailing; or (ii) goods shipped under reservation and satisfaction of the security interest made or tendered. For personal, family, or household goods the right vests when the buyer acquires a special property, even if the seller had not yet repudiated.

rule

Recovering identified goods, § 2-502: a buyer who has paid part or all of the price for goods in which it has a special property may, on making and keeping good a tender of the balance, recover them if (a) goods are bought for personal, family, or household purposes and the seller repudiates or fails to deliver; or (b) in all cases, the seller becomes insolvent within ten days after receipt of the first installment. If the buyer made the identification, the goods must conform (§ 2-502(3)).

  • Identification (§ 2-501): the moment the buyer begins to acquire property rights in specific goods, usually when the seller indicates which goods will fill this contract. Existing identified goods: when the contract is made. Future goods: when shipped, marked, or otherwise designated by the seller.
  • Absent § 2-502, § 2-716, or an Article 9 security interest, the buyer cannot force the goods out of the seller. Prepaying alone gives no right to the goods.
  • A buyer that gets the goods still owes any unpaid price (express in § 2-502(1), and presumably true under § 2-716; see §§ 2-607, 2-709), but may recover damages for the delay (§§ 2-711 cmt. 1, 2-714(1), 2-715, 1-103, 1-305).

Remedy

Prepayment needed?

Limit

Specific performance § 2-716(1)

No

No

Replevin § 2-716(3)

Yes
