sections.title: Problems
sections.html:
Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-1 Goods not unique, but specific performance fits

Inability to cover is the key sign of "other proper circumstances": a long-term output or requirements deal in a shortage, a component only this seller can make on time, or a fungible commodity that cannot be found in time. Outside class materials: § 2-716 cmt. 2 and Laclede Gas v. Amoco are the usual support.

7-2 Clause making specific performance available

Helpful, not binding. § 2-716(1) says "may" and the remedy is the court's. The clause is evidence that damages are inadequate. Draft recitals of why cover is hard and add a backup such as liquidated damages or an Article 9 security interest.

7-3(A) $5,000 car; paid $1,000 / paid nothing; family / business

A specific existing car is identified at contracting. Paid + family use: yes, § 2-502(1)(a), on tender of the balance. Paid + business use: § 2-502 only if seller became insolvent within 10 days after the payment; otherwise § 2-716. No payment (either use): § 2-502 is out; only § 2-716. Need to know: is the car unique, can Buyer cover, is Seller insolvent?

7-3(B)(1) Award plaques, nothing made yet

No goods exist, so nothing is identified: no replevin, no § 2-502 (also business goods). Specific performance is unlikely: others can engrave plaques, and an order to manufacture is hard to supervise. Cover plus damages.

7-3(B)(2) Plaques partly made

Partly made plaques may be "otherwise designated" and so identified, opening § 2-716(3) if Buyer cannot cover. The ceremony deadline helps, but ordering Seller to finish pushes back toward specific performance.

7-3(C) Builder prepaid; beams segregated; seller already insolvent (not assigned)

Prepaid and identified, but not consumer goods, so § 2-502(1)(b) only. Seller was already insolvent, so did it "become" insolvent within 10 days? Argue the literal reading against the protective purpose. Fallback § 2-716 is weak if steel can be bought elsewhere.

sections.title: XVIII. Buyer's Damages After Nondelivery or Repudiation — §§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715
Cancelling
sections.html:
• Cancellation (§ 2-106(3)–(4)): the aggrieved party ends the contract for the other's breach. Buyer's duty to perform is discharged and it keeps its damages claim. No procedure and no notice are prescribed, but word it carefully: do not imply a discharge or waiver (§ 1-306; see also § 2-720, under which "cancellation" language does not renounce a claim for antecedent breach unless a contrary intention clearly appears).
  • Refund first: a buyer that did not receive the goods recovers any price paid (§ 2-711(1)), even with no other damages.
rule

Cover, § 2-712: buyer may cover by making in good faith and without unreasonable delay any reasonable purchase of goods in substitution for those due. Damages = cost of cover − contract price + incidental + consequential − expenses saved. Failure to cover does not bar other remedies (§ 2-712(3)).

rule

Market damages, § 2-713: only if the buyer has not covered (cmt. 5; a purchase that does not qualify as cover does not count). Damages = market price when buyer learned of the breach − contract price + incidental + consequential − expenses saved. Market price is taken at the place for tender, or at the place of arrival after rejection on arrival or revocation.

  • Direction matters. Both formulas are (substitute − contract), never the reverse. The buyer accepted the risk that the market would fall; the seller took the risk that it would rise. If the difference is zero or negative there is no direct-damage award, but incidental and consequential damages may still be available.
  • Worked example (pp. 271–272): State Street Motors, $40,000 car, $1,000 down. Market or cover price $42,000: refund $1,000 + $2,000. Buyer ends up with the car for a net $40,000 ($1,000 + $42,000 − $1,000 − $2,000), exactly the expectancy. Market price $40,000 or less: refund only, plus any incidental or consequential loss.

sections.title: Limits on cover
sections.html:
• Good faith limits overpaying with someone else's money. Buyer need not make herculean efforts to find the lowest price, but the seller should not pay for a markup when goods were readily available for much less.
  • Without unreasonable delay stops the buyer from playing the market at the seller's expense.
  • Reasonable substitute stops upgrades. Some difference in quality is fine, especially if identical goods are unavailable, but the seller does not pay for a significant or unnecessary upgrade.
  • Open questions in the text: (1) covering with the breaching seller: is the higher price a cover or an agreed modification with no breach? If buyer refuses that offer, did it fail to mitigate? (2) Covering by making the goods itself: how is the cost measured?
  • Why cover anyway: the buyer may need the goods, and consequential damages are limited to losses that could not reasonably be prevented "by cover or otherwise" (§ 2-715(2)(a)).

sections.title: Time and place of the market price
sections.html:
• Place: the place for tender comes from the agreement plus gap fillers (F.O.B. seller's city = that city; F.O.B. destination = destination).
  • Time after repudiation is contested. Buyer may wait a commercially reasonable time or treat repudiation as breach at once (§ 2-610). When did it "learn of the breach"? Courts differ: date of tender under the contract (Hess Energy v. Lightning Oil (4th Cir. 2003)) vs. a commercially reasonable time after repudiation (Cosden Oil v. Karl O. Helm (5th Cir. 1984)). Both are cited only, at p. 275 n.17. Outside class materials: A third reading uses the date the buyer learned of the repudiation.
  • Shipment contracts: the seller may breach days before the buyer learns the goods won't arrive. Which date controls is unclear; read § 2-723.
  • § 2-723(1): if an action based on repudiation comes to trial before the time for performance (mainly long-term supply contracts), use the price when the aggrieved party learned of the repudiation.
  • § 2-723(2)–(3), § 2-724: if the price at the right time or place is not readily available, use a reasonable substitute time or place with transport adjustments, on fair notice. Published market quotations are admissible.

sections.title: Expenses saved
sections.html: • Both formulas deduct costs the buyer avoided, so damages match the expectancy. Example: buyer of $100,000 equipment would have spent $1,000 modifying its facility. The seller repudiates first; the buyer does not cover (or buys goods needing no modification). Deduct $1,000.

sections.title: Incidental and consequential damages — § 2-715
sections.html:
Incidental § 2-715(1)

Consequential § 2-715(2)

What

Expenses from the breach itself: inspection, receipt, transport, and care of rightfully rejected goods; commercially reasonable cover costs (e.g., travel to a supplier); other reasonable expense from delay or breach

(a) Loss from general or particular needs the seller had reason to know of at contracting and that could not reasonably be prevented by cover or otherwise; (b) injury to person or property proximately resulting from breach of warranty

Test

Caused by the breach and reasonably incurred. No foreseeability test

(1) Caused by the breach; (2) foreseeable: reason to know at contracting; (3) not reasonably avoidable; (4) proved with reasonable certainty (cmt. 4; § 1-103(b))

Example

Cost of traveling to check a substitute supplier

Lost business while a mill waits for a crank shaft

sections.title: When the formula overcompensates
sections.html:
• The formulas sometimes conflict with § 1-305(a). Treat them as tools for reaching the expectancy. The two recurring fact patterns are a buyer that passes its extra cost to someone else (Problem 7-9) and a buyer with a fixed-price resale (Problem 7-10).
  • Problem 7-9 (not assigned): builder on a cost-plus contract covers at $90,000 instead of $70,000 and passes the cost to the developer. Compare KGM Harvesting v. Fresh Network (Cal. Ct. App. 1995) (cited only, p. 280). Outside class materials: KGM allowed cover damages even though the buyer passed the increase along.
  • Problem 7-5 (not assigned): a buyer that makes several purchases must show which ones replaced the breached contract. Blue Sky needed 200,000 gallons but bought 600,000; the earliest purchases best satisfy "without unreasonable delay" (100,000 at $5.20 + 100,000 at $5.40 = $60,000 over contract). Whether fuel delivered to Atlanta is a reasonable substitute for Chicago fuel depends on whether Blue Sky can use it the same way.
  • Problem 7-8 (not assigned): 10-year gravel supply, repudiated in year 5. Trial in year 7: § 2-723(1) applies to performance not yet due. Trial after the term has run: § 2-723(1) does not apply.

sections.title: Problems
sections.html:
Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-4 $40,000 car; $42,000 substitute with heated seats and moon roof, no $500 entertainment system

Refund $1,000. Start at $42,000 − $40,000 = $2,000, then adjust: same make and model is likely a reasonable substitute, but subtract the value of the extras and add $500 for the missing system. Other facts: was an identical car available, did the price reflect the extras, how long was the search, can the system be added later?

7-6(A) 10 desks, $5,000 F.O.B. Phoenix, $100 down, freight ~$500. Repudiated May 20. Cover $6,000 delivered; metal, bigger

"Different model at $800" is a repudiation, and declining it isn't failure to mitigate. "Cancel... refund" does not waive damages. Refund $100. Cover: $6,000 − $5,000 = $1,000 − $500 freight saved = $500 if the metal desks are a reasonable substitute (upgrade fight). Plus search costs (incidental). Wages and lost sales are consequential: reason to know, avoidability, certainty.

7-6(B) Cover for $4,000

No cover damages; Buyer is better off on price. Still the $100 refund, plus incidental and consequential damages, less expenses saved. Having covered, Buyer can't switch to § 2-713, unless the desks aren't a true substitute.

7-6(C) No purchase; expansion dropped for the economy (not assigned)

§ 2-713 at Phoenix when Buyer learned of the breach. Freight cancels (both prices are at Phoenix). No consequential damages: the economy, not the breach, caused the loss. Seller argues § 1-305 limits a buyer that never wanted the desks.

7-7 5,000 lbs of lobster at $10/lb ($50,000), F.O.B. Bar Harbor, July 1; repudiated June 1; prime rib bought June 15. Bar Harbor prices: June 1 $12; June 15 $13; July 1 $14

Prime rib is not a reasonable substitute, so no cover; use § 2-713. Place for tender: Bar Harbor, so Long Island prices are out. Time depends on the rule: June 1 learned of repudiation: $2 × 5,000 = $10,000; June 15 commercially reasonable time: $3 × 5,000 = $15,000; July 1 performance date: $4 × 5,000 = $20,000. The $2,000 freight is not deducted on this reasoning: the Bar Harbor market price also excludes freight. Seller will argue it is an expense saved.

7-10(A) Broker: buy $2.50 F.O.B. New Orleans; resale at $2.70; market $4.50 New Orleans, $4.70 St. Louis. Customer holds Broker liable

§ 2-713 gives ($4.50 − $2.50) × 100,000 = $200,000. Broker's real loss is its liability to Customer ($4.70 − $2.70 = $2.00 × 100,000 = $200,000) plus lost profit ($270,000 − $250,000 − $5,000 − $500 = $14,500), so about $214,500 if the resale was foreseeable and cover impossible. A broker's resale is plainly foreseeable. Don't stack market damages on top of the same liability.

7-10(B) Customer waives its claims

Broker's real loss is $14,500; the formula says $200,000. Split: H-W-H Cattle and Allied Canners on one side, TexPar and Tongish on the other (all cited only, p. 280). Outside class materials: The first pair caps recovery near actual loss under the § 1-305 principle; the second allows the market measure, on the view that it keeps the market incentive and prevents a windfall to the breaching seller. Check the opinions before relying on this.

7-10(C) Broker would have burned the oil itself

No resale to compare, so the market differential is the measure, with any consequential loss. Buyer's use, not resale, was the expectancy.

sections.title: The choice the buyer must make
sections.html:
• After a tender the buyer must accept or reject. It can't do both (§ 2-607(2)) and can't do neither (§ 2-606(1)(b)), though it may accept some and reject the rest. Section XXI covers acceptance.
  • Rejection is a refusal of the seller's tender. It is not a rescission or repudiation of the contract.
  • Two separate questions: (1) did the buyer have the right to reject (was the tender nonconforming)? (2) was the rejection effective (timely, clear notice)? A rejection can be effective even if it is not rightful.
rule

Perfect tender, § 2-601: subject to § 2-612 and to agreed limits (§§ 2-718, 2-719), if the goods or the tender fail in any respect to conform, the buyer may
(a) reject the whole,
(b) accept the whole, or
(c) accept any commercial unit or units and reject the rest. "Conforming" = in accordance with the obligations under the contract (§ 2-106(2)).

sections.title: Limits on perfect tender
sections.html:
• Agreement. The parties may limit rejection, e.g., to major defects. Courts may be reluctant to read an exclusive liquidated-damages term as removing the right to reject, and may apply it only to accepted goods.
  • Trade terms and good faith. Course of performance, course of dealing, and usage of trade can bar rejection for minor defects, and so can § 1-304 good faith.
  • Shipment contracts. Under § 2-504, a failure to make a proper contract with the carrier or to notify is a ground for rejection only if material delay or loss ensues.
  • Installment contracts, § 2-612. See below.
  • Commercial units (§ 2-105(6)). Partial rejection must follow units. Buyer of three laptops may keep two and reject one, but can't reject one laptop's hard drive or one shoe of a pair.
rule

Installment contracts, § 2-612: one requiring or authorizing delivery in separate lots to be separately accepted, even if it says each delivery is a separate contract. Reject an installment only if (1) the nonconformity substantially impairs the value of that installment and (2) cannot be cured (or is a defect in required documents). If seller gives adequate assurance of cure, buyer must accept unless § 2-612(3) applies. Cancel the whole only if nonconformity in one or more installments substantially impairs the value of the whole contract. Buyer reinstates the contract by accepting a nonconforming installment without seasonably notifying of cancellation, suing only on past installments, or demanding future performance.

  • Agreeing to pay in installments doesn't make an installment contract; delivery in separate lots does (p. 284 n.22).
  • "Substantial impairment" is undefined. Some courts analogize to material breach (R2d § 241 factors:
    (a) benefit lost,
    (b) adequacy of compensation,
    (c) forfeiture,
    (d) likelihood of cure,
    (e) good faith). It's judged by the normal and specifically known purposes of the contract (§ 2-612 cmt. 4), so a brief delay can qualify if seller knows it will cause serious trouble. The parties may define it or remove it (n.25).
  • Why a higher bar? The text offers two rationales: preserving an ongoing relationship, and stopping a buyer on the wrong side of a market shift from getting picky to escape the deal.

sections.title: Making a rejection effective
sections.html:
• Article 2 says what is not effective rather than what is. Buyer must avoid anything that counts as acceptance (§ 2-606): saying it will keep the goods despite the nonconformity, or acting inconsistently with the seller's ownership. Merely taking possession to inspect isn't acceptance (§ 2-513). Reselling generally is.
  • § 2-602(1): reject within a reasonable time after delivery or tender, and seasonably notify the seller (§§ 1-205, 1-202). Late or no notice = acceptance, with liability for the price, though the claim for the nonconformity survives.
  • Reasonable time tracks the time reasonably needed to inspect, which depends on the goods' complexity.
rule

Failure to particularize, § 2-605(1): failure to state a particular defect ascertainable by reasonable inspection bars the buyer from relying on it to justify rejection or establish breach (a) where the seller could have cured had it been stated seasonably; or (b) between merchants, when the seller after rejection has made a written request for a full and final written statement of all defects. The rejection is still effective, but may become wrongful, turning the seller's breach into the buyer's.

Problems 7-13, 7-14 matrix

Timely notice

Untimely notice

Right to reject

Rightful and effective. No acceptance. Seller breached. Buyer gets § 2-711 remedies. (If § 2-605 bars the defect: effective but wrongful, so buyer breached.)

Ineffective, so accepted. Buyer owes the price. Seller still breached: buyer has § 2-714 damages if § 2-607(3)(a) notice is given.

No right to reject

Wrongful but effective. No acceptance. Buyer breached; seller has § 2-703 remedies.

Accepted. No seller breach. Buyer owes the price.

sections.title: Problems
sections.html:
Problem 7-11 (1,000 bushels of Early Girl tomatoes, F.O.B. seller, ship by July 15)

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

(A)(1) 990 bushels on time

May reject all. Any shortfall fails to conform, absent a trade term or bad faith.

(A)(2) 10 bushels of the wrong variety

May reject all, for the same reason.

(A)(3) All shipped July 16

May reject: late shipment is a nonconforming tender. § 2-504's materiality limit covers carrier arrangements and notice, not a missed shipment date.

(A)(4) Shipped July 14; seller's bad instruction; arrives 4 days late

§ 2-504: improper contract with the carrier. Reject only if material delay or loss ensues. Four days is likely material for a perishable crop.

(B)(1) 50 bushels rotten: keep 950?

Yes, if a bushel is a commercial unit (§§ 2-601(c), 2-105(6)).

(B)(2) Keep only 500 good bushels?

Yes on the text: once the tender fails, buyer may accept any commercial units and reject the rest. Good faith is the only check.

(C)(1) Installments: first load 10 short; or 10 rotten; or 1 day late

Installment contract, so § 2-612(2). Rejecting all needs substantial impairment of that installment plus no cure. 10% short or rotten is curable, so buyer must accept with adequate assurance. One day late is unlikely to impair.

(C)(2) String of problems, then 10 wrong bushels in load 5: reject load 5 and cancel?

Rejecting load 5 alone is hard: 10% is curable. Cancelling needs substantial impairment of the whole, based on the pattern. Accepting earlier bad loads without notifying of cancellation reinstates the contract (§ 2-612(3)). Cancelling on this record is risky; a § 2-609 demand is the safer step.

7-12, 7-15 (not assigned)

Drafting: seller wants a materiality standard, a cure right, and short inspection and notice periods. Buyer of custom cranes wants clear inspection on each delivery, the right to reject each crane without proving impairment, and a long enough time. Cover what § 2-612 would otherwise control.

sections.title: XX. Cure, Care of Rejected Goods & Rejection Damages — §§ 2-508, 2-602 to 2-604, 2-711(3)
sections.html:
• After rejection the seller usually does one of three things: offers to cure, takes the goods back and refunds, or refuses to take them back.
rule

Seller's cure, § 2-508: (1) if the rejected tender was nonconforming and the time for performance has not expired, seller may seasonably notify buyer of its intent to cure and make a conforming delivery within the contract time. (2) If seller had reasonable grounds to believe the tender would be acceptable (with or without a money allowance), it may, on seasonable notice, have a further reasonable time to substitute a conforming tender.

  • One-way right. § 2-508 gives the seller a right to cure and imposes no duty. The buyer can't force a cure under § 2-508, though if the breach is a failure to repair, specific performance under § 2-716 might be available (p. 291 n.31). The contract can expand or limit cure.
  • What counts as cure: something that negates the breach and puts buyer where proper performance would have. It may be repair or replacement, depending on the breach. A cure that doesn't conform is no cure.
  • Late delivery can't be cured. Unless the seller can reverse time, buyer can only waive or settle.
  • After a cure, buyer may still claim damages for the delay (§§ 2-714(1), (3), 2-715). If buyer refuses a cure seller had a right to make, the result is unclear, perhaps a waiver of the curable breach.

sections.title: Care of rejected goods
sections.html:
• Buyer in possession is essentially a bailee (§ 2-401(4)) and must hold the goods with reasonable care for a time sufficient for the seller to remove them (§ 2-602(2)(b)).
  • Merchant buyer, § 2-603: when the seller has no agent or place of business at the market of rejection, must follow the seller's reasonable instructions and, absent instructions, make reasonable efforts to sell goods that are perishable or decline rapidly in value.
  • § 2-604: if seller gives no instructions, buyer may store, reship, or sell for the seller's account and remit the proceeds less expenses.
  • Security interest, § 2-711(3): a buyer that paid any of the price, or incurred expenses on the goods, has a lien and may hold the goods and resell under § 2-706. Cover or market damages are not part of what the lien secures; nor are consequential damages or some incidental damages.
  • §§ 2-602 to 2-604 appear limited to rightfully rejected goods, but a wrongful rejecter should still take reasonable care; its resale would probably be an acceptance (n.32).

sections.title: Using the goods after rejection
sections.html:
• Use beyond those rights risks being treated as acceptance (§ 2-606 cmt. 4) or conversion. Don't run rejected resin through production.
  • Unavoidable use is fine: the buyer can walk on rejected carpet over a weekend.
  • Evolving majority: use that is reasonable and necessary under the circumstances is neither acceptance nor conversion. Typical case: a consumer who must keep using a car or mobile home because the seller won't take it back.
note case

Johannsen v. Minnesota Valley Ford Tractor Co. (Minn. 1981) — factors for post-rejection use

Source: note case: the casebook quotes the opinion, p. 297 (n.34). No class slides.

Held: Reasonableness of the buyer's continued use is a jury question on all the facts. Factors: (1) the seller's instructions after revocation; (2) the buyer's economic and other hardship if use stopped; (3) whether use was a reasonable way to mitigate damages; (4) prejudice to the seller; (5) the seller's bad faith.

Why it matters: The checklist to run whenever a buyer keeps using goods it has rejected or revoked.

sections.title: Rejection and damages
sections.html: • After a rightful rejection the buyer stands as if the seller never delivered: refund of price paid, cover or market damages (§ 2-711), incidental and consequential damages (§ 2-715). Section XVIII applies.

sections.title: Problems
sections.html:
Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-16 Clause giving buyer a right to demand cure

Buyer wants it because Article 2 gives none, and custom equipment can't easily be replaced. Seller resists an open-ended duty, but would welcome it as an exclusive remedy limiting damages (§ 2-719).

7-17 Reasonable grounds to think the tender acceptable

Household example: buyer orders a washer; store delivers the newer model with better features at the same price, reasonably expecting buyer to be pleased. Buyer rejects; seller gets a further reasonable time to bring the model ordered. A past course of accepting similar substitutes also supports it.

7-18(A) Mirror falls off; dealer will reattach

Cure. A trivial defect is fully fixed by repair.

7-18(B)(1) New starter next day, no charge

Cure.

7-18(B)(2) Three business days, unless Barbara pays for express

Still likely cure within a further reasonable time; she need not pay for express shipping. See Travelers v. Maho (cited only).

7-18(C) Salvaged parts for a new car's exhaust

Likely no cure: used parts on a new car don't conform. Compare Bowen and Zabriskie with Wilson v. Scampoli (cited only). Outside class materials: Zabriskie is the "shaken faith" case; Wilson allowed a seller to try a minor repair.

7-18(D) Repeated electrical failures; dealer offers more repair; Barbara wants a new car

After repeated failed attempts seller's offer is likely not cure. She can't force a new car, but she can reject or revoke and get her money back with damages.

7-19 (not assigned)

Late bolts can't be cured, but an installment needs substantial impairment. Replacement next morning likely must be accepted under § 2-612(2). A pattern can justify cancelling the whole. Draft cure on buyer's option plus a defined termination trigger.

7-20 Bancroft keeps a scratched laptop and uses it on a trip

Installing software after seeing the scratch risks acceptance under § 2-606(1)(c). Use after rejection: apply Johannsen. Against Bancroft: seller said send it back, and the use was avoidable if another laptop could be found. For Bancroft: seller refused to replace first and the trip was close. Outcome is fact-dependent.

sections.title: XXI. Acceptance, Notice of Breach & § 2-714 Damages — §§ 2-606, 2-607, 2-714, 2-717
sections.html:
rule

Acceptance, § 2-606(1): buyer accepts when, after a reasonable opportunity to inspect, it
(a) signifies the goods conform or that it will keep them despite nonconformity;
(b) fails to make an effective rejection; or
(c) does any act inconsistent with the seller's ownership.

Effect of acceptance

Rule

Owes the price

§ 2-607(1)

Must notify of breach within a reasonable time or be barred from any remedy

§ 2-607(3)(a)

Bears the burden of proving breach

§ 2-607(4). (After rejection, the burden falls on whichever party sues.)

Loses the right to reject

§ 2-607(2)

Loses the right to cancel, and cover or market damages

Unless buyer revokes. An installment contract may differ: §§ 2-612(3), 2-711(1)

Gains value-difference damages + incidental and consequential

§§ 2-714, 2-715

  • Losing the right to reject means buyer can't force goods back on the seller to escape a falling market.

sections.title: Notice of breach
sections.html:
• Purposes (Aqualon v. MAC Equipment (4th Cir. 1998), quoted p. 301):
    (1) prevent surprise and let the seller recommend how to fix the problem;
    (2) let the seller investigate and prepare;
    (3) open the way to settlement;
    (4) protect against stale claims. Also lets the seller preserve rights against its own supplier (Hebron v. American Isuzu).
  • Because losing all remedies is draconian, courts are lenient, but many hold that some pre-suit notice is required; filing a complaint generally isn't enough. Reasonable time is a fact question (§§ 1-205, 1-202; Golden v. Den-Mat). Content: see § 2-607 cmt. 4.
  • Don't confuse: § 2-605 applies to rejected goods; § 2-607(3)(a) applies to accepted goods.
  • The parties may fix a reasonable time (§§ 1-205(b), 1-302). Whether they could dispense with notice altogether is an open question in the text.

sections.title: Damages for accepted goods
sections.html:
rule

§ 2-714:
(1) for any nonconforming tender (e.g., late or short), the loss resulting in the ordinary course of events, determined in any reasonable manner.
(2) For breach of warranty, value as warranted − value as accepted, at the time and place of acceptance, unless special circumstances show proximate damages of a different amount.
(3) Incidental and consequential damages in a proper case.

rule

Deducting from the price, § 2-717: on notifying the seller, buyer may deduct all or part of its damages from any price still due under the same contract.

  • Contract price plays no part in the § 2-714(2) formula. A buyer that struck a bad bargain keeps its bad bargain, and one that struck a good bargain keeps that too.
  • Repair cost is a common proxy for value difference, not the statutory test. The text asks whether cost of repair or cost of replacement better measures the lost expectancy. Where repair costs more than the drop in value, the seller argues for the smaller figure; if repair leaves the goods worth less, the buyer adds the leftover loss.
  • Consequential damages carry the same four limits as in Section XVIII and can far exceed the price.

sections.title: Problems
sections.html:
Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-21 Baker: replacement parts promised by April 4 haven't come

Trick: nothing was accepted, so § 2-607(3)(a) doesn't apply. No notice is required for nondelivery. Still tell Supplier about the mounting loss, demand delivery, and start looking for cover, which protects consequential damages.

7-22 Notice clause for kitchen appliances

Set a specific period running from when buyer discovers or should discover the defect (e.g., 30 days), and state how to give notice. Keep it reasonable: § 1-302(b) bars manifestly unreasonable time limits, and a clause that cuts off hidden-defect claims risks §§ 2-302, 2-719. Be more generous to consumers than to restaurants.

7-23(A) (not assigned) #1 tomatoes contract $10; tender #2; at acceptance #1 = $9, #2 = $7

($9 − $7) × 10,000 = $20,000 to deduct. The $10 contract price isn't used.

7-23(B) (not assigned) #1 = $12, #2 = $9

$3 × 10,000 = $30,000.

7-24(A) 500 rail cars at $20,000; repair $10,000; repaired value $19,000

Railroad's $11,000 is right only if cars as delivered were worth $9,000: it is using repair cost as a proxy for value lost. Seller answers that § 2-714(2) measures value, not cost. If delivered value was $15,000, damages are $5,000 per car; spending $10,000 on a $5,000 problem doesn't raise the measure, unless special circumstances apply.

7-24(B) Repair $10,000; repaired value $22,000

Railroad comes out ahead of what was promised ($22,000 vs. $20,000). Subtract the $2,000 betterment: $8,000.

7-25(A) (not assigned)

Add up: excess cost of replacement boards, cost of installing replacements, repair of sold computers, shipping, and disposal, then test each for foreseeability and proof. The future repairs of the remaining 3,000 computers raise certainty.

sections.title: XXII. Revocation of Acceptance — § 2-608
sections.html:
rule

§ 2-608(1): buyer may revoke acceptance of a lot or commercial unit whose nonconformity substantially impairs its value to him if he accepted it (a) on the reasonable assumption the nonconformity would be cured and it has not been seasonably cured; or (b) without discovery, where acceptance was reasonably induced by the difficulty of discovery or by the seller's assurances. § 2-608(2): within a reasonable time after buyer discovers or should have discovered the ground, and before any substantial change in the goods' condition not caused by their own defects. Not effective until buyer notifies seller.

Rejection

Revocation

Standard

Any nonconformity (§ 2-601)

Substantial impairment of value "to him"

Compared with § 2-612

—

§ 2-612 lacks "to him"; whether that changes the test is an open question in the text

Timing

Reasonable time after tender; shorter

Reasonable time after discovery; apparently longer (cmt. 4)

Notice content

§ 2-605 can bar unstated defects

No specific content required (cmt. 5)

Wrongful but effective?

Yes

No such thing. Revocation works only if it is both justified and properly notified (§ 2-709 cmt. 5)

Effect

Not an acceptance

Undoes the acceptance; not a cancellation (cmt. 1)

  • After a justified, effective revocation: buyer doesn't owe the price, may cancel, and has every remedy of a buyer that rightfully rejected (§ 2-711(1)), including the same rights and duties for goods in its possession and the § 2-711(3) lien (§ 2-608(3)).
  • Seller's cure after revocation is unsettled. The syllogism says yes: same rights and duties as rejection, and rejection allows cure. The answer: § 2-608(3) speaks of duties "with regard to the goods," not the seller's performance. And after § 2-608(1)(a) revocation, cure has already had its chance; a (1)(b) revocation may be different. See Lile v. Kiesel (Ind. Ct. App. 2007) (no right to cure after revocation) (cited only, n.44).

sections.title: Problems
sections.html:
Problem 7-26 (not assigned)

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

(A) Shirts discolor; 45 of 100 bolts used

Revoke for the unused bolts. For the 45 used, the change came from the defect only if discoloration is the defect, not from cutting and sewing. Commercial units help.

(B) Motorcycle burns up

The defect caused the change, so that bar doesn't apply. Revocation mostly adds the refund; injury is consequential.

(C) Promised fuel-line repair never made

§ 2-608(1)(a).

(D) Repeated leaks; roof to be sawn off

Each failed repair strengthens substantial impairment; refusing a major repair is reasonable.

(E) Assorted-color binders; replacements never come

Notably easy to see, so (1)(b) fails; (1)(a) fits.

Problem 7-27 (Steelsmith / Ballistics)

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

Was the machine accepted?

Likely yes. Two-hour test, "a little more time," then a month's use with the problem known by June 21: § 2-606(1)(a)–(c). So rejection is too late, and revocation is the question.

Can Ballistics revoke?

Yes, probably. 40 instead of 50 bullets a minute is substantial impairment to a buyer needing that rate. Acceptance was induced by difficulty of discovery: a two-hour test didn't show it, and even its engineers couldn't find the cause. July 1 notice is within a reasonable time after discovery, and the notice needs no particular content.

Must it accept repair?

Unsettled. § 2-508(1) is out: the time for performance has passed. § 2-508(2) needs reasonable grounds to think the tender acceptable. Lile says no cure after revocation; the syllogism says otherwise. If a court finds a cure right, refusing repair may be Ballistics' breach.

Use until September 1?

Reasonable and necessary under the Johannsen factors: keeps production going and mitigates. Expect an offset for value of the use.

Result

If revocation stands: Ballistics owes no balance, recovers the $125,000 down payment, and takes cover: $750,000 − $500,000 = $250,000 if Epoch's machine is a reasonable substitute and not an upgrade. It holds a § 2-711(3) lien on the machine for the money it paid. If revocation fails: it owes the $375,000 balance, less § 2-714(2) damages (machine at 50 per minute vs. 40), deducted under § 2-717.

7-28 Standard Plywood (not assigned)

Usage of trade may decide if 90 sheets per pallet conforms. 45 pallets instead of 50 is a shortfall, and inspection was wrongly refused. Selling for $80 and the 24-day delay raise acceptance and § 2-604 issues.

sections.title: XXIII. Privity & Remote Sellers — § 2-318
sections.html:
• A contract claim normally needs privity. Vertical privity: a buyer in the chain of title suing a seller further up the chain (consumer vs. manufacturer). Horizontal privity: a non-buyer outside the chain, injured by the goods. Vertical privity exists only between immediate links; a buyer who didn't buy directly from a seller is "remote."
  • First ask whether the remote seller made any warranty to this buyer. Express warranty under § 2-313? Implied warranty under § 2-314? Or a warranty to the distributor or retailer that extends to the buyer?
  • Article 2 barely addresses privity. § 2-318 offers three alternatives, and comment 3 leaves room for case law on the distributive chain.

§ 2-318

Who is protected

Injury covered

Vertical privity

Alt. A (majority)

Natural persons in buyer's family or household, or guests in buyer's home

Injury in person

Silent; left to case law

Alt. B

Any natural person reasonably expected to use, consume, or be affected

Injury in person

Implicitly abolished

Alt. C

Any person reasonably expected to use, consume, or be affected

"Injured": some states include property or economic loss

Eliminated

  • A seller can't exclude § 2-318's reach, but disclaimers and remedy limits that bind the buyer bind beneficiaries too (§ 2-318 cmt. 1). Section VI has the overview of § 2-318.
main case

Hyundai Motor America, Inc. v. Goodin (Ind. 2005) — no vertical privity for a consumer's implied warranty claim

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 328–337. No class slides.

Facts: Sandra Goodin bought a new Hyundai Sonata from a dealer, with a 5-year/60,000-mile manufacturer warranty. Brake trouble began almost at once, and eight months of repairs didn't fix it. Her lawyer sought a refund; she sued Hyundai under the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act. The jury found for Hyundai on express warranty but for Goodin on the implied warranty of merchantability, awarding $3,000. The Court of Appeals reversed for lack of privity, feeling bound by a footnote in Martin Rispens.

Held: Indiana doesn't require vertical privity between a consumer and a manufacturer for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability, even for economic loss. The footnote was dicta. Alternative A speaks only to horizontal privity and leaves vertical privity to the courts. Privity's freedom-of-contract rationale has "eroded to the point of invisibility" for many consumer goods: goods reach consumers through intermediaries; warranties are marketing tools; consumers expect merchantability; the law spreads the cost of lemons across all buyers; and a disclaimer in the dealer's buyer's order would otherwise leave her without a remedy. The privity bar began as a limit on tort claims (Winterbottom) and was undercut by MacPherson and Henningsen.

Why it matters: The modern consumer rule, but courts remain divided. Limits: it speaks to a consumer against a manufacturer, for goods subject to Magnuson-Moss. Damages are usually the § 2-714(2) value difference.

sections.title: After Goodin
sections.html:
• Express warranty: even privity states may not require it. A manufacturer shouldn't escape its public claims because the buyer bought through a dealer (p. 337).
  • Open questions when privity falls away (pp. 338–339): Can a remote buyer reject or revoke and get a refund from the manufacturer, and of which price? May it recover § 2-712 or § 2-713 damages? Must notice go to the manufacturer, or is notice to the retailer enough? Are consequential damages tested by what the manufacturer or the retailer knew? When does the limitations period start? Which state's law applies when only one has abolished privity? Does a distributor owe the same duty?
  • Only sellers make implied warranties. "Seller" = one who sells or contracts to sell (§ 2-103(1)(d)), and a sale passes title (§ 2-106(1)). Auctioneers, brokers, and other agents without title almost always aren't sellers.
  • Amazon: for third-party vendors' goods, courts have held Amazon isn't a seller and makes no warranty, despite listing, payment processing, storage, and shipping. The § 2-403(2) entrustment argument fails for three reasons: Amazon may never possess the goods, and the vendor's identity is disclosed; an entrustee isn't necessarily "the seller"; and Amazon's terms disclaim implied warranties anyway.

sections.title: Problems
sections.html:
Problem 7-31 (copier: Manufacturer warrants 3 years from purchase, sold June 1, 2021; Distributor disclaims all, sold Dec. 1, 2021; Retailer warrants 1 year, sold to Buyer April 1, 2022)

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

(A)(1) Privity abolished; fails Nov. 1, 2022

Retailer: yes, on the 1-year warranty (through April 1, 2023) and on merchantability, unless disclaimed. Manufacturer: yes, on its express warranty and implied warranty if they reach Buyer. Whether a warranty on order forms Buyer never saw extends to it is a real issue. Distributor: no; its disclaimer works and it binds those below it.

(A)(2) Fails Nov. 1, 2023

Retailer's 1-year warranty has expired. Implied warranty requires a defect at tender, and the four years hasn't run. Manufacturer's 3 years still runs on either reading of "date of purchase."

(A)(3) Fails Nov. 1, 2024

Manufacturer: covered only if "purchase" means Buyer's purchase (through April 1, 2025), not Distributor's (ended June 1, 2024). Implied warranties remain only if the defect existed at tender and suit is timely (§ 2-725).

(B) Privity not abolished

Implied claim only against Retailer. Express claim against Manufacturer may survive, though this warranty wasn't a public statement. Retailer has no recourse past Distributor's disclaimer: the gap privity creates.

(C) Fire destroys VP's home; no injury to anyone

VP isn't the buyer, so this is horizontal. Alt. A: no. VP isn't family, household, or a guest of a corporate buyer, and wasn't injured in person. Alt. B: no; property loss only. Alt. C: yes where "injured" includes property, against Retailer (and Manufacturer, since vertical privity is gone). Distributor still protected by disclaimer. Tort remains.

7-32 Homeowner and Renovator, privity state

Make Homeowner a party in privity with the appliance seller: have Homeowner buy directly, or have Renovator buy as Homeowner's agent. Or have Renovator assign its warranty rights to Homeowner (§ 2-210), and get the seller to name Homeowner an intended beneficiary. The renovation contract alone can't bind the seller. Add Renovator's own express warranty.

sections.title: XXIV. Seller's Remedies: Roadmap & When the Buyer Has the Goods — §§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702
sections.html:
• Buyer's basic duties: accept and pay in accordance with the contract (§ 2-301).
  • Walk the facts in order. Was the seller's refusal to tender justified (buyer failed to pay first, or to answer a proper demand for assurance)? Or was it a breach? Or does neither party breach, e.g., goods destroyed without fault? Is the buyer's breach excused? Are the seller's remedies limited?
  • § 2-703 is an incomplete catalog. It has no "and" or "or," so it doesn't say which remedies combine (cmt. 1). The answer comes from § 1-305: no overcompensation. As with the buyer, the remedies depend on the nature of the breach and who has the goods.

Situation

Seller's remedy

Cite

Buyer accepted and won't pay

The price + incidental damages. Buyer may offset for nonconformity (§§ 2-714, 2-717)

§§ 2-709, 2-607(1)

Buyer has goods; payment device fails; or buyer took goods on credit while insolvent

Limited reclamation

§§ 2-507, 2-702(2)

Seller has the goods or they are in transit: repudiation, failure to pay before delivery, wrongful rejection, refused cure, wrongful revocation

Withhold or stop delivery; cancel; resale, market, or lost-profit damages; rarely the price

§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705, 2-706, 2-708, 2-709

Any of these

Incidental damages, not consequential

§§ 2-710, 1-305(a)

rule

Action for the price, § 2-709(1): when buyer fails to pay the price as it becomes due, seller may recover the price, with incidental damages, of (a) goods accepted, or conforming goods lost or damaged within a commercially reasonable time after risk of loss passed to buyer; and (b) goods identified to the contract if seller is unable after reasonable effort to resell them at a reasonable price, or circumstances reasonably indicate that effort would be unavailing.

  • "Commercially reasonable time" limits only the lost-or-damaged goods, not accepted goods (p. 399 n.1).
  • Worked example (p. 400): custom sign, $6,400; accepted; color wrong; buyer spends $1,300 reprinting brochures to match. Buyer owes $6,400, less any § 2-714 value difference and, if recoverable under § 2-715, the $1,300, deducted under § 2-717.

sections.title: Getting goods back from a buyer that won't pay
sections.html:
• The general rule surprises people: an unpaid seller doesn't get the goods back. The principal right is the price, which is only as good as the buyer's ability to pay. Two exceptions:
  • (1) Article 9 security interest. The seller who takes one may repossess peaceably or by replevin on default (§ 9-609). One sentence creates it: "seller retains a security interest in the goods sold to secure the buyer's obligations under this agreement." A clause that seller "retains title" does the same thing and no more, because title passes on delivery and the reservation is limited to a security interest (§§ 1-201(b)(35), 2-401(1), 9-109(a)(5)).
  • (2) Reclamation. A restitutionary remedy, not an expectancy measure. Not self-help: if buyer doesn't return the goods voluntarily, seller must go to court.

§ 2-507 (failed payment)

§ 2-702(2) (credit sale to an insolvent)

When

Cash sale: payment due on delivery; payment device fails, e.g., a check bounces. A check at delivery counts (§ 2-511 cmts. 4–6). A credit sale or post-dated check does not

Seller sold on credit and discovers buyer received the goods while insolvent (§ 1-201(b)(23))

Deadline

Reasonable time after the payment fails

Demand within 10 days after receipt, unless buyer misrepresented solvency to this seller in writing within 3 months before delivery

Other remedies

No similar limit

Successful reclamation excludes all other remedies as to those goods (§ 2-702(3)), apparently even incidental damages

Subject to

Rights of good faith purchasers, covered in Chapter 10 (not assigned)

Buyers in ordinary course and good faith purchasers (§ 2-702(3))

  • Why the § 2-702(3) bar? Possibly reclamation rests on a rescission for fraud, so no expectancy remains; and the insolvent buyer's other creditors shouldn't be pushed further behind.
  • Practice point: a seller on credit should take a security interest; reclamation is too narrow to rely on.
  • Problem 9-1 (4,000 gallons of milk, into a vat with 5,000 others; half the vat becomes ice cream; demand June 7 for June 1 delivery): demand is within 10 days and the sale was on credit, so § 2-702(2) applies. Treat the milk as fungible: § 2-105(4) lets an undivided share of a bulk be identified. Supplier's share is 4/9. Half the vat remains (4,500 gallons), so Supplier can reclaim about 2,000 gallons. Nothing for the ice cream, which is no longer the goods sold. The casebook cites Wheeling-Pittsburgh and Charter and gives no answer; the result is worked from the statute.

sections.title: XXV. When the Seller Has the Goods: Withhold, Stop, Cancel — §§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705, 2-612
sections.html:
• Withhold = seller has the goods. Stop = a carrier or other bailee has them.
rule

Withholding: seller may withhold delivery if buyer
(1) wrongfully rejects,
(2) wrongfully revokes,
(3) fails to make a payment due, or
(4) repudiates (§ 2-703(a)). If seller discovers buyer is insolvent, it may refuse delivery except for cash, including payment for all goods already delivered under the contract (§ 2-702(1)).

rule

Stopping in transit, § 2-705(1): seller may stop delivery in a carrier's or bailee's possession when it discovers buyer's insolvency (any size of shipment). For repudiation, failure to make a payment due before delivery, or any other right to withhold or reclaim, it may stop only carload, truckload, planeload, or larger shipments. § 2-705(2): the right ends on buyer's receipt; a bailee's (non-carrier) acknowledgment to buyer that it holds for buyer; a carrier's such acknowledgment by reshipment or as a warehouse; or negotiation to buyer of a negotiable document of title.

  • Three questions:
    (1) does seller have the right as against buyer?
    (2) must the carrier obey?
    (3) who is liable if the carrier obeys or disobeys?
  • Carrier, § 2-705(3): seller must give notice enabling the carrier, by reasonable diligence, to prevent delivery. The carrier must then hold and deliver as seller directs, and seller is liable for ensuing charges or damages. If a negotiable document was issued, the carrier need not obey until the document is surrendered. A carrier with a nonnegotiable bill need not obey a stop order from anyone but the consignor.
  • Stopping is limited because of the burden on carriers (cmt. 1). Related: shipping under reservation (§ 2-505), which in effect gives seller a security interest and lets it withhold the goods until paid.
rule

Cancellation, § 2-703(f): in a non-installment contract, seller may cancel on any buyer breach. No notice is required. Cancellation ends future performance and doesn't waive damages (§ 2-106(4)). Installment contracts: seller may cancel the whole only if the breach substantially impairs the value of the whole contract (§§ 2-612(3), 2-703). Short of that it may demand assurance and suspend (§ 2-609; § 2-612 cmt. 6).

sections.title: Problems
sections.html:
Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

9-2(A) Diamonds shipped F.O.B. seller; negotiable bill naming seller as consignee; buyer misses funds transfer

A parcel isn't a carload, so nonpayment alone gives no right to stop. Only insolvency would. A default to its main lender is evidence of insolvency (§ 1-201(b)(23)) but not conclusive: ask whether buyer has generally ceased paying debts or can't pay as they come due. Holding the bill in its own name also gives seller practical control (§ 2-505).

9-2(B) Must Federated obey?

§ 2-705(3)(c): not until the negotiable bill is surrendered. If it delivers to buyer without the bill, it risks misdelivery liability to the holder, seller. It should hold and ask for the bill.

9-2(C) Nonnegotiable bill

§ 2-705(3)(d): the carrier need not obey anyone but the consignor. Seattle Gems is the consignor, so Federated must follow § 2-705(3)(b), with seller liable for charges and damages. Rightfulness against buyer is still the question in Part A.

9-3 500 stoves in two lots; first 250 accepted; $20,000 check bounces; 250 in warehouse

Advise: (1) withhold the second lot (§ 2-703(a)). (2) Sue for the $20,000 due; a bounced check leaves the debt alive. (3) Possible § 2-507 reclamation, but only the 20% was due on delivery, so it is at best a partial cash sale, and act fast. (4) Check insolvency (§ 2-702): cash terms, and a 10-day demand if goods came on credit while insolvent. (5) Demand adequate assurance (§ 2-609) and suspend. (6) Cancel only if the breach substantially impairs the whole (§ 2-612(3)). Failure to give assurance within 30 days is repudiation, which supports cancelling and reselling the 250.

sections.title: XXVI. Seller's Damages — §§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708, 2-709, 2-710
sections.html:
• Four alternatives, all protecting the expectancy (§ 1-305), all with incidental damages: resale, market, lost profit, price. Seller can't stack resale and market.
  • Worked example (pp. 408–410): $10,000 lithograph, buyer defaults. Worth $9,000: resell and get $1,000 (§ 2-706), or keep it and get $1,000 (§ 2-708(1)). Worth $11,000 or $10,000: no resale or market damages. Unlimited supply: the resale isn't a substitute, because Dealer would have made both sales, so its loss is the profit on one extra sale (§ 2-708(2)). Nobody else wants it: the price (§ 2-709), and buyer gets the print.
  • Market damages are the more traditional remedy: they resemble the seller reselling to itself at market (n.11).

Measure

Formula

Key conditions

Plus / less

Resale § 2-706

Contract − resale

Good faith; commercially reasonable in every aspect; notice

+ incidental − saved

Market § 2-708(1)

Contract − market at time and place for tender

Proof of market price (§§ 2-723, 2-724)

+ incidental − saved

Lost profit § 2-708(2)

Profit (including reasonable overhead) + costs reasonably incurred

§ 2-708(1) inadequate; typically lost-volume sellers

+ incidental

Price § 2-709

Contract price

Accepted, or lost after risk passed, or can't be resold at a reasonable price

+ incidental; hold goods for buyer

sections.title: Resale — § 2-706
sections.html:
rule

§ 2-706: where resale is in good faith and commercially reasonable, seller may recover contract price − resale price, + incidental damages, − expenses saved. Every aspect (method, manner, time, place, terms) must be commercially reasonable, and the resale must be reasonably identified as referring to the broken contract. Private sale: reasonable notification to buyer of the intent to resell (§ 2-706(3)). Public sale (auction):
(1) only identified goods unless there is a recognized futures market;
(2) at a usual place if available;
(3) reasonable notice of time and place, except perishables;
(4) goods available for inspection if not in view;
(5) seller may buy.

  • Resale isn't required. Seller resells because market price may be hard to prove and the resale price is known, and because sellers rarely want the goods.
  • A bad resale doesn't cost seller its claim. It only loses this measure and falls back on § 2-708 (§ 2-706 cmt. 2).
  • Good-faith purchaser takes free of the original buyer, even if seller botched the requirements (§ 2-706(5)). Seller keeps any profit on resale (§ 2-706(6)).
  • Unidentified goods: the goods need not exist or be identified at breach (§ 2-706(2)), and § 2-704(1) lets seller identify conforming goods in its possession or control when it learned of the breach. With fungible goods, proving which sale replaced the broken contract can be hard, like a buyer proving which purchase was cover. Wisconsin Cranberry v. Groupe Alimonco (Wis. Ct. App. 2016): other sales weren't substitutes (different product, special contracts, much smaller load). Apex Oil v. Belcher (2d Cir. 1988): resale six weeks later unusable; delay unreasonable and seller had sold conforming oil the next day (cited only, n.15).
rule

Unfinished goods, § 2-704(2): seller may, in the exercise of reasonable commercial judgment to avoid loss and for effective realization, either complete manufacture and wholly identify the goods, or cease and resell for scrap or salvage, or proceed in any other reasonable manner. § 2-704(1)(b) lets it resell unfinished goods demonstrably intended for the contract.

sections.title: Market — § 2-708(1)
sections.html:
rule

§ 2-708(1): unpaid contract price − market price at the time and place for tender, + incidental damages, − expenses saved. Ignore the word "unpaid" for now: prepayments are handled separately (Section XXVII). The formulas are "strongly worded suggestions"; if one misses the expectancy, follow § 1-305.

  • Seller's timing rule differs from the buyer's: time for tender, not when the party learned of the breach. The text asks why a seller treating repudiation as an immediate breach must wait for a later price.
  • § 2-723(1) exception: if a repudiation case comes to trial before the time for performance, use the price when seller learned of the repudiation.
  • Proof is hard for unique goods and easy for fungibles with published quotations (§ 2-724).
note case

Peace River Seed Coop. v. Proseeds Marketing (Or. 2014) — market damages after a resale

Source: note case: the casebook quotes it in nn.17–18, p. 415. No class slides.

Held: An aggrieved seller may claim § 2-708(1) market damages even if it resold and market damages exceed resale damages. A fixed-price contract allocates market risk, so market damages are what the parties bargained for. A seller isn't required to resell, so mitigation can't force it to use the resale price, and the UCC rejects election of remedies.

Why it matters: Answers the question the text poses: resale and market are alternatives, but resale doesn't necessarily lock the seller into its resale price. Counterargument: § 1-305 forbids a recovery above the seller's real loss, and the resale shows that loss. A seller can avoid § 2-706 simply by not identifying the resale to the broken contract (n.19).

  • Resale price vs. market price: the difference may reflect the passage of time (who bears that risk?) or the seller's negotiating skill. If seller recovers market damages and later resells higher, § 2-706(6) suggests no accounting.

sections.title: Lost profit — § 2-708(2)
sections.html:
rule

§ 2-708(2): if § 2-708(1) is inadequate to put seller in as good a position as performance, damages = the profit (including reasonable overhead) seller would have made, + incidental damages, + due allowance for costs reasonably incurred, and due credit for payments or proceeds of resale.

  • Remedy of last resort, and implicitly available only if resale damages are also inadequate.
  • Lost-volume seller: a jobber with unlimited supply is the clearest case; the breach costs it one sale, and any resale would have happened anyway.
note case

R.E. Davis Chem. Corp. v. Diasonics, Inc. (7th Cir. 1987) — who is a lost-volume seller

Source: note case: the casebook quotes the opinion, p. 418 (n.20). No class slides.

Held: Capacity alone isn't enough. Ask not only whether seller could have produced the breached units on top of its actual volume, but whether it would have been profitable to do so. Under diminishing returns, at some volume the next sale stops being worthwhile, and awarding presumed lost profit would overcompensate.

Why it matters: A manufacturer must show capacity and profitability. The usual test on an exam.

Lost-profit math (pp. 419–421)

Why

Profit = sale price − fixed costs − variable costs

Fixed = overhead (rent, CEO salary). Variable = rises with output (raw materials)

Statute adds overhead back: recovery = sale price − variable costs

Saves allocating overhead to one contract

Add unreimbursed reliance costs: recovery = sale price − variable costs + unreimbursed reliance

"Due allowance for costs reasonably incurred": money already spent that seller can't recover, because it gets only profit, not the price

Ignore "due credit for ... proceeds of resale"

Likely a drafting mistake. Applied literally it would almost always leave a lost-volume seller with nothing, contrary to § 1-305

  • Wages and utilities can go either way: fixed if the sale was small against normal output; variable if it needed overtime. Tax treatment has little bearing.
  • Direct, not consequential. A seller's lost profit comes from the breached contract itself, so foreseeability and mitigation limits generally don't apply (contrast a buyer's lost profits on resale, which are consequential).
  • Lost profit is no ceiling. A buyer can't use a low or zero profit to cut market or resale damages: § 2-708(2) applies only when other measures are inadequate, not when they are higher (Trans World Metals v. Southwire (7th Cir. 1985), the leading case, n.26).
  • Problem 9-8 (not assigned): lathe sold for $90,000; cost $80,000 + $2,000 parts + $1,500 preparation. Lost profit = $90,000 − $83,500 = $6,500 (the $500 overhead isn't deducted). Add unreimbursed reliance: $1,000 cancellation fee + $1,200 parts it can't reuse ($2,000 − $800) = $8,700. Market damages are zero ($90,000 market), and § 2-708(1) is inadequate if Sawtooth is lost-volume.

sections.title: The price, when the seller keeps the goods
sections.html:
• Why the price? If seller truly can't resell, resale price is meaningless, market price may not be $0, and lost profit leaves seller stuck with its production costs. So § 2-709(1)(b) gives the contract price.
  • Seller must hold the goods for buyer while suing. If resale becomes possible it may resell before collecting; net proceeds are credited. Payment of the judgment entitles buyer to any goods not resold (§ 2-709(2)).
  • If seller is held not entitled to the price, it still gets § 2-708 damages (§ 2-709(3)).
note case

Foxco Indus. v. Fabric World, Inc. (5th Cir. 1979) — "unable to resell at a reasonable price"

Source: note case: the casebook quotes the opinion, pp. 423–424 (n.27). No class slides.

Held: Seller of specially made spring fabric needed only reasonable efforts to resell at a reasonable price. The goods were made for a customer, were hard to sell after the spring season, and the market fell 50%. The jury could find seller acted reasonably even though it made little resale effort for months and sold part only the next season.

Why it matters: Goods need not be worthless. The test is reasonable effort and a reasonable price, and market collapse and seasonality count.

sections.title: Incidental damages, no consequential damages
sections.html:
rule

§ 2-710: commercially reasonable charges, expenses, or commissions incurred in stopping delivery, in transporting and caring for the goods after breach, in connection with return or resale, or otherwise resulting from the breach. No consequential damages for sellers absent a provision: § 1-305(a), and most courts agree (Validsa v. PDVSA, n.28). So separating incidental from consequential matters. The nature of the loss counts, not its amount: incidental storage costs reached $293 million in Commonwealth Edison v. Allied Chem. (n.29).

sections.title: Problems
sections.html:
Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

9-4(A) Instructions for reselling used copiers

Decide private vs. auction. Private: send buyer notice of intent to resell. Auction: give time and place, make the machines available to inspect, use a usual place. Identify each resale to the broken contract in your records. Resell promptly in the normal channels, on normal terms, at the best reasonable price. Don't delay for a better market; keep records.

9-4(B) 100,000 gal, $5, F.O.B. Miami, 10¢ freight saved. Resold $4.75 F.O.B. Cincinnati; storage $1,000

($5.00 − $4.75) × 100,000 = $25,000 + $1,000 incidental − $10,000 freight saved = $16,000. The 2¢ to Cleveland is the new buyer's cost under F.O.B. Cincinnati.

9-5 $6,400 sign; $4,000 spent, $800 to finish. Salvage nets $100; or $2,000 to modify, 50% chance of $5,000

Salvage: lost profit $1,600 + costs incurred $4,000 − $100 = $5,500 from buyer, plus $100 salvage = $5,600, the same as finishing a paid contract ($6,400 − $800). Modify: expected return 50% × $5,000 = $2,500 − $2,000 = $500, vs. $100. Better on expected value by $400 to $450, depending on salvage if unsold, so it is defensible under § 2-704(2). If the sale works, buyer owes about $2,600; if not, about $7,500. Seller's risk: if a court finds it unreasonable, it eats the $2,000. Salvage is the safe choice. Finishing for $800 makes no sense: no one else wants the sign.

9-6(A) Repudiated Feb. 15; shipment by Feb. 25; delivery by March 1. Market $4 (Feb. 15), $4.25 (Feb. 25), $4.50 (March 1). Resale March 7 at $4.75; notice given

Resale valid: $16,000 as in 9-4(B). Market: F.O.B. destination means tender at Miami on March 1: ($5.00 − $4.50) × 100,000 = $50,000 + $1,000 − $10,000 = $41,000. Under Peace River seller may take market damages despite resale; a court applying § 1-305 strictly would hold it to $16,000.

9-6(B) No notice of resale

Private sale without notice fails § 2-706(3), so § 2-708(1): $41,000. The $4.75 can still be evidence of market value, and § 2-706(6) means no accounting for the difference.

9-7(A) 10,000 gal/yr at $5 for 10 yrs; repudiated Year 6; trial August Year 9

Years 7–9 are past due at trial: use tender-date prices. Year 10 isn't due: § 2-723(1) uses the price when seller learned of repudiation, $4.00. Per gallon, less 10¢ saved: Y7 $0.80, Y8 $0.70, Y9 $0.50, Y10 $0.90 = $2.90 × 10,000 = $29,000.

9-7(B) Trial in Year 11; Year 10 market $5.50

§ 2-723(1) doesn't apply. Y7–Y9 = $20,000. Year 10 is above contract, so no damages for that year; netting its $0.60 gain per gallon, as § 1-305 suggests, gives $14,000. Which one depends on whether the contract is treated as a whole.

9-9(A) Custom container, $3,000; cost $1,800; best offer $1,500; standard units $2,000

Probably no action for the price: $1,500 may be a reasonable price for a customized container, so seller can resell. Resale damages: $3,000 − $1,500 = $1,500 + incidental. If $1,500 isn't reasonable, § 2-709(1)(b). The dollars are similar either way.

9-9(B) Only scrap at $500

Yes: scrap isn't resale at a reasonable price. Recover $3,000, hold the container for buyer, and credit net proceeds if it is sold (§ 2-709(2)).

9-11(A) Pre-breach loan for general operations

Not incidental: an ordinary business cost, unrelated to the breach.

9-11(B) Pre-breach loan to finance this contract

Not incidental: incurred regardless of the breach. It is a cost of performance, which is recovered, if at all, through the price or as reliance.

9-11(C) Post-breach loan for an investment planned with the price

Consequential, so not recoverable: lost use of the money.

9-11(D) Post-breach loan to finish the machine and resell it

Strongest case: "in connection with ... resale" under § 2-710, and the finishing is authorized by § 2-704(2).

sections.title: XXVII. Prepaying Buyers, Casualty & Limitations — §§ 2-718(2)–(4), 2-709(1)(a), 2-510(3), 2-725
sections.html:
rule

Restitution to a breaching buyer, § 2-718(2)–(3): when seller justifiably withholds delivery because of buyer's breach, buyer gets back any amount by which its payments exceed (a) enforceable liquidated damages (§ 2-718(1)); or (b) with no such term, 20% of the value of its total performance or $500, whichever is smaller. Buyer's right is offset to the extent seller establishes (a) a right to damages under other Article 2 provisions and (b) benefits buyer received. Payment in goods counts at its value or resale proceeds (§ 2-718(4)).

  • It works as a type of statutory liquidated damages. Sellers may keep the statutory amount without proving harm, or prove larger damages and offset them.
  • Example (Problem 9-12, not assigned): $90,000 lathe, $20,000 down; market $80,000 at tender. (A) Valid $10,000 LD: return $10,000. (B) No LD: the statutory retention is $500, the smaller of that and 20%, and seller may offset damages it proves (§ 2-718(3)), such as market damages ($90,000 − $80,000) or lost profit, plus incidental damages. Compare Neri v. Retail Marine with McCann v. McSorley (cited only).
  • Problem 9-13 (not assigned): after a wrongful revocation with goods returned: pick market vs. resale at the right place, add storage and freight, and subtract the $20,000 down payment. Note that buyer took and revoked, so § 2-718(2) (withheld delivery) doesn't fit neatly, but the § 1-305 result is the same.

sections.title: Casualty to the goods — p. 428
sections.html:
• Risk of loss principles (Section IX): the party in control, the party likely to be insured, and the party in breach should bear the risk.
  • If risk has passed to buyer and conforming goods are lost or damaged within a commercially reasonable time, buyer owes the price (§ 2-709(1)(a)). Typical case: a shipment contract with loss in transit.
rule

§ 2-510(3): if buyer repudiates or breaches as to conforming goods already identified before risk passes, seller may, to the extent of any deficiency in its effective insurance coverage, treat risk of loss as resting on buyer for a commercially reasonable time.

  • Both parties can hold an insurable interest in identified goods (§ 2-501). After an unjustified revocation Article 2 is silent; presumably risk returns to seller once it takes the goods back (n.30).
  • Problem 9-14 (not assigned): (A) lathes identified, buyer repudiates Oct. 28, lightning fire that night: buyer bears the loss to the extent of any insurance shortfall. (B) In a shipment contract risk passed on tender to the carrier, so transit damage is buyer's loss, and rejection and revocation fail because the goods conformed at tender. Seller gets the price, and buyer's recourse is against the carrier.

sections.title: Statute of limitations — p. 430
sections.html:
rule

§ 2-725: four years; the cause of action accrues when the breach occurs, regardless of the aggrieved party's knowledge. A warranty is breached on tender, unless it explicitly extends to future performance and discovery must await that performance. The parties may shorten the period to not less than one year, and can't extend it.

  • Buyer's breach usually occurs when it fails to pay or wrongfully rejects. After repudiation the seller may wait a commercially reasonable time, and that time is uncertain, so sue within four years of the repudiation.
  • Whether § 2-725 governs a secured seller's deficiency suit is split (nn.31–32).

sections.title: XXVIII. Leases: Scope & Lease vs. Sale — §§ 2A-103, 1-203
sections.html:
• Article 2A (1990) governs leases of goods and is modeled on Article 2, so the study question is where it differs, and why. The differences come from one fact: in a lease the lessor gets the goods back.
rule

Lease, § 2A-103(1)(j): a transfer of the right to possession and use of goods for a term in return for consideration. A sale, a retained security interest, and similar deals are not leases. A sale passes title (§ 2-106(1)); a lease transfers only limited rights, and the lessor keeps a residual interest.

sections.title: Why the sale/lease line matters
sections.html:
Issue

True lease

Disguised sale (security interest)

Governing law

Article 2A

Articles 2 and 9

Tax

Lessor is tax owner, takes depreciation; rent is lessor's income and potentially deductible by lessee

Buyer is tax owner; payments not deductible as rent; seller may have gain or loss

Lessee's bankruptcy

Lessee keeps goods only by performing the lease

Buyer may keep goods paying over time the amounts due or the goods' value, whichever is less

Third parties

Lessor needs no public filing

Seller is a secured party and must perfect, typically by filing. Filing a protective financing statement is not evidence it's a sale (§ 9-505; n.3)

  • Form and intent don't control. Economic substance does (§§ 1-203, 2A-102, 9-109(a)(1)).
rule

§ 1-203(a): lease or security interest is decided on the facts of each case. The real question: is there a reasonable chance the lessor gets the goods back while they still have meaningful economic value? Yes = lease. No = sale with a retained security interest.

rule

§ 1-203(b) bright-line test: a transaction in lease form creates a security interest if the lessee's payment obligation is for the term and not terminable by the lessee, and
(1) original term ≥ remaining economic life of the goods;
(2) lessee is bound to renew for the remaining economic life or is bound to become owner;
(3) lessee may renew for the remaining economic life for no or nominal additional consideration; or
(4) lessee may become owner for no or nominal additional consideration. If this isn't met, go back to the facts under (a).

  • § 1-203(c) "not merely because": none of these alone creates a security interest:
    (1) the PV of rent equals or exceeds the goods' value at signing;
    (2) lessee takes risk of loss;
    (3) lessee pays taxes, insurance, fees, or maintenance;
    (4) lessee has an option to renew or buy;
    (5) a renewal option at or above predictable fair market rent;
    (6) a purchase option at or above predictable fair market value.
  • § 1-203(d) nominal: consideration is nominal if it is less than the lessee's reasonably predictable cost of performing under the lease if the option isn't exercised. It is not nominal if the option price or rent is stated to be fair market value or rent determined when the option is performed.
  • § 1-203(e): remaining economic life and predictable value are judged when the transaction is entered into.
  • 99-year laptop (p. 466): a lease in form, but the goods are dead long before the term ends: a sale.

sections.title: Problems
sections.html:
Problem 11-1 ($200,000 skid loader; construction company pays maintenance, insurance, and the entire $200,000 even if it returns early)

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

Threshold

Payment isn't terminable, so go through § 1-203(b)'s four prongs. Maintenance, insurance, and full payout alone don't make a sale (§ 1-203(c)).

(A)(1) 5 years, $3,900/mo; goods return to dealer

If five years is under the economic life, (b) isn't met. On the facts a five-year-old loader likely has real value, so it's a lease.

(A)(2) Option to buy at $5,000

Is $5,000 nominal? Compare it with the predictable cost of returning (§ 1-203(d)) and with predictable value. If the loader should be worth far more than $5,000, exercise is near certain and it looks like a sale, but this one needs facts.

(A)(3) Option at $100

Nominal. § 1-203(b)(4) met: sale with a security interest.

(B) 25 years, $2,000/mo; goods return

The term likely exceeds economic life, so § 1-203(b)(1): sale.

(C) Lessee may return early with no more payments

Not "non-terminable," so the bright-line test fails in every scenario. Go to the facts under (a). A low option price is still a sign of a sale, but the lessor bears real return risk, so likely a lease.

sections.title: Hybrids and other law
sections.html:
• Hybrid leases, § 2A-102 (2022 Amendments): mirrors § 2-102(2). If the lease-of-goods aspects predominate, Article 2A applies. If not, only the provisions relating primarily to the lease-of-goods aspects apply. A consumer's cable box with cable service is an example. The goods part can be a finance lease (cmt. 6).
  • Other law: Article 2A generally defers to certificate-of-title and consumer-protection law (§§ 2A-104, 2A-105; 15 U.S.C. §§ 1667–1667f; Regulation M). Magnuson-Moss and lemon laws might not apply to leases, one reason sellers structure deals as leases. No international convention governs leases of goods.

sections.title: XXIX. Finance Leases — §§ 2A-103(1)(g), 2A-209, 2A-407
sections.html:
• The idea: the lessee picks the goods from a supplier; a bank or other financer buys them (Article 2 applies to that purchase) and leases them to the lessee. The goods usually go straight to the lessee. In form the financer is a lessor; in substance a lender. It wants no responsibility for quality, and the lessee looks to the supplier.
  • The lease must still be a true lease under § 1-203. Because a finance lessor needs a real residual but doesn't want the goods, these leases often give the lessee a fair-market-value purchase option (n.6).
rule

Finance lease, § 2A-103(1)(g): (i) lessor doesn't select, manufacture, or supply the goods; (ii) lessor acquires the goods or the right to them in connection with the lease; and (iii) one of: (A) lessee receives a copy of the supply contract before signing; (B) lessee's approval of the supply contract is a condition of the lease's effectiveness; (C) lessee receives, before signing, an accurate and complete statement of the supplier's promises, warranties, disclaimers, and remedy limits; or (D) in a non-consumer lease, lessor informs lessee in writing of the supplier's identity and of lessee's rights to the promises and warranties.

Finance lease rule

Ordinary lease

Finance lease

Implied merchantability and fitness

Lessor makes them (§§ 2A-212, 2A-213)

Finance lessor makes neither. May give express warranties, but rarely does

Supplier's warranties

No special rule

Flow to lessee to the extent of its leasehold, subject to the supply contract's terms, disclaimers, and defenses (§ 2A-209(1))

Infringement warranty

Merchant lessor gives it (§ 2A-211(2))

Not given

Interference warranty

Yes (§ 2A-211(1))

Yes, for claims arising from lessor's own act or omission

Duty to pay

Lessee may deduct damages from rent (§ 2A-508(6))

Hell or high water on acceptance if non-consumer (§ 2A-407)

Risk of loss

Stays with lessor (§ 2A-219(1))

Passes to lessee (§ 2A-219)

Revocation

Like § 2-608

Only for lessor's assurances, non-consumer (§§ 2A-517, 2A-516(2))

rule

Hell or high water, § 2A-407: in a non-consumer finance lease, the lessee's promises become irrevocable and independent upon acceptance of the goods. They bind assignees and third parties and aren't subject to cancellation, termination, modification, repudiation, excuse, or substitution without the consent of the party to whom the promise runs. Other law may validate an express covenant (§ 2A-407(3)), which is how consumer leases and backup clauses work.

  • § 2A-209(3): a modification or rescission of the supply contract binds lessee unless supplier had notice of the finance lease; if it binds lessee, lessor assumes the old promises. § 2A-209(4): lessee keeps its own rights against supplier.
  • Common-law defenses may survive: a fraudulent-inducement claim might defeat a hell-or-high-water clause (Faust Printing, n.13).
  • Hybrid: if the goods aspect doesn't predominate, § 2A-407 covers only the goods portion. Allocate payments in the lease, or make the whole obligation irrevocable. Express hell-or-high-water clauses are common as backup (n.14).

sections.title: Problems
sections.html:
Problem 11-3 (Lasting Data negotiates 30 servers with Sensational; Boston Finance edits the draft, buys, and leases to Lasting; servers fail)

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

(A) Finance lease?

(i) Boston didn't select or supply: Lasting chose; editing the draft doesn't change that. (ii) Boston acquired the goods in connection with the lease. (iii) Lasting saw the draft, not the final contract with Boston's changes, so (A) is doubtful. Look for (B), (C), or (D). Likely yes, if one is satisfied.

(B) Sensational's warranties to Lasting

Express warranties and merchantability, flowing through § 2A-209(1). Fitness is disclaimed, and the disclaimer binds Lasting.

(C) Boston's warranties

No implied warranties (§§ 2A-212, 2A-213); no express ones on these facts. Only § 2A-211(1) interference.

(D) Supply deal is a lease, not a sale

Same result. § 2A-209 applies to a supply contract by which the lessor buys or leases goods.

(E) Lasting must buy at the end

Bound to become owner + non-terminable: § 1-203(b)(2) makes it a sale with a security interest. Article 2A and § 2A-209 drop out. Boston is a seller: implied merchantability only if it is a merchant in such goods; disclaim under § 2-316. Lasting's claim against Sensational now hits vertical privity (Section XXIII).

11-4(A) Effect of § 2A-407

If Lasting accepted, it must keep paying Boston despite the defects, and pursue Sensational. If it validly rejected before accepting, § 2A-407 isn't triggered.

11-4(B) Drafting for Boston

An express hell-or-high-water clause (§ 2A-407(3)) as backup; a signed acceptance certificate; waiver of setoff and defenses against the lessor and assignees; a disclaimer of all warranties; assignment of supplier warranties to lessee; default remedies. See Wells Fargo v. B.C.B.U. (cited only).

sections.title: XXX. Lease Formation & Terms — Article 2A Parts 1–2
Formation
sections.html: • Same as Article 2 (§§ 2A-103(1)(k)–(l), 2A-204 to 2A-206), with no analog to § 2-206(1)(b) (prompt-shipment orders), to § 2-207 (battle of the forms), or to the CISG. Why: lessees rarely send orders, and leases are negotiated rather than exchanged on forms.
