  • 2022 Amendments: a signed record replaces a signed writing. UETA reaches the same result elsewhere. Satisfying the statute doesn't prove a lease exists.

sections.title: Unconscionability
sections.html:
• §§ 2A-108(1), (3) repeat § 2-302. Consumer leases add relief for procedural unconscionability: unconscionable conduct inducing the contract or in collecting a claim, with no need for substantive unconscionability (§ 2A-108(2)), and attorney's fees for a consumer lessee who prevails (§ 2A-108(4)).
  • Consumer lease, § 2A-103(1)(e): a lessor regularly in the business of leasing or selling makes a lease to an individual primarily for personal, family, or household purposes [states may set a dollar cap].

sections.title: Terms and gap fillers
sections.html:
• Same concepts of agreement, course of performance, course of dealing, usage of trade, and good faith (§§ 1-303, 1-304). The casebook still cites § 2A-207, but the 2026 statutes show that section deleted, with its rule now in § 1-303.
  • Few gap fillers. Nothing like §§ 2-304, 2-305, 2-306, 2-307, 2-308, 2-309, 2-310, 2-311, 2-503, 2-504, 2-505. Leases tend to be more complete, and no near-universal default exists. The common law fills gaps (§ 1-103).
  • Consumer leases: limits on choice of law and forum (§ 2A-106), which don't reach arbitration.

sections.title: Warranties
sections.html:
• Express (§ 2A-210), merchantability (§ 2A-212), fitness (§ 2A-213): same as Article 2, except a finance lessor gives no implied warranties.
  • Disclaimers: § 2A-214 tracks § 2-316, except that a merchantability disclaimer must also be in writing and conspicuous. It also has an express rule for disclaiming the interference and infringement warranties (§ 2A-214(4)).
  • Third parties: § 2A-216 tracks § 2-318, separate from § 2A-209.
  • Title analog: § 2A-211(1) warranty against interference: no claim arising from the lessor's act or omission will interfere with the leasehold. Compare § 2-312.

Liquidating consequential damages

Expressly may be liquidated or limited (§ 2A-503(3))

Liquidated damages test

Reasonable in light of anticipated or actual harm, difficulty of proof, inconvenience of other remedy (§ 2-718(1))

§ 2A-202, almost identical

Modification

sections.title: XXXI. Lease Performance — Risk of Loss, Excuse & Transfers
sections.html: • Insecurity and repudiation: §§ 2A-401 to 2A-403 follow §§ 2-609 to 2-611.

sections.title: Risk of loss
sections.html:
rule

§ 2A-219: in an ordinary lease, risk stays with the lessor. In a finance lease, risk passes to the lessee, at the time agreed or, if none,
(a) on delivery to the carrier, or tender at the named destination;
(b) on the bailee's acknowledgment of the lessee's right to possession;
(c) otherwise on the lessee's receipt if the lessor, or in a finance lease the supplier, is a merchant; if not, on tender. Parties often shift the risk to the lessee by agreement.

  • Why different from sales? Both parties hold property rights for the whole term, so the question isn't when risk passes but who carries it during the lease.
  • Default, § 2A-220: a nonconforming tender leaves risk on lessor or supplier until cure or acceptance. A rightful revocation lets lessee treat risk as lessor's from the start, to the extent of any insurance shortfall. If lessee repudiates or defaults as to conforming identified goods, lessor or supplier may put risk on lessee for a commercially reasonable time, to the extent of its insurance shortfall.
  • Insurable interest: lessee on identification (§§ 2A-217, 2A-218(1)–(2)). Lessor keeps one until lessee has exercised a purchase option and risk of loss has passed (§ 2A-218(3)). Parties may agree who insures and who takes proceeds (§ 2A-218(5)).

sections.title: Excuse
sections.html:
• § 2A-221 tracks § 2-613, § 2A-404 tracks § 2-614, §§ 2A-405, 2A-406 track §§ 2-615, 2-616.
  • Finance-lease twist: a non-consumer finance lessee that takes damaged goods, or accepts part of a quota, pays full rent, consistent with § 2A-407.

sections.title: Assignment and delegation — § 2A-303
sections.html:
• Lessor's assignment of the right to payment, with or without the residual, is an Article 9 transaction. Anti-assignment clauses generally don't stop the transfer or create a default (§§ 2A-303(2), 9-406(d), 9-407).
  • Lessee's transfer of possession: if the lease makes it a default, lessor has default remedies (§ 2A-303(4)(a)). If it merely prohibits it, the transfer is effective unless damages would be inadequate (§ 2A-303(4)(b)).
  • Delegation doesn't release the rent duty (§ 2A-303(6); compare § 2-210(1)).

sections.title: XXXII. Lessor's Default & Lessee's Remedies — §§ 2A-508 to 2A-522
sections.html:
• Default comes from the agreement and Article 2A (§ 2A-501). Lessee's remedies are in § 2A-508, and the parties may add others. No general duty to notify of default, with exceptions (§ 2A-502).

Lessee's position

Remedy

Compare Article 2

Goods not delivered

Specific performance or replevin (§ 2A-521)

§ 2-716. Standard largely the same

Prepaid, identified goods

Recover if lessor insolvent within 10 days after first payment (§ 2A-522)

§ 2-502(1)(b). No consumer prepayment analog to § 2-502(1)(a)

Cancel

Non-installment: any default (§§ 2A-508(1)(a), 2A-505). Installment: substantial impairment of the whole (§ 2A-510(2))

§§ 2-711, 2-612(3)

Recover rent and security paid

Only so much as is just under the circumstances (§ 2A-508(1)(b)), since lessee may have had use of the goods (cmt. 2)

§ 2-711(1) refunds the price paid

Cover by substantially similar lease

PV of new rent for the comparable period − PV of old rent + incidental + consequential − saved (§ 2A-518(2))

§ 2-712

Cover by purchase, or by a dissimilar lease, or no cover

Market rent: PV of market rent − PV of original rent, as of default, for the remaining term + incidental + consequential − saved (§§ 2A-518(3), 2A-519(1))

§ 2-713. Place for tender, or arrival after rejection (§ 2A-519(2))

Accepted goods

Loss in the ordinary course; for warranty, PV of the difference in the value of the use of goods as accepted and as warranted (§ 2A-519(3)–(4))

§ 2-714

Deducting from rent

Yes, except finance leases under § 2A-407 (§ 2A-508(6))

§ 2-717

  • A purchase can't be measured as cover. Unlike a buyer, a lessee who buys replacements falls to the market-rent formula. And "substantially similar" is hard to meet given negotiated terms (§ 2A-518 cmts. 3–7).
  • Market rent proof: § 2A-507.

sections.title: Nonconforming tender — same model as Article 2
sections.html:
• Reject: non-installment: perfect tender (§ 2A-509(1)). Installment: substantial impairment of the installment and no cure or assurance of cure (§ 2A-510). Within a reasonable time, with seasonable notice (§ 2A-509(2)). Failure to state defects may waive them (§ 2A-514).
  • Cure: same as § 2-508 (§ 2A-513). Care of goods: §§ 2A-511, 2A-512. Lien for prepayments (§ 2A-508(5)). A purchaser from these sales takes free of lessor's or supplier's claims.
  • Acceptance: failing to reject, or signifying conformity or that lessee will keep the goods (§ 2A-515). Lessee has inspection rights, though no section parallels § 2-513. Acceptance means rent is owed and rejection is gone (§ 2A-516(1)–(2)).
  • Notice after acceptance: notify lessor and the supplier, if any, or be barred against the party not notified (§ 2A-516(3)(a)). Lessee bears the burden of showing default (§ 2A-516(3)(c)).
rule

Revocation, § 2A-517: like § 2-608: substantial impairment + (a) reasonable assumption of cure or (b) acceptance induced by lessor's assurances or difficulty of discovery. Also, except in a non-consumer finance lease, lessee may revoke if lessor defaults under the lease in a way that substantially impairs the goods' value (§ 2A-517(2)), and on other defaults if the agreement says so. Finance lease: the assumption-of-cure and difficulty-of-discovery grounds are gone: only lessor's assurances remain, and acceptance with knowledge bars revocation (§ 2A-516(2)). That keeps § 2A-407 working. A consumer finance lessee may also use § 2A-517(2). Timing and duties track § 2-608.

  • After revocation: cover or market rent + incidental + consequential − saved.
  • Limitations, § 2A-506: four years, reducible by contract to one, and unlike § 2-725 not barred from being extended (cmt.). Accrual is more liberal than § 2-725: when the default is or should have been discovered, or when it occurs, whichever is later. Tolling is left to other law.
  • Problem 11-5, worked from the text, not the professor's answer (Boston leases 30 servers to Lasting; purchase agreement sent for approval; 20 installed, 5 fail; 10 never delivered): likely a finance lease ((iii)(A) or (B)). Against Boston: no warranties. For 15 working and 5 failed installed units, if accepted, rent is due under § 2A-407, and revocation only if Boston gave assurances. For the 10 undelivered there is no acceptance, so § 2A-407 doesn't apply; Lasting can refuse rent on them and, if the deal is an installment lease, cancel if the whole is substantially impaired. Against Sensational: warranty and delivery promises through § 2A-209(1): damages for the 5, and for nondelivery of the 10, with consequential damages for customer problems unless excluded. Notify both Boston and Sensational (§ 2A-516(3)(a)). Cover, because that also limits consequential loss.

sections.title: XXXIII. Lessee's Default & Lessor's Remedies — §§ 2A-523 to 2A-532
sections.html:
• Lessor's main aim is usually to recover the goods and then damages. The residual interest gives it a much stronger claim to the goods than a seller has, but no duty to take them. Remedies are in § 2A-523, and the agreement may add others.

Lessor's measure

Formula

Compare Article 2

Substantially similar new lease (§ 2A-527(2))

Accrued unpaid rent at start of new term + (PV remaining old rent − PV comparable new rent) + incidental − saved

§ 2-706

Market rent (§ 2A-528(1)): dissimilar lease, sale, or no disposition

Accrued unpaid rent + (PV remaining rent − PV market rent at the place where goods are located, same term) + incidental − saved

§ 2-708(1)

Lost profit (§ 2A-528(2))

PV of profit incl. reasonable overhead + incidental + costs reasonably incurred, credit for disposition proceeds, with lessor keeping its residual

§ 2-708(2)

Rent (§ 2A-529)

Accrued unpaid rent at judgment + PV of remaining rent + incidental − saved

§ 2-709

  • No consequential damages for lessors, as with sellers. Incidental damages: § 2A-530.
  • Rent is available for goods accepted and not repossessed, for conforming goods lost or damaged within a commercially reasonable time after risk passed, or for identified goods lessor can't dispose of at a reasonable price (§ 2A-529(1)). Lessor must hold the goods for lessee for the remaining term, but may dispose of them before collecting the judgment, and that disposition then runs through § 2A-527 or § 2A-528 (§ 2A-529(2)–(3)).
  • Tender back cuts off rent. Article 2 lets a seller recover the price of accepted goods. Article 2A rejects that: if lessee tenders the goods back, lessor is limited to the damages it would have had, because it holds a residual and will re-let or sell anyway (§ 2A-529 cmt. 1). A lost-volume lessor can still reach full rent through § 2A-528(2) (cmt. 2, five backhoes never all rented).
  • Residual: lessor may also recover for loss of or damage to its residual interest caused by the default, e.g., goods returned in worse condition than the lease requires (§ 2A-532).
  • No notice of disposition is required from a lessor, unlike § 2-706(3). But if the "lease" may be a disguised sale, give notice anyway: § 2-706(3) and § 9-611 could apply (n.16).
  • Before delivery: lessor may withhold, on default or discovering insolvency (§ 2A-525), or stop in transit (§ 2A-526, parallel to § 2-705), and may cancel, subject to substantial impairment for installment leases (§§ 2A-523(1), 2A-510(2)). Unfinished goods: § 2A-524, parallel to § 2-704.
  • Wrongful rejection or revocation where lessor takes goods back: same damages as repudiation (§ 2A-523(1)).
rule

Repossession, § 2A-525(2)–(3): after default lessor may take possession, without judicial process if it can be done without breach of the peace, or by action. It may require lessee to assemble the goods if the lease says so, and may render business goods unusable. Borrowed from § 9-609: no violence or substantial risk of it; trespass is allowed; no breaking and entering, particularly of a home.

  • Prepaying lessee, § 2A-504(3)–(4): if lessor justifiably withholds or stops delivery, lessee gets back payments above enforceable liquidated damages or, absent that, 20% of the then PV of total rent for the balance of the term (in a consumer lease, the lesser of that or $500), subject to offset for proven damages and benefits received. Compare § 2-718(2): sales use the lesser of 20% or $500 for every buyer.
  • Risk after default, limitations: §§ 2A-220(2), 2A-506, as in Sections XXXI and XXXII.

sections.title: Problems
sections.html:
Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's; PV ignored)

11-6 Lathes leased for $80,000 over 3 years; $20,000 down; delivered, accepted, returned a week later at lessee's unjustified demand; market rent Nov. 8: $60,000 Chicago, $55,000 Phoenix; 2-year re-lease in Denver for $50,000

Two-year lease isn't substantially similar to three-year, so § 2A-527(3) sends it to § 2A-528(1). Goods are in Phoenix, so use $55,000: $80,000 − $55,000 = $25,000. Incidental: storage (about 60 days × $100 = $6,000) + $1,500 freight = $7,500. Total $32,500, less $20,000 already paid = about $12,500, plus any rent accrued for the week of use. Counting the $20,000 as rent paid gives the same result ($60,000 − $55,000 + $7,500).

11-7 On default: repossess, all past rent, all future rent, 5% late fee on missed payments, 12% interest on all amounts

Past rent is fine. Future rent + repossession = double recovery: lessor gets the money and the goods. Not reasonable under § 2A-504(1), so it fails and Article 2A's remedies apply (§ 2A-504(2)). Revise with a formula, which § 2A-504(1) allows if reasonable in light of then anticipated harm: past-due rent + PV of future rent + estimated residual, − net proceeds of re-leasing or sale. The § 2A-504 comment calls that formula common. Limit the late fee and 12% interest to overdue sums, not unaccrued rent.

sections.title: XXXIV. Property Rights in Leased Goods — §§ 2A-304 to 2A-308
sections.html:
• Starting point: a transferor gives only what it has. Lessee can transfer the leasehold, and lessor the residual (§ 2A-303). These rules are the exceptions. The text is deliberately brief: know which rule fits. Fixtures, accessions, and titled goods are excluded (n.18).

Transfer

Result

Person with voidable title leases to a good-faith lessee for value (§ 2A-304(1))

Lessee takes free of the original seller's rights. Analog to § 2-403(1)

Lessor leases twice for overlapping terms (§ 2A-304(1))

First in time: second lessee takes subject to the first lease, unless (1) lessor is disposing after breach of the first lease (§ 2A-527(4)), or (2) first lessee entrusted goods back and the second is a lessee in ordinary course (§ 2A-304(2))

Owner entrusts to a merchant, who leases in ordinary course (§ 2A-307(2); § 2A-304 cmt. 3)

Lessee in ordinary course is protected, but owner keeps the residual: it loses the goods only for the term. Analog to § 2-403(2)

Lessee with a voidable leasehold (§ 2A-305(1))

Can transfer a good leasehold to a good-faith sublessee or buyer. Doesn't cut off lessor's residual

Merchant lessee sells or subleases in ordinary course (§ 2A-305(2))

Buyer or lessee in ordinary course takes free of lessor. Eliminates the residual

Lessee disposes after lessor's breach (§§ 2A-511, 2A-512)

Purchaser takes free of lessor's interest (§ 2A-511(4))

sections.title: Creditors
sections.html:
Creditor

Result

Lessor's creditor with a possessory statutory lien for services or materials

Lessee takes subject to it, whenever it arose (§ 2A-306), unless the lien law says otherwise

Lessor's creditor whose lien arose before the lease

Lessee takes subject to it (§ 2A-307(2)–(3)), unless it's an Article 9 security interest and lessee qualifies as a lessee in ordinary course (§ 9-321(c)) or gave value and took possession without knowledge while it was unperfected (§ 9-317(c))

Lessor's creditor whose lien arose after the lease

Subject to lessee's rights, except a statutory lien or a fraudulent transfer (§ 2A-308)

Lessee's creditors

Don't beat lessor's rights (§ 2A-307(1)), except a § 2A-306 possessory lien

sections.title: XXXV. Week 14 Review: Final Exam Checklists
sections.html: • Final format (syllabus): 180 minutes in three parts: 60 minutes of closed-book multiple choice, a 30-minute closed-book short bar essay, and 90 minutes of short answers with a physical statutory supplement and a 5-single-page outline. Worth 70% of the grade. It covers lectures, slides, handouts, readings, and class discussion. The syllabus lists an asynchronous review lecture for Week 14; no Week 15 appears on it.

Anticipated or actual harm

Same

Then anticipated harm only

sections.title: Buyer's remedy decision steps
sections.html:
• (1) Did seller breach? Is that excused? Are remedies limited?
    (2) Who has the goods?
    (3) Goods not delivered or repudiated: get them (§§ 2-502, 2-716), or cancel and take refund + cover or market + § 2-715.
    (4) Delivered: was it accepted? Check § 2-606.
    (5) Not accepted: was rejection rightful (§ 2-601 or § 2-612) and effective (§ 2-602; § 2-605)? Can seller cure (§ 2-508)?
    (6) Accepted: notice under § 2-607(3)(a), then § 2-714 and § 2-717, or revoke under § 2-608.
    (7) Add § 2-715, subtract expenses saved, and test against § 1-305.

sections.title: Seller's remedy decision steps
sections.html:
• (1) Did buyer breach? Excused? Limited?
    (2) Buyer has the goods: price (§ 2-709), or reclamation (§§ 2-507, 2-702), or Article 9.
    (3) Seller or carrier has them: withhold or stop (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705); cancel.
    (4) Pick a measure: resale properly done? Market provable? Lost-volume with capacity and profitability? Can't resell?
    (5) Add § 2-710; never consequential.
    (6) Subtract expenses saved.
    (7) Account for prepayments under § 2-718(2)–(3).

sections.title: Lease spot-check
sections.html:
• (1) Is it a true lease (§ 1-203)?
    (2) Is it a finance lease (§ 2A-103(1)(g))?
    (3) Consumer lease?
    (4) If finance and non-consumer: did lessee accept (§ 2A-407)?
    (5) Who bears risk (§ 2A-219)?
    (6) Apply the PV formulas, and watch which Article 2A difference the facts are built around.
tip

Traps to rehearse. Formula direction (cover − contract, contract − resale). A purchase that isn't a reasonable substitute isn't cover, so § 2-713 applies. § 2-607(3)(a) applies only to accepted goods. No "wrongful but effective" revocation exists. A seller gets no consequential damages. Nonpayment alone doesn't stop a parcel in transit. A retained-title clause is only a security interest. A $100 option on a non-terminable lease is a sale. A lessee's purchase can't serve as cover damages.

cases.name: Daitom, Inc. v. Pennwalt Corp.
cases.title: Daitom, Inc. v. Pennwalt Corp. (10th Cir. 1984) — § 2-207 battle of the forms
cases.html:
main case

Daitom, Inc. v. Pennwalt Corp. (10th Cir. 1984) — § 2-207 battle of the forms

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 47–57. Not named on the slides; the topic is covered at W1-S44 to S47.

Facts: Seller Pennwalt sent a typed proposal (the offer) to sell buyer Daitom two rotary vacuum dryers; its attached printed terms limited warranties and required any suit within 1 year of delivery. Daitom answered with its own purchase order (PO) — boilerplate on the back reserved "all of its rights and remedies available at law" and said acceptance was "expressly limited to such terms." The dryers were delivered in May 1977 but sat in crates while Daitom's plant was built; when finally run in June 1978 they were seriously defective. Daitom sued in March 1980 — too late under the 1-year term, timely under the UCC's 4 years.

Held: (1) The PO was an acceptance, not a counteroffer: "expressly conditional" requires the offeree to clearly say it won't proceed unless its terms are accepted (Dorton) — form language like "expressly limited to such terms" isn't enough. (2) The 1-year term and Daitom's reservation of its legal remedies (which impliedly reserved the statutory period) were different (conflicting) terms → knock-out rule (cmt. 6): both drop out, and the gap filler — § 2-725's 4-year statute of limitations (SOL) — applies. Summary judgment for Pennwalt reversed. (Dissent: would affirm — Daitom accepted Pennwalt's offer.)

Why it matters: the textbook illustration that § 2-207 abolished the mirror-image and "last shot" rules — a nonconforming acceptance still forms a contract, and when the forms conflict neither side's boilerplate wins; the UCC default does. The court stressed the 1-year period would have run before the machines were even installed.

cases.name: Casazza v. Kiser
cases.title: Casazza v. Kiser (8th Cir. 2002) — statute of frauds exceptions
cases.html:
main case

Casazza v. Kiser (8th Cir. 2002) — statute of frauds exceptions

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 75–80. Not named on the slides; the exceptions are covered at W1-S50 to S54.

Facts: Casazza found Kiser's internet listing for the Andante, a 52-foot sailboat, inspected it in Ft. Lauderdale, and (he said) orally agreed to buy it for $200,000, subject to a survey and sea trial. Each side jotted terms on separate sheets and Casazza typed them up, but Kiser never signed anything about the boat. The only document both signed was a license transferring the boat's navigation software, which never mentioned the boat. Casazza booked a survey and a Virginia slip; a week later Kiser backed out and sold the boat to someone else.

Held: Dismissal affirmed — no enforceable contract. Part performance failed: accepting the software wasn't accepting the boat — they aren't one "commercial unit" (software bought years after the boat; boat later sold without it). No sufficient writing: the typed terms were unsigned by Kiser; the signed license didn't refer to a boat sale, so the papers couldn't be read together. Admission: hoping Kiser might admit the deal in a deposition isn't an admission. Promissory estoppel couldn't get around § 2-201 under any test — his reliance wasn't the kind that makes refusal a fraud.

Why it matters: walks through every § 2-201 escape route and shows how narrow each is. Big oral deal + no signature from the party being sued = unenforceable, even between two individuals (Art. 2 still applies).

cases.name: Market Street Assocs. v. Frey
cases.title: Market Street Assocs. v. Frey (7th Cir. 1991, Posner, J.) — what "good faith" in performance means
cases.html:
main case

Market Street Assocs. v. Frey (7th Cir. 1991, Posner, J.) — what "good faith" in performance means

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 92–102 (Brunswick Hills and Vintage Rodeo in the notes, pp. 100–102). Not named on the slides; good faith is covered at W2-S4.

Facts: In a sale-leaseback, J.C. Penney sold properties to the GE Pension Trust and leased them back. ¶ 34 of the lease said that if the tenant asked the Trust to finance improvements and negotiations failed, the tenant could buy the property back at roughly the original price plus 6% a year — potentially far below market. Market Street, which took over the lease on a Milwaukee shopping center, couldn't get outside financing and found the Trust's $3 million asking price too high. So it wrote asking the Trust to finance $2 million of improvements without mentioning ¶ 34. The Trust's slow, unresponsive manager turned the request down without realizing the consequence. Market Street sent a letter saying it would look elsewhere, then a month later exercised the ¶ 34 option at about $1 million and sued for specific performance.

Held: Summary judgment for the Trust was reversed and remanded, because liability turns on Market Street's state of mind. Good faith lies between a fiduciary duty and merely avoiding fraud. Before contracting you may exploit superior knowledge. After contracting, deliberately taking advantage of your partner's oversight about its contract rights — when you could correct it at no cost — is opportunistic "sharp dealing." On remand, the trial court found Orenstein knew the Trust was overlooking ¶ 34 and kept sending ambiguous letters → bad faith, no specific performance (affirmed).

Why it matters: defines good faith in performance (§ 1-304) and the line between formation and performance (common law here — a land lease — but used for the UCC concept). Compare (note cases): Brunswick Hills (N.J.) — a landlord evaded a tenant's requests for 19 months and then declared the option void = bad faith. Vintage Rodeo (Del. Ch.) — a party that merely benefited from the other side's own missed deadline in a heavily negotiated deal did nothing wrong; good faith only fills gaps.

cases.name: Roth Steel Products v. Sharon Steel Corp.
cases.title: Roth Steel Products v. Sharon Steel Corp. (6th Cir. 1983) — modification and good faith
cases.html:
main case ★

Roth Steel Products v. Sharon Steel Corp. (6th Cir. 1983) — modification and good faith

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 105–110. Slide W2-S8.

Facts: In Nov. 1972, with the steel industry at 70% capacity and prices very competitive, Sharon agreed to sell Roth 200 tons/month of hot-rolled steel through 1973 at $148/ton, well below its book price. In 1973 demand boomed and every mill was fully booked. Sharon announced it was ending its 1972 price breaks and threatened to stop selling Roth any steel in the second half of 1973 unless Roth paid more. Roth was short on inventory and couldn't buy elsewhere, so it reluctantly agreed to a higher price. Roth later sued.

Held: The modification was unenforceable. A modification needs no consideration (§ 2-209(1)) but must be sought in good faith, which has two parts: (1) objective — would an ordinary merchant seek it? Yes: the market shift meant Sharon was losing money on the deal. (2) Subjective / honesty in fact — a real reason, not a pretext, obtained without extortion. Sharon's threat to stop performing was evidence of bad faith it never rebutted (its contract-based excuse first appeared at trial). Judgment for Roth affirmed.

Why it matters: shows what good faith adds once consideration is gone. A legitimate reason to ask for a change isn't enough if you extract the change by threatening to breach (§ 2-209 cmt. 2).

cases.name: Rogath v. Siebenmann
cases.title: Rogath v. Siebenmann (2d Cir. 1997) — basis of the bargain
cases.html:
main case ★

Rogath v. Siebenmann (2d Cir. 1997) — basis of the bargain

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 121–126. Slide W2-S32.

Facts: Siebenmann sold Rogath a "Self Portrait" attributed to Francis Bacon for $570,000. The bill of sale warranted that he was the sole owner, that the painting was authentic, and that he knew of no challenge to its authenticity. In fact, the Marlborough Fine Art gallery in London had already told him it doubted the work. Rogath resold the painting for $950,000; that buyer learned of the doubts and demanded a refund, which Rogath paid. Rogath then sued. Siebenmann claimed he had told Rogath about the Marlborough "controversy" before the sale, and Rogath had also heard doubts from a Tate Gallery curator.

Held: The trial court's summary judgment for Rogath was vacated and the case remanded. The question isn't whether the buyer believed the warranted facts, but whether he bought the seller's promise. A buyer who closes knowing facts the seller disclosed that make the warranty false waives the breach unless he expressly preserves his rights. Knowledge from a third party or common knowledge doesn't bar recovery, because the buyer may have bought the warranty as insurance. So the key fact was whether Siebenmann himself told Rogath; that was disputed, so trial was needed.

Why it matters: illustrates that "basis of the bargain" (§ 2-313 cmt. 3) isn't a strict reliance test. An express warranty allocates risk, and the source of the buyer's knowledge decides the case.

cases.name: Webster v. Blue Ship Tea Room
cases.title: Webster v. Blue Ship Tea Room (Mass. 1964) — merchantability of food
cases.html:
cited only

Webster v. Blue Ship Tea Room (Mass. 1964) — merchantability of food

In the casebook: cited only, in Problem 3-10(b) (Boggs chokes on a bone in a salmon fillet), alongside Mexicali Rose and Schafer. The casebook gives no facts or holding.

Outside class materials — facts: a diner ordered fish chowder at a Boston restaurant; a fish bone lodged in her throat and had to be removed. She sued for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability, and a jury found for her.

Outside class materials — held: reversed. Bones are natural to New England fish chowder and to be expected, so the chowder was fit for its ordinary purpose.

Why it matters: merchantability = fit for ordinary purposes (§ 2-314(2)(c)); the problem asks whether a bone in a fillet is different.

cases.name: Ingram River Equip. v. Pott Indus.
cases.title: Ingram River Equip. v. Pott Indus. (8th Cir. 1987) — "particular" purpose
cases.html:
note case

Ingram River Equip. v. Pott Indus. (8th Cir. 1987) — "particular" purpose

Source: note case — the casebook quotes the opinion, pp. 139–141. Not on the slides.

Facts: Ingram bought four tank barges with heating coils from builder Pott to haul heavy petroleum products on the Mississippi and heat them so they would unload in cold weather. Pott argued that carrying and heating heavy oil is the ordinary use of coil-equipped barges — it had built 30+ for exactly that — so no fitness warranty arose.

Held: A fitness warranty could arise. The buyer's use need not be unique; the question is whether it is sufficiently different from the customary use of the goods. That depends on whether the goods are "tank barges" (used for many cargoes) or "heating-coil barges" — like buying climbing shoes at a general shoe store vs. a climbing store. It's a fact question, and the finding for Ingram stood.

Why it matters: draws the line between § 2-315 (particular purpose) and § 2-314 (ordinary purpose).

cases.name: Orange & Rockland Utils. v. Amerada Hess
cases.title: Orange & Rockland Utils. v. Amerada Hess (N.Y. App. Div. 1977) — § 2-306 "unreasonably disproportionate"
cases.html:
note case

Orange & Rockland Utils. v. Amerada Hess (N.Y. App. Div. 1977) — § 2-306 "unreasonably disproportionate"

Source: note case — the casebook quotes the factors and summarizes the result, pp. 151–152. Not on the slides.

Facts (casebook): a requirements contract for oil with stated estimates, which were based on the buyer's plans to burn the oil to produce electricity for its customer base. The buyer then doubled its "requirements," seeking the extra oil in order to sell the additional quantity in the market. Outside class materials: the contract price was fixed, oil's market price had risen far above it, and Hess refused to supply the excess.

Held: "Unreasonably disproportionate" is a limit separate from good faith (it applies "even where one party acts with complete good faith"), judged by the parties' expectations using the five factors above. The doubling was unreasonably disproportionate.

Why it matters: a requirements buyer can't use the contract to speculate on the market. Cf. Problem 4-1(B) (buyer jumps to plant capacity when the market rises to $1.15).

cases.name: Mathis v. Exxon Corp.
cases.title: Mathis v. Exxon Corp. (5th Cir. 2002) — price set by one party, § 2-305(2)
cases.html:
note case ★

Mathis v. Exxon Corp. (5th Cir. 2002) — price set by one party, § 2-305(2)

Source: note case — the casebook summarizes it and quotes the opinion, pp. 154–157 (Autry/HRN excerpt pp. 156–158). Slides W3-S44 and S45 — treat it like a main case.

Facts: Exxon franchise dealers had to buy a minimum amount of gas each month at a price Exxon set (the "dealer tank wagon" price). The dealers claimed Exxon set that price to squeeze them out so it could replace them with company-run stations. Their evidence: Exxon planned to convert stations to company stores; the price exceeded the wholesale (rack) price plus delivery; after 1994 Exxon barred dealers from buying cheaper gas from jobbers; and many dealers became unprofitable. Exxon replied that its price was within the range competitors charged.

Held: The jury's bad-faith finding was upheld. Good faith under § 2-305(2) has both a subjective and an objective part. Comment 3's posted-price safe harbor covers only the "normal case," and an intent to drive the buyer out of business takes the case outside it — even when the price is in the competitive range.

Why it matters / split: shows how good faith limits a price-setter's discretion. The majority rejects Mathis — Shell v. HRN (Tex. 2004) and Autry v. BP (11th Cir. 2009) hold that a commercially reasonable, non-discriminatory price is in good faith regardless of motive, for the sake of certainty.

cases.name: Windows, Inc. v. Jordan Panel Sys.
cases.title: Windows, Inc. v. Jordan Panel Sys. (2d Cir. 1999) — the case behind Problem 4-7
cases.html:
cited only

Windows, Inc. v. Jordan Panel Sys. (2d Cir. 1999) — the case behind Problem 4-7

In the casebook: cited only, in Problem 4-7 (casebook p. 171), whose facts track the case: a South Dakota seller of custom windows; a contract to ship them "properly crated … and delivered to" the buyer's New York construction site; damage in transit. The casebook gives no holding; the slides (W4-S39–40, W5-S21–24) work through the problem.

Outside class materials — what happened and the holding: the carrier's truck had an accident en route; the buyer refused to pay and the seller sued for the price. The court held for the seller: "delivered to" didn't create a destination contract, so risk passed on delivery to the carrier (§ 2-509(1)(a)); and even if the packing was inadequate, the accident — not the packing — caused the loss, so § 2-504/§ 2-510(1) didn't shift risk back to the seller.

Why it matters: the shipment-contract presumption (casebook and slides) plus the causation requirement in § 2-504. The buyer bearing transit risk must go after the carrier (§ 2-722) or its insurer.

cases.name: Razor v. Hyundai Motor America
cases.title: Razor v. Hyundai Motor America (Ill. 2006) — failed limited remedy and the consequential-damages exclusion
cases.html:
main case ★

Razor v. Hyundai Motor America (Ill. 2006) — failed limited remedy and the consequential-damages exclusion

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 202–212. Slide W67-S32.

Facts: A consumer bought a new Hyundai Sonata. Hyundai's written warranty limited her remedy to repair or replacement and separately excluded incidental and consequential damages. The car had a no-start problem that numerous repairs never fixed. The jury found the repair remedy failed of its essential purpose and awarded $5,000 for lost value plus $3,500 for inconvenience and loss of use. The warranty and its exclusion were in the owner's manual in the glove box; she never saw them until after she signed and drove off.

Held: (1) Independent approach (majority; Chatlos): the failure of the repair remedy does not automatically void the consequential-damages exclusion. The exclusion stands unless unconscionable under § 2-719(3) — the "two concentric walls." The court rejected the dependent approach of Adams v. J.I. Case (a tractor stuck in the repair shop for over a year) because it would make exclusions meaningless. (2) This exclusion was unconscionable: a preprinted consumer form with no bargaining power, and decisively, it wasn't available to her before she signed. Clear capital letters don't matter if she couldn't see it. Remanded for a new trial on § 2-714(2) damages.

Why it matters: shows the two separate tests in § 2-719: failure of essential purpose (for the limited remedy) vs. unconscionability (for the consequential exclusion). Dissent: the ruling burdens manufacturers and discourages written warranties.

cases.name: Santa Fe Custom Shutters & Doors v. Home Depot
cases.title: Santa Fe Custom Shutters & Doors v. Home Depot (N.M. App. 2005) — terminating an at-will supply deal
cases.html:
note case

Santa Fe Custom Shutters & Doors v. Home Depot (N.M. App. 2005) — terminating an at-will supply deal

Source: note case — the casebook quotes the opinion, pp. 230–232. Not named on the slides; termination is covered at W8-S22.

Facts: A shutter manufacturer supplied Home Depot under an indefinite, at-will arrangement. Relying on it (and on Home Depot's alleged promises of a profitable partnership and professional marketing), the manufacturer made enormous up-front investments and took on debt to expand production. Home Depot terminated before the investment paid off, and the trial court awarded five years of lost profits. The manufacturer argued good faith barred the termination.

Held: Good faith applies to termination but doesn't override § 2-309(2)'s right to end an indefinite contract "at any time," so the five-year lost-profits award was error. No good reason is required, and the contract needn't have run a reasonable time. "The essence of the at-will doctrine is the right … to cease doing business without liability for future profits." Remaining claims: fraud in the inducement, breaches before termination, and unreasonable notice.

Why it matters: good faith can't contradict an express or statutory right. Termination (§ 2-106(3)) isn't breach — the duty is reasonable notice (enough time to find substitutes).

cases.name: Top of Iowa Cooperative v. Sime Farms, Inc.
cases.title: Top of Iowa Cooperative v. Sime Farms, Inc. (Iowa 2000) — § 2-609 adequate assurance
cases.html:
main case ★

Top of Iowa Cooperative v. Sime Farms, Inc. (Iowa 2000) — § 2-609 adequate assurance

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 235–243. Slide W8-S26.

Facts: Farmer Sime signed "hedge-to-arrive" corn contracts with its grain co-op for 60,000 bushels. The Coop hedged each contract by selling futures, paying margin as prices rose. Sime kept "rolling" (postponing) delivery and sold its 1995 crop elsewhere at high cash prices. By spring 1996 the market had inverted — rolling to December would cost about $1.30/bushel — and Sime had no corn to deliver in July. Sime told the manager he'd get back to the Coop but never did. That same month the Iowa Attorney General (AG) said some of these contracts might be illegal. The Coop wrote demanding, as assurance, (1) payment of margins (or a letter of credit) and (2) a signed promise to deliver; refusal would be treated as repudiation. Sime's lawyer replied that the contracts were illegal and refused.

Held: The jury verdict for the Coop was affirmed. (1) Reasonable grounds for insecurity are judged objectively by commercial standards and need not come from the other party's own conduct. The inverted market, the AG's statement, and Sime's silence were enough. (2) The demand was not unreasonable as a matter of law: "all demands for adequate assurance call for more than was originally promised," and asking for more isn't itself a repudiation (§ 2-610 cmt. 2).

Contrast — PDM v. Brookhaven (7th Cir. 1976) (note case; casebook quotes a concurrence, p. 243): PDM would have been "assured" only by Betke's personal guarantee, escrow financing, or buying an interest in Brookhaven. Those demands were more than "adequate assurance" as a matter of law — § 2-609 doesn't let a party redraft the contract. Outside class materials: PDM was building a water-storage tank for Brookhaven and acted on reports that Brookhaven's financing might fall through.

cases.name: Johannsen v. Minnesota Valley Ford Tractor Co.
cases.title: Johannsen v. Minnesota Valley Ford Tractor Co. (Minn. 1981) — factors for post-rejection use
cases.html:
note case

Johannsen v. Minnesota Valley Ford Tractor Co. (Minn. 1981) — factors for post-rejection use

Source: note case: the casebook quotes the opinion, p. 297 (n.34). No class slides.

Held: Reasonableness of the buyer's continued use is a jury question on all the facts. Factors: (1) the seller's instructions after revocation; (2) the buyer's economic and other hardship if use stopped; (3) whether use was a reasonable way to mitigate damages; (4) prejudice to the seller; (5) the seller's bad faith.

Why it matters: The checklist to run whenever a buyer keeps using goods it has rejected or revoked.

cases.name: Hyundai Motor America, Inc. v. Goodin
cases.title: Hyundai Motor America, Inc. v. Goodin (Ind. 2005) — no vertical privity for a consumer's implied warranty claim
cases.html:
main case

Hyundai Motor America, Inc. v. Goodin (Ind. 2005) — no vertical privity for a consumer's implied warranty claim

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 328–337. No class slides.

Facts: Sandra Goodin bought a new Hyundai Sonata from a dealer, with a 5-year/60,000-mile manufacturer warranty. Brake trouble began almost at once, and eight months of repairs didn't fix it. Her lawyer sought a refund; she sued Hyundai under the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act. The jury found for Hyundai on express warranty but for Goodin on the implied warranty of merchantability, awarding $3,000. The Court of Appeals reversed for lack of privity, feeling bound by a footnote in Martin Rispens.

Held: Indiana doesn't require vertical privity between a consumer and a manufacturer for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability, even for economic loss. The footnote was dicta. Alternative A speaks only to horizontal privity and leaves vertical privity to the courts. Privity's freedom-of-contract rationale has "eroded to the point of invisibility" for many consumer goods: goods reach consumers through intermediaries; warranties are marketing tools; consumers expect merchantability; the law spreads the cost of lemons across all buyers; and a disclaimer in the dealer's buyer's order would otherwise leave her without a remedy. The privity bar began as a limit on tort claims (Winterbottom) and was undercut by MacPherson and Henningsen.

Why it matters: The modern consumer rule, but courts remain divided. Limits: it speaks to a consumer against a manufacturer, for goods subject to Magnuson-Moss. Damages are usually the § 2-714(2) value difference.

cases.name: Peace River Seed Coop. v. Proseeds Marketing
cases.title: Peace River Seed Coop. v. Proseeds Marketing (Or. 2014) — market damages after a resale
cases.html:
note case

Peace River Seed Coop. v. Proseeds Marketing (Or. 2014) — market damages after a resale

Source: note case: the casebook quotes it in nn.17–18, p. 415. No class slides.

Held: An aggrieved seller may claim § 2-708(1) market damages even if it resold and market damages exceed resale damages. A fixed-price contract allocates market risk, so market damages are what the parties bargained for. A seller isn't required to resell, so mitigation can't force it to use the resale price, and the UCC rejects election of remedies.

Why it matters: Answers the question the text poses: resale and market are alternatives, but resale doesn't necessarily lock the seller into its resale price. Counterargument: § 1-305 forbids a recovery above the seller's real loss, and the resale shows that loss. A seller can avoid § 2-706 simply by not identifying the resale to the broken contract (n.19).

cases.name: R.E. Davis Chem. Corp. v. Diasonics, Inc.
cases.title: R.E. Davis Chem. Corp. v. Diasonics, Inc. (7th Cir. 1987) — who is a lost-volume seller
cases.html:
note case

R.E. Davis Chem. Corp. v. Diasonics, Inc. (7th Cir. 1987) — who is a lost-volume seller

Source: note case: the casebook quotes the opinion, p. 418 (n.20). No class slides.

Held: Capacity alone isn't enough. Ask not only whether seller could have produced the breached units on top of its actual volume, but whether it would have been profitable to do so. Under diminishing returns, at some volume the next sale stops being worthwhile, and awarding presumed lost profit would overcompensate.

Why it matters: A manufacturer must show capacity and profitability. The usual test on an exam.

cases.name: Foxco Indus. v. Fabric World, Inc.
cases.title: Foxco Indus. v. Fabric World, Inc. (5th Cir. 1979) — "unable to resell at a reasonable price"
cases.html:
note case

Foxco Indus. v. Fabric World, Inc. (5th Cir. 1979) — "unable to resell at a reasonable price"

Source: note case: the casebook quotes the opinion, pp. 423–424 (n.27). No class slides.

Held: Seller of specially made spring fabric needed only reasonable efforts to resell at a reasonable price. The goods were made for a customer, were hard to sell after the spring season, and the market fell 50%. The jury could find seller acted reasonably even though it made little resale effort for months and sold part only the next season.

Why it matters: Goods need not be worthless. The test is reasonable effort and a reasonable price, and market collapse and seasonality count.

problems.title: Speedy Offset prints & binds 500 art books

parts.html: • Problem 1-2 (Speedy Offset prints & binds 500 art books): printing/binding = services in manufacturing goods → goods predominate → Art. 2 applies; claims concern conformity of the books, so warranty rules apply either way.
• Problem 1-4: Art. 2 governs merchant→merchant, merchant→consumer, consumer→merchant, and consumer→consumer (garage sale) — scope never depends on merchant status.

• Problem 2-10(A) — "sufficient against the sender": the confirmation must satisfy § 2-201(1) against its sender — signed by the sender, indicates a contract, states a quantity. ✓ "This confirms our deal: 500 widgets at $10 — /s/ Seller." ✗ an unsigned invoice, a mere quote, or a confirmation without quantity.
parts.title: "sufficient against the sender"

parts.html:
Facts

Result

(a)

Oral $400 deal → orally doubled to $800

As modified it's $500+ → needs a record → modification unenforceable; the $400 deal stands (may operate as waiver)

(b)

Oral $1,000 deal → orally cut to 40 units/$400

As modified it's under $500 → no record needed → enforceable

(c)

Record: 100/$1,000 → orally 110, same price

Enforceable only to the 100 units shown in the record → SOF bars the extra 10

(d)

Record: 100/$1,000 → orally 90/$900

Split (Costco vs. Zemco): old record still shows a contract and quantity ≥ 90, or a quantity change needs its own record

(e)

Record: delivery June 1 → orally July 1

No SOF problem — only quantity must be in the record (a NOM clause would be a separate barrier)

problems.title: 10,000 widgets/month, delivery to buyer by the 5th

parts.html:
Problem 3-5 (10,000 widgets/month, delivery to buyer by the 5th):

  • (A) One late delivery accepted: no course of performance (single occasion), no modification, no waiver of damages — buyer keeps its claim if it gives timely notice.
  • (B) Three late deliveries accepted: arguable course of performance (but express term prevails if irreconcilable); buyer may retract any waiver for future deliveries by reasonable notice (unless seller materially relied); recovery for the past three requires timely § 2-607(3)(a) notice, and conduct may be a waiver as to them.
  • (C) + NOM clause: no unwritten modification (§ 2-209(2)), but conduct can still be a waiver (§ 2-209(4)); NOM clause weakens estoppel.
  • (D) + anti-waiver clause: courts split — some enforce it; others hold the clause itself can be waived by conduct; estoppel remains possible but weak.

Problem 3-6 statement

Result

"Looks good on you" · "a beautiful painting by a talented artist"

Puffing

"Queen Anne" desk · "Ming" vase · "antique" table

Warranty (descriptions) — question whether "Queen Anne" means period or style

Consumer seller: used washer "works great"

Close call (Petti) — present condition (fact) vs. casual opinion

"The ball David Ortiz hit for a grand slam, Game 2, 2013 World Series"

Warranty — specific, verifiable

"Replacement parts are readily available"

Likely warranty — specific, measurable

"The safest car in its class"

Split — superlative puffery vs. measurable by crash ratings

Used yacht is "seaworthy"

Split — the problem cites Keith v. Buchanan (warranty) vs. Sessa v. Riegle (cited only). Outside class materials: in Keith, a sales brochure called a 41-foot sailboat "seaworthy"; it wasn't → express warranty, no proof of reliance needed. Sessa involved a statement about a racehorse's soundness.

problems.title: HVAC: heating, ventilation, and air conditioning

parts.html: • Problem 3-7 (HVAC: heating, ventilation, and air conditioning): rep's "300,000 BTU [British thermal units]/hr" → warranty · "you'll be very happy" → puffing · brochure "under 100 decibels" → warranty (buyer skimmed it) · owner's manual "free of defects for one year" → likely warranty (post-sale term; future-performance promise).

• Problem 3-8: (A) signed deal for a skid loader, silent on delivery → enforceable; § 2-308 → delivery at seller's place of business → buyer breached by refusing to pick up. (B) history of seller delivering → course of dealing fills the term → seller breached.

Problem 3-9 seller

Makes the warranty?

Artisan (accountant) selling her stained-glass baubles at a semi-annual craft fair

Likely yes — regularly makes and sells goods of that kind; the day job isn't decisive

Rental company selling oldest fleet cars every 4 months

Likely yes — regular, recurring used-car sales

Contractor (60% services/40% materials; clients pick materials)

Hybrid — warranty rules still apply to the goods; likely a merchant in what it regularly supplies

Decorator paid a finder's fee by the client

No — not the seller

Problem 3-10

Breach?

New mower fails on 4th use

Likely — early failure is circumstantial proof of a defect at sale (unless misuse)

Bone in a salmon fillet

Depends on the approach — the problem cites Webster (no breach) against Mexicali Rose and Schafer. Outside class materials: these are usually called the "foreign-natural" test (Webster) and the "reasonable-expectation" test (Schafer); a fillet sold as boneless is the stronger claim under the latter.

Yarn color varies across five dye lots

Likely not if within trade-usage variations (§ 2-314(2)(d))

Car meets all safety rules but rates low in crashes

Likely not — needs minimal, not top, safety (different under fitness if buyer stated a safety need)

• Problem 4-1:
    (a)     fixed 50,000 sq ft/yr → buyer can't cut to 20,000 without seller's assent (fixed quantity; demand risk is buyer's).
    (b)     "requirements," no estimate: 25,000 → 32,500 → 35,000 → 60,000 (plant capacity) when market rose to $1.15 → seller can resist as disproportionate and opportunistic.
    (c)     drop to 5,000 in a recession at 90¢ market → seller argues disproportion and buying elsewhere; a genuine lack of orders may be good faith.

• Problem 4-2 (90,000, then 100,000): good faith but disproportionate — buyer honestly lands a huge new customer and needs 400,000. Proportionate but bad faith — buyer orders a normal 110,000 to resell at a higher market price, or 85,000 because it's secretly buying cheaper elsewhere.

Problem 4-3 (1,000 sacks; Feb. 1 market $7)

Result

(a) "To be agreed at delivery"; seller demands $15; market $12; buyer covers at $13

Contract exists (intent to be bound) → reasonable price ≈ $12 → seller breached; buyer recovers cover difference

(b) "Chicago Board price on March 15"; board closed; Mar. 13 price $12; buyer buys at $11

Standard failed → reasonable price (≈ $12) → contract exists; buyer's rejection likely a breach

(c) "Set by a third party both agree on"; buyer refuses to name anyone; market $13

Failure is buyer's fault → seller may cancel or fix a reasonable price (≈ $13) and sue

Problem 4-4 (100 bushels at $4; seller tenders first):

Facts

Proper tender?

Only 95 bushels + broken loading auger

No — nonconforming quantity (single lot); auger turns on who must load (trade usage); seller may cure

Moldy wheat

No — nonconforming goods

"Pick it up within 2 hours or I sell it"

Probably no — must hold for a reasonably necessary period

Pick up at a warehouse 300 miles away

Only if both knew at contracting the identified goods were there (§ 2-308(b))

Buyer brings a small truck, wants half now, half tomorrow

Seller's tender is fine — single lot; buyer must furnish suitable facilities

Seller arrives at buyer's farm on time; buyer's bins aren't ready

Seller's tender is fine — buyer failed to cooperate; seller excused for delay (§ 2-311(3))

• Problem 4-5: (a) seller demands payment before inspection → buyer is right (inspect first unless otherwise agreed). (b) buyer wants a 2-week genetically modified organism (GMO) lab test → reasonable only if GMO-free is a contract term and the test is a reasonable manner/time; buyer may hold the wheat for testing without accepting; buyer pays test costs unless the wheat fails and is rejected; agree on a protocol.

• (a) Seller drives the wheat in its own truck; truck burns en route → the seller's own truck is not a carrier → § 2-509(3). Merchant: no receipt → seller's risk. Non-merchant: risk passes at the completion of tender, which never happened → seller's risk. Seller bears it either way (fungible wheat → must re-tender).
  • (b) Seller says "ready for pickup"; fire destroys it before buyer arrives → merchant seller: seller bears (no receipt); non-merchant: buyer bears (tender complete). Merchant status decides the case.
  • Rationale (cmt. 3): a merchant seller still controls and can insure the goods — risk stays even if buyer has paid.

problems.title: custom windows, South Dakota → New York

parts.html:
Problem 4-7 (custom windows, South Dakota → New York)

Who bears the loss?

(a) "Delivered to" the site; properly packaged; destroyed in transit

Buyer — shipment contract (Windows v. Jordan Panel)

(b) "Delivered at" the site

Arguably seller — destination contract

(c) How to make it a destination contract

"F.O.B. buyer's site" or "seller bears risk until tender at the site"

(d)(1) Improperly packaged; damage caused by packaging

Seller — improper shipment caused the loss (§§ 2-504, 2-510(1))

(d)(2) Damage caused by the carrier's fault (slide: properly packaged)

Buyer — risk already passed; sue the carrier. Even with bad packaging, no shift unless the packaging caused the loss
• Non-modifiable (Problem 5-1(b)): § 2-302 unconscionability · § 2-102 scope · §§ 2-204–2-207 formation · § 2-403 rights of third-party purchasers · also § 2-201 (cmt. 1).
parts.title: Non-modifiable

parts.html: • Problem 5-1(a): buyer setting a good-faith standard for a seller-set fuel price → tie it to an objective index or seller's lowest price to similar customers (or use an index price instead). Seller limiting requirements → stated estimate with min/max, fuel actually consumed by the existing fleet, notice of changes.

• Problem 5-3 — every way to disclaim fitness: conspicuous writing (need not say "fitness") · "no warranties beyond the face hereof" · "as is"/"with all faults" · buyer's examination or refusal after seller's demand · CoD/CoP/UoT.

problems.title: fisherman's engine; disclaimer on the back of a delivery receipt

parts.html: • Problem 5-4 (fisherman's engine; disclaimer on the back of a delivery receipt): both implied warranties arose (merchant dealer; boat specs + reliance on dealer's recommendation); a post-sale receipt term is likely not part of the contract (§§ 2-207/2-209); if it is, it mentions merchantability and covers "all implied warranties," but is it conspicuous on the back? Consumer buyer: additional terms are mere proposals; consumer law may void it. Non-merchant dealer: no merchantability warranty at all; fitness can still arise.

• Problem 5-5 (title): buyer accepts an express title disclaimer when provenance is uncertain and the price reflects the risk (quitclaim-style, estate or liquidation sales). Circumstances alone: storage-unit auctions, executor/trustee or police auctions, lien sales.

problems.title: oven LD: $1,000/day; 30 days late = $30,000; actual lost profit $2,500

parts.html: • Problem 5-6 (oven LD: $1,000/day; 30 days late = $30,000; actual lost profit $2,500): the "anticipated OR actual" wording lets a clause reasonable when made survive — negotiated by merchants, based on profit discussions, hard-to-prove harm, time of the essence → likely enforceable; the seller argues the 12x gap makes it a penalty.

• Problem 5-7 — failure of essential purpose: Circuit City store credit (retailer goes bankrupt; credit worthless); repair-or-replace that never fixes the defect; replacement parts when the whole machine is destroyed.

• LD vs. limitation (Problem 5-9): LD fixes damages in advance (higher or lower than actual) and is tested for reasonableness/penalty; a limitation eliminates or caps categories, buyer still proves actual loss, tested by failure of essential purpose / unconscionability.

Problem 5-10 — the PER chart (slides W67-S37, W8-S8):

Evidence offered

Final (partial)

Complete & exclusive

Supplementary — oral, prior

Admissible

Inadmissible

Supplementary — oral, contemporaneous

Admissible

Inadmissible

Admissible

Inadmissible

Admissible

N/A (part of the record)

Supplementary — UoT / CoD / CoP

Admissible

Admissible

Contradictory — oral, prior

Inadmissible

Inadmissible

Contradictory — oral, contemporaneous

Inadmissible

Inadmissible

Inadmissible

Inadmissible
