Admissible

N/A

Contradictory — UoT / CoD / CoP

§ 2-202(a) / § 1-303(e)

§ 2-202(a) / § 1-303(e)

Problem 5-11 clause

Effect

1. "Represents the final agreement"

Only partial integration — not a true merger clause

2. "Complete and exclusive statement… no other agreements"

Best — tracks § 2-202(b)

3. "Supersedes all prior agreements, written or oral"

Helpful but misses contemporaneous terms; pair with #2

4. "May not be modified except by a signed writing"

NOM clause — about future changes, not a merger clause

problems.title: fiber supplier; both forms say "complete and exclusive"

parts.html:
• Problem 5-12 (fiber supplier; both forms say "complete and exclusive"):
    (a) usage of trade that a supplier sells for the carpet style's market life → admissible (UoT supplements even complete records unless carefully negated);
    (b) same term from prior oral discussions → inadmissible (full integration);
    (c)(1) UoT to explain "support the integration of all materials" → admissible; (c)(2) prior talks to explain it → depends (some courts require ambiguity).

• Problem 5-13 (used car: "never been in an accident" + "we'll fix it within 30 days"; signed "AS IS… no warranty, express or implied"): the oral statements are express warranties, and § 2-316(1) would make the disclaimer inoperative — but it's subject to § 2-202: if the writing is final on warranties, the prior oral contradictory warranties are excluded → disclaimer stands; "as is" kills the implied warranties. Buyer's best route: fraud (not barred by the PER), or argue the writing wasn't final (consumer form).

Problem 6-1

Assignment by buyer (right to goods)

Assignment by seller (right to payment)

Delegation by buyer (duty to pay)

Delegation by seller (duty to deliver)

No prohibition

OK unless it materially changes the other party's duty, burden, risk, or chance of return performance — § 2-210(2)

Same; assigning the right to payment rarely affects buyer — § 2-210(3)

OK unless other party has a substantial interest in original performance — § 2-210(1)

Same — § 2-210(1)

Contract prohibits

Not permitted (except a claim for breach of the whole, or after buyer fully performed)

Permitted — §§ 2-210(2)–(3), 9-406

Not permitted

Not permitted

• Problem 6-2 (100 steel I-beams, $20,000):
    (a)     seller assigns its rights to Bank → after notice, buyer must pay Bank (keeps defenses).
    (b)     contract says assignment is "prohibited and void" → still effective for the right to payment (§ 9-406(d)).
    (c)     seller assigns "the contract" to Manufacturer → assignment + delegation; standard beams → no substantial interest → buyer must accept Manufacturer's conforming goods and pay Manufacturer; seller stays liable; buyer may demand assurances.

• Problem 6-3 (custom goods; pay 15 days after each delivery; buyer's credit downgraded, paying others late, changed banks):
    (a)     don't demand cash on delivery — § 2-702(1) allows that only if buyer is insolvent; unilaterally changing credit terms risks repudiation → use § 2-609.
    (b)     seller demands a letter of credit and withholds delivery; buyer only professes ability to pay → grounds are reasonable; a letter of credit (LOC) is a common assurance (Top of Iowa) but insisting only on it may be too much; a bare promise from a shaky buyer is likely inadequate, but real proof of solvency may be adequate — then seller's continued withholding becomes the breach.
    (c) Demand letter:     list the specific grounds; ask for adequate assurance with several options (LOC, guaranty, payment in advance/on delivery, "other assurances might also be adequate"); reserve the right to suspend; set a deadline within 30 days.

• Problem 6-4 (Big Discount's one-sided clauses): the clause letting Big Discount demand "whatever assurances it deems appropriate" whenever it wants sets an arbitrary standard → ineffective (cmt. 6; § 1-302(b); cf. § 1-309). Barring the supplier from ever demanding assurance is vulnerable as unconscionable given the take-it-or-leave-it market power.

• Problem 6-5 (Ace's email: first valve installment will be late; "we expect you will cover the extra expenses"; will catch up by the second): a definite repudiation of installment 1; the cost demand isn't a repudiation unless performance is conditioned on it; canceling the whole requires substantial impairment of the whole contract (§§ 2-610, 2-612). Buyer's real motive (needing only half the valves) is not a valid reason. Advice: don't cancel yet — send a § 2-609 demand (perform at the contract price, give a catch-up schedule), reserve rights, suspend payments; if Ace conditions performance on extra money or gives no adequate assurance → repudiation → cancel, recover the 25% advance, cover.

Problem

Answer

6-6(a) Art dealer's Picasso etching burns overnight before buyer's pickup

Merchant seller → risk not passed (no receipt) → identified goods, total loss → avoided — if no fault: a neglected coffee pot (negligence) = seller breaches; lightning = excused

6-6(b) Etching was stolen; true owner reclaims it

Not a casualty — a title failure → seller breaches (no § 2-613 excuse)

6-6(c) Print #10 water-damaged; seller has #12

If #10 specifically → § 2-613(b): buyer avoids or accepts with allowance; if prints are interchangeable → must deliver #12

6-6(d) Buyer's options under § 2-613

Total loss → avoided (refund); partial → inspect, then avoid or accept with allowance

Problem

Answer

6-8(a) Town cancels the sewer project; fittings have no other use

Frustration of purpose likely (shared basic assumption; § 2-615 cmt. 9)

6-8(b) Buyer's bank seized, account frozen

Not excused — § 2-614(2): buyer must provide a substantially equivalent payment method

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-1 Goods not unique, but specific performance fits

Inability to cover is the key sign of "other proper circumstances": a long-term output or requirements deal in a shortage, a component only this seller can make on time, or a fungible commodity that cannot be found in time. Outside class materials: § 2-716 cmt. 2 and Laclede Gas v. Amoco are the usual support.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-2 Clause making specific performance available

Helpful, not binding. § 2-716(1) says "may" and the remedy is the court's. The clause is evidence that damages are inadequate. Draft recitals of why cover is hard and add a backup such as liquidated damages or an Article 9 security interest.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-3(A) $5,000 car; paid $1,000 / paid nothing; family / business

A specific existing car is identified at contracting. Paid + family use: yes, § 2-502(1)(a), on tender of the balance. Paid + business use: § 2-502 only if seller became insolvent within 10 days after the payment; otherwise § 2-716. No payment (either use): § 2-502 is out; only § 2-716. Need to know: is the car unique, can Buyer cover, is Seller insolvent?

7-3(B)(1) Award plaques, nothing made yet

No goods exist, so nothing is identified: no replevin, no § 2-502 (also business goods). Specific performance is unlikely: others can engrave plaques, and an order to manufacture is hard to supervise. Cover plus damages.

7-3(B)(2) Plaques partly made

Partly made plaques may be "otherwise designated" and so identified, opening § 2-716(3) if Buyer cannot cover. The ceremony deadline helps, but ordering Seller to finish pushes back toward specific performance.

7-3(C) Builder prepaid; beams segregated; seller already insolvent (not assigned)

Prepaid and identified, but not consumer goods, so § 2-502(1)(b) only. Seller was already insolvent, so did it "become" insolvent within 10 days? Argue the literal reading against the protective purpose. Fallback § 2-716 is weak if steel can be bought elsewhere.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-4 $40,000 car; $42,000 substitute with heated seats and moon roof, no $500 entertainment system

Refund $1,000. Start at $42,000 − $40,000 = $2,000, then adjust: same make and model is likely a reasonable substitute, but subtract the value of the extras and add $500 for the missing system. Other facts: was an identical car available, did the price reflect the extras, how long was the search, can the system be added later?

• Problem 7-5 (not assigned): a buyer that makes several purchases must show which ones replaced the breached contract. Blue Sky needed 200,000 gallons but bought 600,000; the earliest purchases best satisfy "without unreasonable delay" (100,000 at $5.20 + 100,000 at $5.40 = $60,000 over contract). Whether fuel delivered to Atlanta is a reasonable substitute for Chicago fuel depends on whether Blue Sky can use it the same way.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-6(A) 10 desks, $5,000 F.O.B. Phoenix, $100 down, freight ~$500. Repudiated May 20. Cover $6,000 delivered; metal, bigger

"Different model at $800" is a repudiation, and declining it isn't failure to mitigate. "Cancel... refund" does not waive damages. Refund $100. Cover: $6,000 − $5,000 = $1,000 − $500 freight saved = $500 if the metal desks are a reasonable substitute (upgrade fight). Plus search costs (incidental). Wages and lost sales are consequential: reason to know, avoidability, certainty.

7-6(B) Cover for $4,000

No cover damages; Buyer is better off on price. Still the $100 refund, plus incidental and consequential damages, less expenses saved. Having covered, Buyer can't switch to § 2-713, unless the desks aren't a true substitute.

7-6(C) No purchase; expansion dropped for the economy (not assigned)

§ 2-713 at Phoenix when Buyer learned of the breach. Freight cancels (both prices are at Phoenix). No consequential damages: the economy, not the breach, caused the loss. Seller argues § 1-305 limits a buyer that never wanted the desks.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-7 5,000 lbs of lobster at $10/lb ($50,000), F.O.B. Bar Harbor, July 1; repudiated June 1; prime rib bought June 15. Bar Harbor prices: June 1 $12; June 15 $13; July 1 $14

Prime rib is not a reasonable substitute, so no cover; use § 2-713. Place for tender: Bar Harbor, so Long Island prices are out. Time depends on the rule: June 1 learned of repudiation: $2 × 5,000 = $10,000; June 15 commercially reasonable time: $3 × 5,000 = $15,000; July 1 performance date: $4 × 5,000 = $20,000. The $2,000 freight is not deducted on this reasoning: the Bar Harbor market price also excludes freight. Seller will argue it is an expense saved.
• Problem 7-8 (not assigned): 10-year gravel supply, repudiated in year 5. Trial in year 7: § 2-723(1) applies to performance not yet due. Trial after the term has run: § 2-723(1) does not apply.

• Problem 7-9 (not assigned): builder on a cost-plus contract covers at $90,000 instead of $70,000 and passes the cost to the developer. Compare KGM Harvesting v. Fresh Network (Cal. Ct. App. 1995) (cited only, p. 280). Outside class materials: KGM allowed cover damages even though the buyer passed the increase along.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-10(A) Broker: buy $2.50 F.O.B. New Orleans; resale at $2.70; market $4.50 New Orleans, $4.70 St. Louis. Customer holds Broker liable

§ 2-713 gives ($4.50 − $2.50) × 100,000 = $200,000. Broker's real loss is its liability to Customer ($4.70 − $2.70 = $2.00 × 100,000 = $200,000) plus lost profit ($270,000 − $250,000 − $5,000 − $500 = $14,500), so about $214,500 if the resale was foreseeable and cover impossible. A broker's resale is plainly foreseeable. Don't stack market damages on top of the same liability.

7-10(B) Customer waives its claims

Broker's real loss is $14,500; the formula says $200,000. Split: H-W-H Cattle and Allied Canners on one side, TexPar and Tongish on the other (all cited only, p. 280). Outside class materials: The first pair caps recovery near actual loss under the § 1-305 principle; the second allows the market measure, on the view that it keeps the market incentive and prevents a windfall to the breaching seller. Check the opinions before relying on this.

7-10(C) Broker would have burned the oil itself

No resale to compare, so the market differential is the measure, with any consequential loss. Buyer's use, not resale, was the expectancy.

problems.title: 1,000 bushels of Early Girl tomatoes, F.O.B. seller, ship by July 15

parts.html:
Problem 7-11 (1,000 bushels of Early Girl tomatoes, F.O.B. seller, ship by July 15)

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

(A)(1) 990 bushels on time

May reject all. Any shortfall fails to conform, absent a trade term or bad faith.

(A)(2) 10 bushels of the wrong variety

May reject all, for the same reason.

(A)(3) All shipped July 16

May reject: late shipment is a nonconforming tender. § 2-504's materiality limit covers carrier arrangements and notice, not a missed shipment date.

(A)(4) Shipped July 14; seller's bad instruction; arrives 4 days late

§ 2-504: improper contract with the carrier. Reject only if material delay or loss ensues. Four days is likely material for a perishable crop.

(B)(1) 50 bushels rotten: keep 950?

Yes, if a bushel is a commercial unit (§§ 2-601(c), 2-105(6)).

(B)(2) Keep only 500 good bushels?

Yes on the text: once the tender fails, buyer may accept any commercial units and reject the rest. Good faith is the only check.

(C)(1) Installments: first load 10 short; or 10 rotten; or 1 day late

Installment contract, so § 2-612(2). Rejecting all needs substantial impairment of that installment plus no cure. 10% short or rotten is curable, so buyer must accept with adequate assurance. One day late is unlikely to impair.

(C)(2) String of problems, then 10 wrong bushels in load 5: reject load 5 and cancel?

Rejecting load 5 alone is hard: 10% is curable. Cancelling needs substantial impairment of the whole, based on the pattern. Accepting earlier bad loads without notifying of cancellation reinstates the contract (§ 2-612(3)). Cancelling on this record is risky; a § 2-609 demand is the safer step.

7-12, 7-15 (not assigned)

Drafting: seller wants a materiality standard, a cure right, and short inspection and notice periods. Buyer of custom cranes wants clear inspection on each delivery, the right to reject each crane without proving impairment, and a long enough time. Cover what § 2-612 would otherwise control.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-16 Clause giving buyer a right to demand cure

Buyer wants it because Article 2 gives none, and custom equipment can't easily be replaced. Seller resists an open-ended duty, but would welcome it as an exclusive remedy limiting damages (§ 2-719).

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-17 Reasonable grounds to think the tender acceptable

Household example: buyer orders a washer; store delivers the newer model with better features at the same price, reasonably expecting buyer to be pleased. Buyer rejects; seller gets a further reasonable time to bring the model ordered. A past course of accepting similar substitutes also supports it.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-18(A) Mirror falls off; dealer will reattach

Cure. A trivial defect is fully fixed by repair.

7-18(B)(1) New starter next day, no charge

Cure.

7-18(B)(2) Three business days, unless Barbara pays for express

Still likely cure within a further reasonable time; she need not pay for express shipping. See Travelers v. Maho (cited only).

7-18(C) Salvaged parts for a new car's exhaust

Likely no cure: used parts on a new car don't conform. Compare Bowen and Zabriskie with Wilson v. Scampoli (cited only). Outside class materials: Zabriskie is the "shaken faith" case; Wilson allowed a seller to try a minor repair.

7-18(D) Repeated electrical failures; dealer offers more repair; Barbara wants a new car

After repeated failed attempts seller's offer is likely not cure. She can't force a new car, but she can reject or revoke and get her money back with damages.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-19 (not assigned)

Late bolts can't be cured, but an installment needs substantial impairment. Replacement next morning likely must be accepted under § 2-612(2). A pattern can justify cancelling the whole. Draft cure on buyer's option plus a defined termination trigger.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-20 Bancroft keeps a scratched laptop and uses it on a trip

Installing software after seeing the scratch risks acceptance under § 2-606(1)(c). Use after rejection: apply Johannsen. Against Bancroft: seller said send it back, and the use was avoidable if another laptop could be found. For Bancroft: seller refused to replace first and the trip was close. Outcome is fact-dependent.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-21 Baker: replacement parts promised by April 4 haven't come

Trick: nothing was accepted, so § 2-607(3)(a) doesn't apply. No notice is required for nondelivery. Still tell Supplier about the mounting loss, demand delivery, and start looking for cover, which protects consequential damages.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-22 Notice clause for kitchen appliances

Set a specific period running from when buyer discovers or should discover the defect (e.g., 30 days), and state how to give notice. Keep it reasonable: § 1-302(b) bars manifestly unreasonable time limits, and a clause that cuts off hidden-defect claims risks §§ 2-302, 2-719. Be more generous to consumers than to restaurants.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-23(A) (not assigned) #1 tomatoes contract $10; tender #2; at acceptance #1 = $9, #2 = $7

($9 − $7) × 10,000 = $20,000 to deduct. The $10 contract price isn't used.

7-23(B) (not assigned) #1 = $12, #2 = $9

$3 × 10,000 = $30,000.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-24(A) 500 rail cars at $20,000; repair $10,000; repaired value $19,000

Railroad's $11,000 is right only if cars as delivered were worth $9,000: it is using repair cost as a proxy for value lost. Seller answers that § 2-714(2) measures value, not cost. If delivered value was $15,000, damages are $5,000 per car; spending $10,000 on a $5,000 problem doesn't raise the measure, unless special circumstances apply.

7-24(B) Repair $10,000; repaired value $22,000

Railroad comes out ahead of what was promised ($22,000 vs. $20,000). Subtract the $2,000 betterment: $8,000.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

7-25(A) (not assigned)

Add up: excess cost of replacement boards, cost of installing replacements, repair of sold computers, shipping, and disposal, then test each for foreseeability and proof. The future repairs of the remaining 3,000 computers raise certainty.

Problem 7-26 (not assigned)

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

(A) Shirts discolor; 45 of 100 bolts used

Revoke for the unused bolts. For the 45 used, the change came from the defect only if discoloration is the defect, not from cutting and sewing. Commercial units help.

(B) Motorcycle burns up

The defect caused the change, so that bar doesn't apply. Revocation mostly adds the refund; injury is consequential.

(C) Promised fuel-line repair never made

§ 2-608(1)(a).

(D) Repeated leaks; roof to be sawn off

Each failed repair strengthens substantial impairment; refusing a major repair is reasonable.

(E) Assorted-color binders; replacements never come

Notably easy to see, so (1)(b) fails; (1)(a) fits.

Problem 7-27 (Steelsmith / Ballistics)

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

Was the machine accepted?

Likely yes. Two-hour test, "a little more time," then a month's use with the problem known by June 21: § 2-606(1)(a)–(c). So rejection is too late, and revocation is the question.

Can Ballistics revoke?

Yes, probably. 40 instead of 50 bullets a minute is substantial impairment to a buyer needing that rate. Acceptance was induced by difficulty of discovery: a two-hour test didn't show it, and even its engineers couldn't find the cause. July 1 notice is within a reasonable time after discovery, and the notice needs no particular content.

Must it accept repair?

Unsettled. § 2-508(1) is out: the time for performance has passed. § 2-508(2) needs reasonable grounds to think the tender acceptable. Lile says no cure after revocation; the syllogism says otherwise. If a court finds a cure right, refusing repair may be Ballistics' breach.

Use until September 1?

Reasonable and necessary under the Johannsen factors: keeps production going and mitigates. Expect an offset for value of the use.

Result

If revocation stands: Ballistics owes no balance, recovers the $125,000 down payment, and takes cover: $750,000 − $500,000 = $250,000 if Epoch's machine is a reasonable substitute and not an upgrade. It holds a § 2-711(3) lien on the machine for the money it paid. If revocation fails: it owes the $375,000 balance, less § 2-714(2) damages (machine at 50 per minute vs. 40), deducted under § 2-717.

7-28 Standard Plywood (not assigned)

Usage of trade may decide if 90 sheets per pallet conforms. 45 pallets instead of 50 is a shortfall, and inspection was wrongly refused. Selling for $80 and the 24-day delay raise acceptance and § 2-604 issues.

Problem 7-31 (copier: Manufacturer warrants 3 years from purchase, sold June 1, 2021; Distributor disclaims all, sold Dec. 1, 2021; Retailer warrants 1 year, sold to Buyer April 1, 2022)

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

(A)(1) Privity abolished; fails Nov. 1, 2022

Retailer: yes, on the 1-year warranty (through April 1, 2023) and on merchantability, unless disclaimed. Manufacturer: yes, on its express warranty and implied warranty if they reach Buyer. Whether a warranty on order forms Buyer never saw extends to it is a real issue. Distributor: no; its disclaimer works and it binds those below it.

(A)(2) Fails Nov. 1, 2023

Retailer's 1-year warranty has expired. Implied warranty requires a defect at tender, and the four years hasn't run. Manufacturer's 3 years still runs on either reading of "date of purchase."

(A)(3) Fails Nov. 1, 2024

Manufacturer: covered only if "purchase" means Buyer's purchase (through April 1, 2025), not Distributor's (ended June 1, 2024). Implied warranties remain only if the defect existed at tender and suit is timely (§ 2-725).

(B) Privity not abolished

Implied claim only against Retailer. Express claim against Manufacturer may survive, though this warranty wasn't a public statement. Retailer has no recourse past Distributor's disclaimer: the gap privity creates.

(C) Fire destroys VP's home; no injury to anyone

VP isn't the buyer, so this is horizontal. Alt. A: no. VP isn't family, household, or a guest of a corporate buyer, and wasn't injured in person. Alt. B: no; property loss only. Alt. C: yes where "injured" includes property, against Retailer (and Manufacturer, since vertical privity is gone). Distributor still protected by disclaimer. Tort remains.

7-32 Homeowner and Renovator, privity state

Make Homeowner a party in privity with the appliance seller: have Homeowner buy directly, or have Renovator buy as Homeowner's agent. Or have Renovator assign its warranty rights to Homeowner (§ 2-210), and get the seller to name Homeowner an intended beneficiary. The renovation contract alone can't bind the seller. Add Renovator's own express warranty.

• Problem 9-1 (4,000 gallons of milk, into a vat with 5,000 others; half the vat becomes ice cream; demand June 7 for June 1 delivery): demand is within 10 days and the sale was on credit, so § 2-702(2) applies. Treat the milk as fungible: § 2-105(4) lets an undivided share of a bulk be identified. Supplier's share is 4/9. Half the vat remains (4,500 gallons), so Supplier can reclaim about 2,000 gallons. Nothing for the ice cream, which is no longer the goods sold. The casebook cites Wheeling-Pittsburgh and Charter and gives no answer; the result is worked from the statute.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

9-2(A) Diamonds shipped F.O.B. seller; negotiable bill naming seller as consignee; buyer misses funds transfer

A parcel isn't a carload, so nonpayment alone gives no right to stop. Only insolvency would. A default to its main lender is evidence of insolvency (§ 1-201(b)(23)) but not conclusive: ask whether buyer has generally ceased paying debts or can't pay as they come due. Holding the bill in its own name also gives seller practical control (§ 2-505).

9-2(B) Must Federated obey?

§ 2-705(3)(c): not until the negotiable bill is surrendered. If it delivers to buyer without the bill, it risks misdelivery liability to the holder, seller. It should hold and ask for the bill.

9-2(C) Nonnegotiable bill

§ 2-705(3)(d): the carrier need not obey anyone but the consignor. Seattle Gems is the consignor, so Federated must follow § 2-705(3)(b), with seller liable for charges and damages. Rightfulness against buyer is still the question in Part A.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

9-3 500 stoves in two lots; first 250 accepted; $20,000 check bounces; 250 in warehouse

Advise: (1) withhold the second lot (§ 2-703(a)). (2) Sue for the $20,000 due; a bounced check leaves the debt alive. (3) Possible § 2-507 reclamation, but only the 20% was due on delivery, so it is at best a partial cash sale, and act fast. (4) Check insolvency (§ 2-702): cash terms, and a 10-day demand if goods came on credit while insolvent. (5) Demand adequate assurance (§ 2-609) and suspend. (6) Cancel only if the breach substantially impairs the whole (§ 2-612(3)). Failure to give assurance within 30 days is repudiation, which supports cancelling and reselling the 250.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

9-4(A) Instructions for reselling used copiers

Decide private vs. auction. Private: send buyer notice of intent to resell. Auction: give time and place, make the machines available to inspect, use a usual place. Identify each resale to the broken contract in your records. Resell promptly in the normal channels, on normal terms, at the best reasonable price. Don't delay for a better market; keep records.

9-4(B) 100,000 gal, $5, F.O.B. Miami, 10¢ freight saved. Resold $4.75 F.O.B. Cincinnati; storage $1,000

($5.00 − $4.75) × 100,000 = $25,000 + $1,000 incidental − $10,000 freight saved = $16,000. The 2¢ to Cleveland is the new buyer's cost under F.O.B. Cincinnati.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

9-5 $6,400 sign; $4,000 spent, $800 to finish. Salvage nets $100; or $2,000 to modify, 50% chance of $5,000

Salvage: lost profit $1,600 + costs incurred $4,000 − $100 = $5,500 from buyer, plus $100 salvage = $5,600, the same as finishing a paid contract ($6,400 − $800). Modify: expected return 50% × $5,000 = $2,500 − $2,000 = $500, vs. $100. Better on expected value by $400 to $450, depending on salvage if unsold, so it is defensible under § 2-704(2). If the sale works, buyer owes about $2,600; if not, about $7,500. Seller's risk: if a court finds it unreasonable, it eats the $2,000. Salvage is the safe choice. Finishing for $800 makes no sense: no one else wants the sign.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

9-6(A) Repudiated Feb. 15; shipment by Feb. 25; delivery by March 1. Market $4 (Feb. 15), $4.25 (Feb. 25), $4.50 (March 1). Resale March 7 at $4.75; notice given

Resale valid: $16,000 as in 9-4(B). Market: F.O.B. destination means tender at Miami on March 1: ($5.00 − $4.50) × 100,000 = $50,000 + $1,000 − $10,000 = $41,000. Under Peace River seller may take market damages despite resale; a court applying § 1-305 strictly would hold it to $16,000.

9-6(B) No notice of resale

Private sale without notice fails § 2-706(3), so § 2-708(1): $41,000. The $4.75 can still be evidence of market value, and § 2-706(6) means no accounting for the difference.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

9-7(A) 10,000 gal/yr at $5 for 10 yrs; repudiated Year 6; trial August Year 9

Years 7–9 are past due at trial: use tender-date prices. Year 10 isn't due: § 2-723(1) uses the price when seller learned of repudiation, $4.00. Per gallon, less 10¢ saved: Y7 $0.80, Y8 $0.70, Y9 $0.50, Y10 $0.90 = $2.90 × 10,000 = $29,000.

9-7(B) Trial in Year 11; Year 10 market $5.50

§ 2-723(1) doesn't apply. Y7–Y9 = $20,000. Year 10 is above contract, so no damages for that year; netting its $0.60 gain per gallon, as § 1-305 suggests, gives $14,000. Which one depends on whether the contract is treated as a whole.

• Problem 9-8 (not assigned): lathe sold for $90,000; cost $80,000 + $2,000 parts + $1,500 preparation. Lost profit = $90,000 − $83,500 = $6,500 (the $500 overhead isn't deducted). Add unreimbursed reliance: $1,000 cancellation fee + $1,200 parts it can't reuse ($2,000 − $800) = $8,700. Market damages are zero ($90,000 market), and § 2-708(1) is inadequate if Sawtooth is lost-volume.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

9-9(A) Custom container, $3,000; cost $1,800; best offer $1,500; standard units $2,000

Probably no action for the price: $1,500 may be a reasonable price for a customized container, so seller can resell. Resale damages: $3,000 − $1,500 = $1,500 + incidental. If $1,500 isn't reasonable, § 2-709(1)(b). The dollars are similar either way.

9-9(B) Only scrap at $500

Yes: scrap isn't resale at a reasonable price. Recover $3,000, hold the container for buyer, and credit net proceeds if it is sold (§ 2-709(2)).

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

9-11(A) Pre-breach loan for general operations

Not incidental: an ordinary business cost, unrelated to the breach.

9-11(B) Pre-breach loan to finance this contract

Not incidental: incurred regardless of the breach. It is a cost of performance, which is recovered, if at all, through the price or as reliance.

9-11(C) Post-breach loan for an investment planned with the price

Consequential, so not recoverable: lost use of the money.

9-11(D) Post-breach loan to finish the machine and resell it

Strongest case: "in connection with ... resale" under § 2-710, and the finishing is authorized by § 2-704(2).

• Example (Problem 9-12, not assigned): $90,000 lathe, $20,000 down; market $80,000 at tender. (A) Valid $10,000 LD: return $10,000. (B) No LD: the statutory retention is $500, the smaller of that and 20%, and seller may offset damages it proves (§ 2-718(3)), such as market damages ($90,000 − $80,000) or lost profit, plus incidental damages. Compare Neri v. Retail Marine with McCann v. McSorley (cited only).

• Problem 9-13 (not assigned): after a wrongful revocation with goods returned: pick market vs. resale at the right place, add storage and freight, and subtract the $20,000 down payment. Note that buyer took and revoked, so § 2-718(2) (withheld delivery) doesn't fit neatly, but the § 1-305 result is the same.

• Problem 9-14 (not assigned): (A) lathes identified, buyer repudiates Oct. 28, lightning fire that night: buyer bears the loss to the extent of any insurance shortfall. (B) In a shipment contract risk passed on tender to the carrier, so transit damage is buyer's loss, and rejection and revocation fail because the goods conformed at tender. Seller gets the price, and buyer's recourse is against the carrier.

Problem 11-1 ($200,000 skid loader; construction company pays maintenance, insurance, and the entire $200,000 even if it returns early)

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

Threshold

Payment isn't terminable, so go through § 1-203(b)'s four prongs. Maintenance, insurance, and full payout alone don't make a sale (§ 1-203(c)).

(A)(1) 5 years, $3,900/mo; goods return to dealer

If five years is under the economic life, (b) isn't met. On the facts a five-year-old loader likely has real value, so it's a lease.

(A)(2) Option to buy at $5,000

Is $5,000 nominal? Compare it with the predictable cost of returning (§ 1-203(d)) and with predictable value. If the loader should be worth far more than $5,000, exercise is near certain and it looks like a sale, but this one needs facts.

(A)(3) Option at $100

Nominal. § 1-203(b)(4) met: sale with a security interest.

(B) 25 years, $2,000/mo; goods return

The term likely exceeds economic life, so § 1-203(b)(1): sale.

(C) Lessee may return early with no more payments

Not "non-terminable," so the bright-line test fails in every scenario. Go to the facts under (a). A low option price is still a sign of a sale, but the lessor bears real return risk, so likely a lease.

Problem 11-3 (Lasting Data negotiates 30 servers with Sensational; Boston Finance edits the draft, buys, and leases to Lasting; servers fail)

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's)

(A) Finance lease?

(i) Boston didn't select or supply: Lasting chose; editing the draft doesn't change that. (ii) Boston acquired the goods in connection with the lease. (iii) Lasting saw the draft, not the final contract with Boston's changes, so (A) is doubtful. Look for (B), (C), or (D). Likely yes, if one is satisfied.

(B) Sensational's warranties to Lasting

Express warranties and merchantability, flowing through § 2A-209(1). Fitness is disclaimed, and the disclaimer binds Lasting.

(C) Boston's warranties

No implied warranties (§§ 2A-212, 2A-213); no express ones on these facts. Only § 2A-211(1) interference.

(D) Supply deal is a lease, not a sale

Same result. § 2A-209 applies to a supply contract by which the lessor buys or leases goods.

(E) Lasting must buy at the end

Bound to become owner + non-terminable: § 1-203(b)(2) makes it a sale with a security interest. Article 2A and § 2A-209 drop out. Boston is a seller: implied merchantability only if it is a merchant in such goods; disclaim under § 2-316. Lasting's claim against Sensational now hits vertical privity (Section XXIII).

11-4(A) Effect of § 2A-407

If Lasting accepted, it must keep paying Boston despite the defects, and pursue Sensational. If it validly rejected before accepting, § 2A-407 isn't triggered.

11-4(B) Drafting for Boston

An express hell-or-high-water clause (§ 2A-407(3)) as backup; a signed acceptance certificate; waiver of setoff and defenses against the lessor and assignees; a disclaimer of all warranties; assignment of supplier warranties to lessee; default remedies. See Wells Fargo v. B.C.B.U. (cited only).

• Problem 11-5, worked from the text, not the professor's answer (Boston leases 30 servers to Lasting; purchase agreement sent for approval; 20 installed, 5 fail; 10 never delivered): likely a finance lease ((iii)(A) or (B)). Against Boston: no warranties. For 15 working and 5 failed installed units, if accepted, rent is due under § 2A-407, and revocation only if Boston gave assurances. For the 10 undelivered there is no acceptance, so § 2A-407 doesn't apply; Lasting can refuse rent on them and, if the deal is an installment lease, cancel if the whole is substantially impaired. Against Sensational: warranty and delivery promises through § 2A-209(1): damages for the 5, and for nondelivery of the 10, with consequential damages for customer problems unless excluded. Notify both Boston and Sensational (§ 2A-516(3)(a)). Cover, because that also limits consequential loss.

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's; PV ignored)

11-6 Lathes leased for $80,000 over 3 years; $20,000 down; delivered, accepted, returned a week later at lessee's unjustified demand; market rent Nov. 8: $60,000 Chicago, $55,000 Phoenix; 2-year re-lease in Denver for $50,000

Two-year lease isn't substantially similar to three-year, so § 2A-527(3) sends it to § 2A-528(1). Goods are in Phoenix, so use $55,000: $80,000 − $55,000 = $25,000. Incidental: storage (about 60 days × $100 = $6,000) + $1,500 freight = $7,500. Total $32,500, less $20,000 already paid = about $12,500, plus any rent accrued for the week of use. Counting the $20,000 as rent paid gives the same result ($60,000 − $55,000 + $7,500).

Problem

Answer (worked from the text; not the professor's; PV ignored)

11-7 On default: repossess, all past rent, all future rent, 5% late fee on missed payments, 12% interest on all amounts

Past rent is fine. Future rent + repossession = double recovery: lessor gets the money and the goods. Not reasonable under § 2A-504(1), so it fails and Article 2A's remedies apply (§ 2A-504(2)). Revise with a formula, which § 2A-504(1) allows if reasonable in light of then anticipated harm: past-due rent + PV of future rent + estimated residual, − net proceeds of re-leasing or sale. The § 2A-504 comment calls that formula common. Limit the late fee and 12% interest to overdue sums, not unaccrued rent.
